claims.statement: The multicellular organism is not a colony of independent cells: a continuous field of force runs through the entire organism, not restricted to protoplasmic continuity, and shapes it independently of the number, size and form of its cells.
claims.quote: And such a continuous field of force, somehow shaping the whole organism, independently of the number, magnitude and form of the individual cells, which enter, like a froth, into its fabric, seems to me certainly and obviously to exist.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claims.statement: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.
claims.quote: So far then, as growth goes on, unaffected by pressure or other external force, the fluidity of protoplasm, its mobility internal and external, and the manner in which particles move with comparative freedom from place to place within, all manifestly tend to the production of swelling, rounded surfaces, and to their great predominance over plane surfaces in the contour of the organism.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claims.statement: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.
claims.quote: Among the forces which determine the forms of cells, whether they be solitary or arranged in contact with one another, this force of surface-tension is certainly of great, and is probably of paramount importance.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claims.statement: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.
claims.quote: Such symmetry is in a high degree characteristic of organic forms, and is rarely absent in living things,—save in such cases as amoeba, where the equilibrium on which symmetry depends is likewise lacking.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claims.statement: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.
claims.quote: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claims.statement: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.
claims.quote: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claims.statement: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.
claims.quote: In the case of the naked protoplasmic cell, as the amoeboid phase is emphatically a phase of freedom and activity, of chemical and physiological change, so, on the other hand, is the spherical form indicative of a phase of rest or comparative inactivity.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claims.statement: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.
claims.quote: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claims.statement: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.
claims.quote: The little organism as a whole is not a figure of equilibrium or of minimal area; but each new bud or separate chamber is such a figure, conditioned by the forces of surface tension, and superposed upon the complex aggregate of similar bubbles after these latter have become consolidated one by one into a rigid system.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claims.statement: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.
claims.quote: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
claims.statement: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.
claims.quote: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const}; surfaces of revolution: plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid

morpholib.note: The audit fits Delaunay sphere, cylinder and unduloid composites to the meridional profiles of real Lagena and other unilocular tests, checking that these cells take constant-mean-curvature forms.
morpholib.label: Thompson (1917) T1917-014 — Lagena and other unilocular tests vs. the Plateau/Delaunay catalogue (Pass 2) faithfully reproduces Lagena spp., Oolina sp., Fissurina sp. (monothalamic Foraminifera); 13 Thompson/Brady drawings + 5 photographs; Globobulimina and Quinqueloculina as polythalamous controls morphology
morpholib.organism: Lagena spp., Oolina sp., Fissurina sp. (monothalamic Foraminifera)

claims.label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claims.statement: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.
claims.quote: the normal height of the spherical cap over the end of the cylindrical cell is just a very little more than one-eighth of the diameter of the cylinder, or of the radius of the sphere. And these are the proportions which we recognise, under normal circumstances, in such a case as the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra where its free end is capped by a portion of a sphere.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: R_{cap} = 2R; cap subtends a cone of 60^\circ; cap height = R(2 - \sqrt{3}) \approx 0.27R

claims.label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claims.statement: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.
claims.quote: But this liquid cylinder has its limit of stability when its length equals its own circumference, and therefore just at the points so defined it tends to disrupt into separate segments
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: liquid cylinder of radius r unstable for length l > 2\pi r; breaks into equal, equally spaced beads

claims.label: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claims.statement: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.
claims.quote: In the case of the hydroid calycle (Fig. 72), we are led to the conclusion that the two common and conspicuous features of notching or indentation of the cup, and of constriction or annulation of the long cylindrical stem, are phenomena of the same order and are due to surface-tension in both cases alike.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claims.statement: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.
claims.quote: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claims.statement: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.
claims.quote: To the fact that these little organisms belong to an order of magnitude in which form is mainly, if not wholly, conditioned and controlled by molecular forces, is due the limited range of forms which they actually exhibit.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claims.statement: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.
claims.quote: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claims.statement: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.
claims.quote: The cups of the various species of Vorticella (Fig. 75) are nothing in the world but a beautiful series of unduloids, or partial unduloids, in every gradation from a form that is all but cylindrical to one that is all but a perfect sphere.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const} (unduloid between two unequal supporting rings)

claims.label: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claims.statement: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a protective purpose, explains their form.
claims.quote: that this surface pellicle or membrane was inevitably bound, by molecular forces, to become a surface of the least possible area which the circumstances permitted
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent
claims.statement: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or common stock.
claims.quote: when we attempt to extend it to minute organisms whose specific characters are few and simple, whose simplicity becomes much more manifest when we regard it from the point of view of physical and mathematical description and analysis, and whose form is referable, or (to say the least of it) is very largely referable, to the direct and immediate action of a particular physical force.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: The unduloid Lagena shell is formed while hanging vertically in the sea
claims.statement: The flask-shaped (unduloid) shell of Lagena is formed while the organism hangs vertically, in a position of symmetry about its vertical axis, like a hanging drop; flattened or winged forms are those formed when this symmetry of position was absent and the shell lay horizontally.
claims.quote: but we may be pretty sure that it is suspended vertically in the sea, that is to say in a position of symmetry as regards its vertical axis, about which the unduloid surface of revolution is symmetrically formed.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely
claims.statement: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.
claims.quote: The manner in which our little Lagena-shell tends to fold or wrinkle, longitudinally in its wider part, and transversely or annularly in its narrow neck, is thus completely and easily explained.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially
claims.statement: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them.
claims.quote: Since the attraction exercised by this surface tension is symmetrical around the filament, the latter will be pulled equally in all directions; in other words it will tend to be set normally to the surface of the sphere, that is to say radiating directly outwards from the centre.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: The trypanosome undulating membrane is a liquid film drawn up along a flagellum
claims.statement: The undulating membrane of trypanosomes and related flagellates forms when the flagellum lies near and parallel to the body and the fluid surface protoplasm is drawn up as a film along it, as a soap-film would be; the membrane is thus a liquid film of constant mean curvature whose undulations are produced by molecular tensions, not by its own active mobility.
claims.quote: It is a plausible assumption to suppose that, as the flagellum waves about, it comes to lie near and parallel to the body of the cell, and that the frill or undulating membrane is formed by the clear, fluid protoplasm of the surface layer springing up in a film to run up and along the flagellum, just as a soap-film would be formed in similar circumstances.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const} (undulating membrane as a liquid film)

claims.label: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
claims.statement: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.
claims.quote: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.notation: biconcave corpuscle: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \neq \text{const}, so not a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone

test_contract.expected_observation: Most isolated red cells in quantitative phase maps have a central thickness minimum and a rim maximum, giving opposite-sign mean curvature at centre and rim on the same face; spheres analysed identically do not.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Red cells have dome-like (centrally maximal) thickness profiles like the spheres, i.e. no centre-rim sign change in mean curvature, consistent with a constant-mean-curvature drop.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Quantitative thickness or phase maps, or 3D reconstructions, of individual unfixed or lightly fixed mammalian red cells at a resolution of >= 12 pixels across a cell, together with a sphere control imaged on the same instrument; public licence; independent of Thompson.
test_contract.inference_method: Segmentation of isolated objects, azimuthal thickness profile, sign of the central quadratic coefficient vs the crest curvature, fraction of cells with a sign change compared with the bead control against the pre-registered 70%/30%/10% thresholds.

claims.label: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claims.statement: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentration.
claims.quote: we see that what we call its normal appearance is just one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage, brought about by the abstraction of fluid from its interior as the result of an osmotic pressure greater outside than inside the cell
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claims.statement: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.
claims.quote: In all probability we must in like manner attribute the peculiar spiral and other forms, for instance of many Infusoria, to the presence, among the multitudinous other differentiations of their protoplasmic substance, of such more or less elastic fibrillae, which play as it were the part of a microscopic skeleton
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface
claims.statement: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.
claims.quote: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claims.statement: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.quote: it is highly characteristic of the whole process of spicule-formation for the deposits to be laid down just in the “interfacial” boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and that the form of the spicular structures tends in many cases to be regulated and determined by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Membranes and cysts form only after protoplasm rounds up with positive surface tension
claims.statement: Because adsorption requires a surface tension greater than zero, films or threads of creeping protoplasm do not form an encysting membrane, and an organism forms its cyst or cell-wall only when its protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension and gathered into a roughly spherical body.
claims.quote: It is for this reason that films or threads of creeping protoplasm shew little tendency, or none, to cover themselves with an encysting membrane; and that it is only when, in an altered phase, the protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension, and has accordingly gathered itself up into a more or less spherical body, that the tendency to form a membrane is manifested
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption
claims.statement: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.
claims.quote: We may in all probability ascribe to this fact and to its converse, or at least associate with it, such phenomena as the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter, or the frequent formation of strong shells or membranous capsules in “winter-eggs.”
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claims.statement: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.
claims.quote: while, from the physical point of view we are tempted to see but little mystery in the whole phenomenon, and to ascribe it, in all probability and in general terms, to the gathering or “clumping” together, under surface tension, of various constituents of the heterogeneous cell-content, and to the drawing out of these little clumps along the axis of the cell towards one or other of its extremities
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Potassium salts concentrate where cell-surface tension is weak
claims.statement: Potassium salts, like inorganic substances generally, raise surface tension and therefore concentrate at those parts of a cell surface where the tension is weak, so their localised accumulation (shown by Macallum's cobalt-nitrite method) indicates inequalities of surface tension.
claims.quote: and we may safely take it that our potassium salts, like inorganic substances in general, tend to _raise_ the surface tension, and will therefore be found concentrating at a portion of the surface whose tension is weak
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Conjugation outgrowths and root-hairs arise at sites of potassium concentration
claims.statement: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.
claims.quote: This bulge is, in the first place, a sign of weakened surface tension on one side of the cell, which as a whole had hitherto been a symmetrical cylinder; in the second place, we see that the bulging area corresponds to the position of a great concentration of the potassic salt
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Potassium accumulates at the bases of cilia and flagella
claims.statement: Ciliate and flagellate cells show a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of their cilia, which accounts (through weakened surface tension) for the small protuberance where a flagellum arises and the ridge at the base of a row of cilia.
claims.quote: In the case of ciliate or flagellate cells, there is to be found a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of the cilia.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces
claims.statement: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.
claims.quote: we have arrived at the conclusion, as regards unicellular organisms, that not only their general configuration but also _their departures from symmetry_ may be correlated with the molecular forces manifested in their fluid or semi-fluid surfaces.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claims.statement: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.
claims.quote: we shall probably find, and we may at least begin by assuming, that the agency of surface tension is especially manifest and important. The effect of this surface tension will chiefly manifest itself in the production of surfaces _minimae areae_
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form
claims.statement: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.
claims.quote: such validity as the rule possesses is due to the fact that among plant-tissues it very frequently happens that one cell-wall has become solid and rigid before another and later partition-wall is developed in connection with it.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.notation: fluid partition meets a rigid wall at 90^\circ (Sachs's rule)

claims.label: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
claims.statement: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.
claims.quote: These various conditions depend, according to what we have already learned, upon the relative magnitudes of the tensions at the surface of the cells and at the boundary between them
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.statement: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
claims.quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.

test_contract.expected_observation: In planar sections of a cellular tissue, the three angles at each three-way wall junction cluster near 120 degrees: junction-angle SD and T-junction fraction are both below those of a random Voronoi tiling of the same cell count.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Junction angles in a tissue are as dispersed as, or more dispersed than, a random Voronoi tiling, or T-junctions (one angle near 180 degrees) are the majority, as in cell-file tissues such as grass epidermis.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Public micrographs of planar (one-cell-thick or surface) tissue with resolvable cell walls, segmentable to label images; not drawings or diagrams; not images used to illustrate the claim in the source; licence permitting reuse. Segmenter output must be calibrated against synthetic tilings with known junction statistics (see revisions).
test_contract.inference_method: Cellpose-SAM segmentation, three-way junction extraction from the label image, angle SD and T-junction fraction per tissue, compared with a perfect hexagonal lattice and a random Voronoi control; pass if both statistics fall below the random control, with segmenter bias measured on synthetic tilings and subtracted from the margin. Planned ridge-based re-measurement (no learned boundary model): fit a straight line to each wall ridge in an annulus starting several blur widths from the vertex and take angles between fitted lines; validate on the synthetic tilings first and sweep the inner annulus radius, reporting the radius at which the brick-wall T fraction plateaus as the measurement floor (cautions from nanoswarm, Moltbook, 2026-10-31).

claims.label: An epidermis’s physical characters follow simply from its lying on the outside
claims.statement: The fundamental character of an epidermis is that it lies on the outside of the cell mass, and its main physical features (flattened, rectangular cells meeting partitions at near right angles) follow from that position through unequal and consolidated tensions in its outer walls.
claims.quote: the fundamental character of an epidermis simply is that it lies on the outside, and that its main physical characteristics follow, as a matter of course, from the position which it occupies and from the various consequences which that situation entails.

claims.label: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claims.statement: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.
claims.quote: the cells, uniform in size, are flattened out to a uniform thickness by the fluid pressure acting radially; and their reaction on each other converts the flattened discs into regular hexagons.

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. For every corrected RPE segmentation ROI of the 10 participants in Granger et al. 2018 (in vivo adaptive-optics imaging of the human RPE mosaic), identify the cells not touching the ROI border, their pixel areas and their numbers of neighbours. For ROIs with >= 30 interior cells compute the coefficient of variation of cell area (CV_A), the fraction of six-sided cells (f6) and the standard deviation of neighbour number (SD_n). The claim is supported if, across ROIs, Spearman's rho between f6 and CV_A is <= -0.3 with p < 0.01, and the mean f6 of the quartile of ROIs with the lowest CV_A exceeds that of the highest-CV_A quartile by at least 0.10 (ten percentage points). SD_n versus CV_A (expected positive) is reported as a consistency check.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if Spearman's rho between f6 and CV_A is >= 0, or if the relation is not significant (p >= 0.05) with the quartile difference in f6 below 0.05, i.e. hexagon regularity does not track size uniformity. Intermediate results (e.g. significant but weak, rho in (-0.3, 0)) are 'mixed'. If fewer than 20 ROIs qualify the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).
test_contract.inference_method: Each corrected-segmentation TIFF was decoded with a minimal TIFF reader; cells were taken as 4-connected components of non-boundary pixels and two cells counted as neighbours when their labels co-occur in the 3 x 3 neighbourhood of a boundary pixel. Cells touching the image border, oversized components (unsegmented area) and cells adjacent to oversized components were excluded, leaving 813 fully-surrounded cells in the 21 ROIs (8 participants) with at least 30 counted cells. Per ROI, CV of pixel area, fraction of six-sided cells and SD of neighbour number were computed; Spearman correlations across ROIs and the f6 difference between the lowest- and highest-CV_A quartiles were evaluated against the pre-registered thresholds. A non-pre-registered sensitivity analysis repeated the correlation with 15- and 20-cell minimum thresholds.

claims.statement: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.

claims.label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
claims.statement: The hive-bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism closed at one end by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron meeting at about 109° 28′, the configuration that encloses a given volume with the least surface.
claims.quote: The bee’s cell, then, is this figure incompletely formed: it is a hexagonal prism with one open or unfinished end, and one trihedral apex of a rhombic dodecahedron.

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. From a public micro-CT or 3-D scan of natural (foundationless) worker comb, fit planes to the three basal facets of each measurable cell and compute the rhombus obtuse angle at the apex of the base. The claim is supported if the median apex angle over >= 20 cells lies within 109.47 +/- 3 degrees and the facet-plane fit residuals are small relative to wall thickness (planar facets), with the prismatic walls meeting at 120 +/- 5 degrees in cross-section.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. Refuted if the median apex angle differs from 109.47 degrees by more than 6 degrees (e.g. if bases are rounded or formed of a single curved surface with no three-facet structure in the majority of cells), or if fewer than half of the cells show three identifiable planar basal facets. Results in between are 'mixed'. If no public 3-D data of bee-built cell bases can be obtained, the verdict is inconclusive with reason data-unavailable.
test_contract.inference_method: No analysis was run. The file inventories and README files of the two candidate Dryad datasets were examined via the Dryad API (datasets endpoint and /files listing) and the README of dryad.z8w9ghxmw was read. Neither contains 3-D geometry of bee-built cell bases: dryad.z8w9ghxmw (Peleg lab, 19.2 GB) holds X-ray microscopy of comb built on 3-D-printed plastic foundation frames, whose cell bases are the printed plastic, plus cell-size tables and cell tilt angles; dryad.r4xgxd2f3 (Yang 2022) holds cell orientation (in-plane rotation) angles and cell counts of natural combs in spreadsheets, with no basal geometry. MorphoSource and other scan repositories require a login. No other public micro-CT or 3-D scan of natural comb was located.

morpholib.label: Thompson (1917) T1917-022 — isoperimetric/minimal-area hollow & aggregate partitions faithfully reproduces Ophiurid pluteus; plant tissue partitions; pollen; radiolarian analogues (Commons) morphology
morpholib.organism: Ophiurid pluteus

claims.label: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane
claims.statement: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.
claims.quote: that one portion by anything less than about three-tenths of the whole, or three-sevenths of the other portion, there will be a tendency for the cell to divide, not by means of a plane transverse partition, but by means of a curved, cylindrical wall cutting off one corner of the original cell
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.notation: unequal division of a cube: quarter-cylinder in a corner minimal for V_{small}/V \lesssim 0.3; spherical octant for V_{small}/V \lesssim 0.15

claims.label: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side
claims.statement: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.
claims.quote: Now we find that a flattened cell which is approximately a quadrant of a circle invariably divides after the manner of Fig. 145, C, that is to say, by an approximately circular, _anticlinal_ wall
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.notation: bisecting a quadrant: circular arc \perp side and periphery, cutting off 55^\circ 22' of the arc, starting \approx 0.3r from the centre

claims.label: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally
claims.statement: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
claims.quote: We see from this, then, that what we have called an anticlinal partition, as _MP_, is only likely to occur in a triangular or prismatic cell whose angle of arc lies between 90° and 62½°. In all narrower or more tapering cells, the periclinal partition will be of less area, and will therefore be more and more likely to occur.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.notation: sector cell divides anticlinally iff 62\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ \lesssim \theta \le 90^\circ, otherwise periclinally

claims.label: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claims.statement: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
claims.quote: For it shews us that a uniform and symmetrical growth of the organism (symmetrical, that is to say, under the limitations of a plane surface, or plane section) by no means involves a uniform or symmetrical growth of the individual cells, but may, under certain conditions, actually lead to inequality among these
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.notation: after bisecting a quadrant: triangular cell reaches division size at 1.345r, quadrilateral at 1.517r

claims.label: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis
claims.statement: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
claims.quote: we shall consequently have a superficial or peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells, with sides approximately parallel, that is to say what we are accustomed to call _an epidermis_.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claims.statement: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.
claims.quote: is a particular arrangement of cell-partitions to be looked upon (as the published figures of the embryologist are apt to suggest) as a _specific character_, or at least a constant or normal character, of the particular organism? The answer to this question is a direct negative
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types
claims.statement: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.
claims.quote: all possible groupings or arrangements whatsoever of eight cells (where all take part in the _surface_ of the group, none being submerged or wholly enveloped by the rest) are referable to some one or other of _thirteen_ types or forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.notation: n cells meeting three at a time with a common outer boundary need n - 3 partitions; n = 8 gives 13 types

claims.label: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them
claims.statement: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.
claims.quote: But it would appear that the most stable arrangements are those in which the total number of contacts is most evenly divided, and the least stable are those in which some one cell has, as in type _f_, a predominant number of contacts.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Few partition patterns recur across organisms regardless of classification
claims.statement: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.
claims.quote: This is the simple reason why we meet in such a case as we have been discussing (viz. the arrangement of a group or system of eight cells) with the same few types recurring again and again in all sorts of organisms, plants as well as animals, and with no relation to the lines of biological classification
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation
claims.statement: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.
claims.quote: Where a single fossula occurs, we are usually told that it is a symptom of “bilaterality”; and this is in turn interpreted as an indication of a higher grade of organisation than is implied in the purely “radial symmetry” of the commoner types of coral. The mathematical aspect of the case gives no warrant for this interpretation.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claims.statement: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).
claims.quote: It is obvious that in the case of the oblong cells of the epidermis in the hyacinth the stomata will be found arranged in regular rows, while they will be irregularly distributed over the surface of the leaf in such a case as we have depicted in Sedum.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claims.statement: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.
claims.quote: the pollen-grains afterwards fall apart, and their individual form will depend upon whether or no their walls have solidified before this liberation takes place.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells
claims.statement: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.
claims.quote: As a direct and immediate consequence of this we might expect a tendency for special outgrowths, or “buds,” to arise from the triangular rather than from the quadrangular cells; and this turns out to be not merely a tendency towards which theoretical considerations point, but a widespread and important factor in the morphology of the cryptogams.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.statement: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
claims.quote: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claims.statement: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.
claims.quote: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm
claims.statement: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
claims.quote: for the actual _precipitation_ takes place, as a rule, not in actively living, but in dead or at least inactive tissue: that is to say in the “formed material” or matrix which (as for instance in cartilage) accumulates round the living cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claims.statement: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
claims.quote: the eggs of sea-urchins reared in lime-free water develop in apparent health, into larvae entirely destitute of the usual skeleton of calcareous rods, and in which, accordingly, the long arms of the Pluteus larva, which the rods support and distend, are entirely suppressed.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight
claims.statement: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
claims.quote: an example limited but yet crucial (_if confirmed_), of an asymmetric force, non-vital in its origin, which might conceivably be the starting-point of that asymmetry which is characteristic of so many organic products.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites
claims.statement: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
claims.quote: The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

morpholib.note: The audit compares the radiate-concentric structure of Harting's calcospherites with natural analogues, including plaice otoliths, which this claim says share that structure.
morpholib.label: Thompson (1917) T1917-023 — calcospherites grow by radial deposition about a centre (Harting 1872 artificial CaCO3 concretions in egg albumen) faithfully reproduces Harting calcospherites (CaCO3 in egg albumen); natural analogues: plaice otoliths (Fig. 209), Jurassic ooids, silver-chromate Liesegang rings morphology
morpholib.organism: Harting calcospherites (CaCO3 in egg albumen)

claims.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claims.statement: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
claims.quote: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claims.statement: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
claims.quote: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
claims.statement: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
claims.quote: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic
claims.statement: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
claims.quote: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.notation: spicule follows a geodesic of the cell surface: \kappa_g = 0

claims.label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry
claims.statement: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
claims.quote: the Holothurian spicules are composed of calcium carbonate while those which we have just described in the case of sponges are usually, if not always, siliceous: this being just another proof of the fact that in such cases the form of the spicule is not due to its chemical nature or molecular structure, but to the external forces
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claims.statement: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
claims.quote: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.notation: three equal cells \Rightarrow triradiate spicule, rays at 120^\circ; four cells \Rightarrow tetraradiate, rays at \approx 109^\circ 28'

morpholib.note: Ray angles of Grantia triradiate spicules measured on SEM plates are checked against the 120-degree and unequal-tension cell-junction geometry this claim predicts.
morpholib.label: Thompson (1917) spicule rays as Plateau borders of the secreting cell field vs Grantia ray angles (Pass 2: null control, sweep closure, ablations, three samples) faithfully reproduces Grantia aff. indica Dendy, 1913 (SEM plate, ZMA Por. 11556b); Grantia sp. (spread); Haeckel/Thompson Fig. 214 drawings morphology
morpholib.organism: Grantia aff. indica Dendy, 1913 (SEM plate, ZMA Por. 11556b)

claims.label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles
claims.statement: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
claims.quote: the cells or vesicles by which they are conformed are not arranged in what is known as “closest packing,” but in linear series; so that in their arrangement, and by their mutual compression, we tend to get a pattern, not of hexagons, but of squares: or, looking to the solid, not of dodecahedra but of cubes or parallelopipeda.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claims.statement: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
claims.quote: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill
claims.statement: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
claims.quote: The formation of an “agglutinated” shell is thus seen to be a purely physical phenomenon, and indeed a special case of a more general physical phenomenon which has many other important consequences in biology.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
claims.statement: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
claims.quote: it will at once follow that they will show a tendency to aggregate in the grooves which separate the vesicles, and the result will be the development of a most delicate sphere composed of tiny rods arranged in a regular hexagonal network
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

morpholib.note: Sumper phase separation deposits silica in the interstices between close-packed droplets to give hexagonal pore lattices, a direct formalisation of Thompson mechanism of silica collecting in grooves between packed surface vesicles (though for diatoms rather than radiolarians).
morpholib.label: Sumper (2002) & Lenoci-Camp (2008) hierarchical Cahn-Hilliard diatom biosilica phase separation (Pass 3: centrifugal precipitation front + 3-stage single-domain quench) faithfully reproduces Coscinodiscus wailesii (Centric marine diatom frustule valve pores: foramen, cribrum, cribrella; radial costae) morphology
morpholib.organism: Coscinodiscus wailesii (Centric marine diatom frustule valve pores: foramen, cribrum, cribrella

claims.label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles
claims.statement: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
claims.quote: This is only another proof (if proof be needed) that the peculiar conformation of these little skeletons is not due to the material of which they are composed, but to the moulding of that material upon an underlying vesicular structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells
claims.statement: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
claims.quote: It is obvious at a glance that this is such a skeleton as may have been formed (I think we may go so far as to say _must_ have been formed) at the interfaces of a little tetrahedral group of cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.notation: six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120^\circ; edges meeting at \approx 109^\circ 28'

claims.label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning
claims.statement: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
claims.quote: If we may safely judge from Haeckel’s figures, the pentagonal dodecahedron of the Radiolarian is perfectly regular, and we must presume, accordingly, that it is not brought about by principles of space-partitioning similar to those which manifest themselves in the phenomenon of crystallisation.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claims.statement: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
claims.quote: The true symmetry of this figure, then, is hexagonal, with a polar axis, produced into two polar spicules; with six equatorial spicules, or rays; and with two sets of six spicular rays, interposed between the polar axis and the equatorial rays, and alternating in position with the latter.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics
claims.statement: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
claims.quote: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics
claims.statement: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.
claims.quote: These three systems are all of frequent occurrence, and are all illustrated in the local thickenings of the wall of the cylindrical cells or vessels of plants.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.notation: geodesics on a cylinder of radius r: circles z = c, lines \theta = c, helices z = a\theta

claims.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
claims.statement: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
claims.quote: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.notation: spiral geodesic on a right cone (\kappa_g = 0) coils more closely as the cone narrows

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least 90% of specimens have R > 1, i.e. the suture coils more times than any geodesic of the enveloping cone can, so the sutural line cannot be a conical geodesic. Between 10% and 90% is 'mixed'. If the tables cannot be retrieved or parsed, inconclusive with reason data-unavailable. The claim's first part (coils tighten toward the apex) is shared by a geodesic and by the logarithmic helico-spiral and is not discriminating; the verdict rests on the identification of the suture with a geodesic.
test_contract.inference_method: fetch.py downloads the article PDF, records its SHA-256 and transcribes Tables 2-6 with pdfplumber into derived/pandita2013_turritellidae.csv (49 rows; all published ratio columns Wang:L and Wsut:L were recomputed from the transcribed measurements and agree, confirming the transcription). analysis.py computes for each of the 34 specimens with both apical angle and whorl number the maximum number of turns of a geodesic on a right cone of that apical angle, N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)), the ratio R = whorls/N_geo, the same ratio after subtracting two whorls (allowance for the protoconch/early whorls), and the apical angle that would have been needed for the observed whorl count to fit a geodesic.

claims.label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns
claims.statement: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.quote: and it is also common to find the two systems interfering with one another, and forming a criss-cross, or reticulated arrangement. This is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves
claims.statement: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
claims.quote: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.notation: fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface takes the shortest path: \kappa_g = 0

claims.label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube
claims.statement: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
claims.quote: these systems of muscular fibres, geodetic to begin with, remain geodetic (in the sense in which we are using the word) after all the twisting to which the primitive cylindrical tube or tubes have been subjected.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claims.statement: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
claims.quote: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
claims.statement: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
claims.quote: Of the spiral forms which we have now mentioned, every one (with the single exception of the outline of the cordate leaf) is an example of the remarkable curve known as the Logarithmic Spiral.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.notation: r = a e^{\theta \cot\alpha}

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Only the molluscan-shell class can be tested with public data located (see interpretation). For every gastropod specimen in Collins et al. 2021 with >= 5 digitised successive half-whorl apertures, take the square root of aperture area as the linear whorl size at angles 0, pi, 2 pi, ...; for every ammonoid species in Korn & Walton 2018 with >= 5 half-whorl diameters, take conch diameter at each half whorl. Fit the three two-parameter models by least squares in the size domain and compare root-mean-square residuals. The claim (for molluscan shells) is supported if the logarithmic model has the lowest RMSE in >= 80% of gastropod specimens and in >= 80% of ammonoid species, and the median ratio RMSE(Archimedean) / RMSE(logarithmic) exceeds 1.5 in both groups. Because horns, foraminifera and sunflower capitula remain untested, the confidence attached to a supporting verdict is capped at 0.5.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted (for molluscan shells, and hence as a universal) if the logarithmic model is best in fewer than 50% of specimens in either group, or if the median RMSE ratio Archimedean / logarithmic is below 1.0 in either group. Intermediate results are 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: For 145 gastropod specimens (>= 5 apertures) the series sqrt(aperture area in mm^2) versus angle (0, pi, 2pi, ...) and for 179 ammonoid species the series conch diameter versus whorl angle were each fitted by nonlinear least squares with a logarithmic spiral a e^(b theta), an Archimedean spiral a + b theta and a Fermat spiral a sqrt(theta + theta0); the model with the lowest RMSE was recorded per series and the median RMSE ratios Archimedean/logarithmic and Fermat/logarithmic computed per group. Pre-registered thresholds were then applied.

morpholib.note: The audit fits logarithmic against Archimedean and power spirals to segmented Nautilus and Conus shells, checking that molluscan shell spirals are logarithmic.
