claims.quote: computers are not just limited to working out consequences of mathematical equations. And indeed, what we have seen in this chapter is that there are fundamental discoveries that can be made if one just studies directly the behavior of even some of the very simplest computer programs.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
claims.statement: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.quote: the only way to find phenomena that one does not already know exist is to do very systematic and general experiments, and then to look at the results with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
claims.statement: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
claims.quote: one of the main reasons that the discoveries I describe in this chapter were not made before the 1980s is just that computer technology did not yet exist powerful enough to do the kinds of exploratory experiments that were needed.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
claims.statement: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
claims.quote: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
claims.statement: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
claims.quote: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Generate all primes below N = 10^8 by sieve; validate against the OEIS A000040 b-file (first 10000 primes must match exactly) and the published value pi(10^8) = 5761455 (OEIS A006880). Simulate the Cramer model on the same range with numpy seed 20261031 and run every statistic on both. Seven respects, each with a threshold for 'random-like': R1 coarse gap distribution: for primes in [N/2, N], maximum over j of |F_emp(30 j) - (1 - exp(-30 j / mean gap))| < 0.03, where F_emp is the empirical CDF of gaps; R2 Pearson correlation of consecutive gaps in [N/2, N]: |rho| < 0.05; R3 equidistribution over the four residue classes coprime to 12: maximum deviation of a class share from 1/4 below 0.005 (the Cramer model is evaluated on its own coprime-to-12 events); R4 counts of primes in consecutive disjoint intervals of length H = round(ln N) in [N/2, N]: total variation distance between the empirical count distribution and Poisson with the same mean < 0.02; R5 discrete Fourier transform of the indicator of primes among the 2^22 odd numbers just below N: ratio of the largest non-zero-frequency power to the mean power < 30 (a Gumbel-scale maximum for random indicators is about ln(2^21) ~ 15); R6 sequential compressibility: lzma size of the sequence of half-gaps (clipped at 255) in [N/2, N] divided by the lzma size of a seeded random permutation of the same sequence >= 0.98; R7 maximum over x <= N of |pi(x) - Li(x)| / sqrt(x / ln x) < 3. A respect is calibrated only if the Cramer simulation satisfies its threshold; miscalibrated respects are dropped and reported. PASS (supports) if the primes are random-like in at least (K - 2) of the K calibrated respects (so 5 of 7 if all are calibrated).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if the primes are random-like in at most K - 4 of the K calibrated respects (3 of 7), or if the gap sequence is plainly regular (lzma ratio of the raw half-gap byte sequence below 0.1, or a single Fourier frequency carrying more than half the non-DC spectral power). MIXED for exactly K - 3 random-like respects (4 of 7). If the OEIS validation fails the generator is wrong and the result is 'inconclusive' (other). If the OEIS files cannot be fetched, validation falls back to the published pi(10^8) value only and this is reported.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py sieves all primes below 10^8 (pi(10^8) = 5761455, matching OEIS A006880; first 10000 primes match the OEIS A000040 b-file), simulates Cramer's model on the same range with seed 20261031, and evaluates the seven pre-registered respects on both: coarse gap CDF versus exponential, consecutive-gap correlation, equidistribution over residues coprime to 12, Poisson fit of counts in intervals of length 18, Fourier spectrum of the prime indicator over 2^22 odd numbers below 10^8, lzma compressibility of the half-gap sequence relative to its shuffle, and the scaled fluctuation of pi(x) - Li(x). All seven thresholds were satisfied by the Cramer simulation, so all seven respects were calibrated. Runtime about 3 min.

claims.label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
claims.statement: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
claims.quote: despite many hints over the course of several centuries, the basic phenomenon that I have described in this chapter was never discovered before.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs
claims.statement: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.
claims.quote: whatever kind of underlying rules one uses, the behavior that emerges turns out to be remarkably similar to the basic examples that we have already seen in cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary (two-color, nearest-neighbor) cellular automata started from a single black cell, about two-thirds produce patterns that stay of fixed size and about one-third produce patterns that grow forever, with about 14% yielding patterns more complicated than repetition.
claims.quote: In about two-thirds of all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages [54, 55, 56], the patterns produced remain of a fixed size. But in about one-third of cases, the patterns instead grow forever.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: run all 256 rules for T = 4096 steps on a ring of 2T + 64 cells (so the light cone never wraps). Width w(t) = extent of cells differing from the background value at time t, where the background follows b_{t+1} = f(b_t, b_t, b_t). A rule is 'fixed size' if max_{t in [T/2, T]} w(t) equals max_{t in [T/4, T/2]} w(t), otherwise 'growing'. A growing rule is 'repetitive' if some temporal period P <= 16 and spatial shift |s| <= 16 satisfy grid[t + P, x + s] == grid[t, x] for every t in [T/2, T - P] and every x in [-t + 16, t - 16]; otherwise it is 'more complicated than repetition'. The claim passes if the fixed-size fraction lies in [0.60, 0.73], the growing fraction in [0.27, 0.40] and the more-complicated fraction in [0.10, 0.18], and if the three-way classification of every rule is identical for T = 2048 and T = 4096 (no rule changes class with the cutoff).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the fixed-size fraction is below 0.55 or above 0.78, or the more-complicated fraction is outside [0.07, 0.21]; 'mixed' if the fractions fall between the pass and refute bands, or if more than 4 rules change class between T = 2048 and T = 4096 (indicating the cutoff, not the rules, decides the shares); 'inconclusive' if the periodicity search is not able to classify the growing patterns (e.g. because the width of the periodic window is inadequate for some rule) in a way that is stable across cutoffs.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves each of the 256 rules for 4096 steps from a single black cell on an 8256-cell ring, tracks the background value from a cell outside the light cone (odd rules make it alternate), and measures the width of the pattern (cells differing from the background) in every row. A rule is fixed-size if the maximum width over rows 2048..4096 equals the maximum over rows 1024..2048; otherwise growing. For growing rules it searches temporal periods P <= 16 and shifts |s| <= 16 such that the space-time pattern repeats over rows 2048..4096-P inside the interior mask; a growing rule with such a period is repetitive, otherwise more complicated. Two interior masks are evaluated: the pre-registered light-cone mask |x| <= t - 16, and an extent mask (inside the pattern's actual extent at time t minus 16 cells each side), added after the first run showed that for rules 57 and 99, whose patterns grow at half a cell per step, the light-cone mask includes background cells that the growing pattern later overwrites, so their period-3 interiors were being scored as non-periodic. The whole classification is repeated with cutoff T = 2048 using the first 2048 rows. Run time about 3 minutes.

claims.label: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
claims.statement: Of the 256 elementary cellular automata started from a single black cell, 10 produce patterns that seem in many respects random, falling into three basic forms, while 24 produce nested patterns falling into only three fundamentally different forms.
claims.quote: And out of the 256 rules discussed here, it turns out that 10 yield such apparent randomness. There are three basic forms, as illustrated on the facing page.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Each rule is run for T = 4096 steps from a single black cell on a white background (zero boundary, width 2T+1). Statistics: (i) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / cells of the central strip (columns -64..63 relative to the seed, rows 1024..4095, one byte per cell, preset 9); (ii) periodic: the strip rows are time-periodic with some period p <= 64 over rows 2048..4095; (iii) growing: the black-cell extent of row 4095 is at least 1.2 times that of row 2047, or the extent of row 4095 exceeds 64 cells while the strip is not periodic. Calibration (performed before the rules are run): random references are i.i.d. fair bits (numpy seed 20260303) in a 128 x 3072 strip; nested references are the same-size central strips of the Sierpinski gasket (Pascal's triangle mod 2), Pascal's triangle mod 3 thresholded to nonzero, and the outer products t_i XOR t_j of the Thue-Morse and of the period-doubling sequences; periodic references are random patterns of period 1..64 in time and 1..16 in space. tau_random = geometric mean of the smallest random-reference rho and the largest nested-reference rho. Classification: 'random-looking' iff rho >= tau_random; 'nested' iff not random-looking, not periodic, and growing; 'regular' otherwise. Symmetry classes: orbits under reflection (swap left and right inputs) and complementation (conjugation by colour swap). Secondary, reported but not decisive: for nested rules, the black-cell count exponent D = log2(N(4096)/N(2048)) with N(t) = black cells in rows 0..t-1, and the width exponent log2(width(4095)/width(2047)); the number of clusters when D is binned to 0.1 and the width exponent to {about 1, about 0.5} is compared with Wolfram's 'three fundamentally different forms'. 'supports' if the random-looking count is in [8, 12] and forms exactly 3 symmetry classes, and the nested count is in [20, 28].
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the random-looking count is <= 5 or >= 16, or the nested count is <= 14 or >= 36, under the calibrated criterion. Otherwise 'mixed' (e.g. counts near but outside the pass windows, or random-looking rules forming a number of symmetry classes other than 3). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate random from nested references.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py first calibrates the strip-compressibility statistic rho (bits per cell after lzma, 128 x 3072 central strip) on i.i.d. random bits (rho = 1.110-1.116), four classical nested patterns (0.009-0.033) and six periodic tilings (0.004-0.013), giving tau = 0.190. It then runs each of the 256 rules for 4096 steps from a single black cell (array width 2(T+128)+1 so that zero-boundary defects of background-flipping rules cannot reach the strip), computes rho, tests the strip for time-periodicity with period <= 64 over rows 2048-4095, measures the black-cell extent at rows 2047 and 4095, and classifies: random-looking if rho >= tau; nested if not random, not periodic and growing; regular otherwise. Random-looking rules are grouped into orbits under reflection and complementation. Run time about 50 s.

claims.label: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
claims.statement: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.
claims.quote: at least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules for a system does not ultimately lead to more complex overall behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
claims.statement: About 85% of the 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular, while the remainder include rules with seemingly random behavior and rules with interacting localized structures like rule 110.
claims.quote: About 85% of all three-color totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Each code c in 0..2186 (Wolfram's convention: base-3 digit k of c is the new colour for neighbourhood sum k in 0..6; colours 0 = white, 1 = gray, 2 = black) is run for T = 3000 steps from a single gray cell on a white background with an array wide enough that boundary effects cannot reach the central 128 columns. Statistics on the central strip (columns -64..63): (i) periodic: rows 2250..2999 are time-periodic with some period p <= 256; (ii) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / (cells * log2(3)) over rows 1500..2999. Calibration (performed before the codes are run): nested references are the same-size strips of Pascal's triangle mod 3 (3 symbols), Pascal's triangle mod 2, and the Thue-Morse and period-doubling outer-product patterns (normalised by log2 of their own alphabet size); irregular references are the strips of elementary rules 110, 124, 137, 193 (localised structures) and 30, 45 (random) run from a single black cell with the same geometry. tau = geometric mean of the largest nested-reference rho and the smallest irregular-reference rho. A code is 'regular' iff it is periodic or rho < tau. 'supports' if the regular fraction lies in [0.80, 0.90].
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the regular fraction is below 0.70 or above 0.95. 'mixed' if it lies in [0.70, 0.80) or (0.90, 0.95]. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested rho >= smallest irregular rho). The number of irregular codes that are random-looking (rho above the smallest random reference) versus structured-irregular is reported but not decisive.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py ran all 2187 three-colour totalistic codes from a single gray cell for T = 3000 steps on an array of width 2*(T+128)+1 (boundaries cannot reach the centre), then classified the central 128-column strip: time-periodic with p <= 256 over rows 2250..2999, or lzma compressibility rho over rows 1500..2999 below tau. Calibration before the census: nested references rho = 0.017..0.037 (Pascal mod 2 / mod 3, Thue-Morse and period-doubling outer products), irregular references rho = 0.099..0.136 (elementary rules 110, 124, 137, 193) and 1.11..1.12 (rules 30, 45); classes separated, tau = sqrt(0.0367 * 0.0985) = 0.0601. Result: 1706 codes periodic, 145 non-periodic but nested-compressible (rho <= 0.042), 336 irregular (rho 0.12..1.11, median 0.90; 169 with rho >= 0.9); regular fraction 1851/2187 = 0.8464, inside the pre-registered [0.80, 0.90] band.

claims.label: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
claims.statement: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.
claims.quote: Of the 65,536 possible mobile automata with rules of the kind discussed so far it turns out that not a single one shows more complex behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Encoding: the behaviour of a mobile automaton is summarised by its step sequence s_t in {0,1,2,3} = 2 * (new colour of the active cell) + (1 if the active cell moves right else 0); for the extended family s_t additionally records the two neighbour colours written (16 symbols), and the sequence of active-cell positions is determined by it. Calibration (performed before the mobile automata are run, on reference sequences only): rho(L) = 8 * lzma_size(sequence of L symbols, one byte each, preset 9) / (L * log2(alphabet size)). References over a 4-symbol alphabet: periodic sequences with periods 1..500 (numpy seed 20260306), nested sequences (Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci word, paper-folding, ruler sequence mod 4), and random sequences (numpy random symbols; rule 30 centre bits paired). The complexity threshold tau is the geometric mean of the largest rho(8000) over the periodic and nested references and the smallest rho(8000) over the random references. Stage 1: all 65,536 basic rules, 2000 steps (vectorised); a rule is 'periodic' if its last 1000 symbols have a period p <= 500. Stage 2: every non-periodic rule is run for 16000 steps and rho is computed on symbols 8000..16000 (tail); a rule is 'complex' if rho > tau. Stage 3: any rule flagged complex is re-run for 64000 steps and rho on symbols 32000..64000 is required to still exceed tau (guards against long transients). Extended family: 100,000 rules sampled uniformly (numpy seed 20260306), same three stages with the 16-symbol alphabet and a 16-symbol calibration run analogously. 'supports' if no basic rule is complex after stage 3 and the fraction of complex extended rules is <= 1 %. Secondary check reported but not decisive: the number of basic rules with non-periodic step sequences, which Wolfram gives as 218 (p. 72).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at least one basic rule is complex after stage 3 (its tail step sequence compresses no better than the geometric midpoint between nested and random references at 32000 symbols). 'mixed' if no basic rule is complex but the extended family's complex fraction exceeds 1 %. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested/periodic rho >= smallest random rho).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py first calibrates the compressibility statistic rho(L) = 8*lzma_bytes/(L*log2 A) on reference sequences (periodic with 14 periods up to 500, Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci, paper-folding and ruler sequences, numpy random symbols and paired rule 30 centre bits): for A = 4 the non-random references give rho <= 0.162 and the random ones >= 1.27, so tau = 0.454; for A = 16, tau = 0.323. It then simulates all 65,536 basic mobile automata in parallel for 2000 steps from an all-white tape, labels a rule periodic if its last 1000 step symbols have a period <= 500, re-runs the non-periodic rules for 16000 steps and computes rho on the second half, and would re-run any rule above tau for 64000 steps. The same three stages were applied to 100,000 uniformly sampled neighbour-updating rules (seed 20260306) with the 16-symbol alphabet. Run time about one minute.

claims.label: Complex behavior correlates with many cells being active at once
claims.statement: In generalized mobile automata, complex behavior almost never occurs unless many cells are active simultaneously, and this correlation between overall activity and complexity helps explain why complexity is much more common in cellular automata than in mobile automata.
claims.quote: complex behavior almost never occurs except when large numbers of cells are active at the same time.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
claims.statement: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.
claims.quote: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Stage 1: run every machine for 1000 steps and record the letters (state, colour read) for steps 201..1000 (alphabet 6 for s = 3, 4 for s = 2); compute the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of this 800-letter window; machines with p(12) <= 200 are classed low-complexity (repetitive or nested), the rest are flagged. Stage 2: run flagged machines for 20000 steps and compute p(64) over the letters of steps 10001..20000 (window of 10000; maximum possible 9937): p(64) >= 2500 is 'complex', p(64) <= 1280 (= 20 x 64, a generous linear bound for nested sequences) is low-complexity, otherwise 'unclear'. Stage 3: 'unclear' machines run for 200000 steps with the window of the last 100000 letters: p(64) >= 25000 complex, <= 1280 low-complexity, otherwise unclear. Controls run through the same statistics: a periodic letter sequence, a Thue-Morse (nested) letter sequence, and uniformly random letters, which must be classed low, low and complex respectively. PASS (supports) if no two- or three-state machine is classed complex and no machine remains unclear after Stage 3.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if at least one two- or three-state two-colour machine is classed complex at Stage 2 or Stage 3 (it is reported with its NKS number and complexity profile). MIXED if no machine is complex but some remain unclear after Stage 3, or if the controls are misclassified (criterion not discriminating).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves every two-state (4096) and three-state (2,985,984) two-colour Turing machine under the NKS numbering (p. 888) from a blank tape with the head in state 1, vectorised over chunks of 100000 machines, and records the letter sequence (state, colour read). Stage 1 computes the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of the letters of steps 201-1000 and flags machines with p(12) > 200 for Stage 2 (20000 steps, p(64) over steps 10001-20000; complex if p(64) >= 2500, low if <= 1280) and Stage 3 (200000 steps, p(64) over the last 100000 letters, complex if >= 25000). Periodic, Thue-Morse and uniformly random control sequences pass through the same statistics. As a supplementary (non-criterion) check the 200 highest-p(12) machines of each family are run through Stage 2 anyway, and the single highest-p(64) machine of each family is profiled at Stage-3 scale (p(n) for n = 8..512, lzma ratio, head extent and sweep lengths). Runtime about 4 minutes.

claims.label: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
claims.statement: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.
claims.quote: With four states, however, more complicated behavior immediately becomes possible. Indeed, in about five out of every million rules of this kind, one gets patterns with features that seem in many respects random
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
claims.statement: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.
claims.quote: To get behavior that is more complicated than simple nesting, it follows therefore that one must consider substitution systems whose rules depend not only on the color of a single element, but also on the color of at least one of its neighbors.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: enumerate exhaustively (a) all 225 neighbour-independent systems with 2 colours and replacement strings of length 0..3, and (b) all 2197 systems with 3 colours and replacement strings of length 0..2; start each from each single colour and iterate until the string has at least 2^15 symbols (or the string dies out, stays bounded for 60 steps, or exceeds 10^6 symbols). For every run that reaches 2^15 symbols ('growing'), compute the subword complexity p(n) (number of distinct length-n factors) of the first min(len, 2^17) symbols for n = 1..20. The claim passes if every growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) <= 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (a quadratic law gives 4, an exponential law about 2^10), and if the Thue-Morse system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 10} reproduces OEIS A010060 and the Fibonacci system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 0} reproduces OEIS A003849 term for term over the available b-file terms. Discriminating power: the neighbour-dependent control family (2 colours, replacement of each element determined by the pair (element, right neighbour), replacement strings of length 1 or 2, 1296 systems, right-most element paired with colour 0) must contain at least one system whose growing run has p(20) > 2 x 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) > 8; otherwise the test cannot separate the two families and the verdict is at most 'inconclusive'.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if any growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) > 10^4 or p(20)/p(10) > 8, or if the Thue-Morse or Fibonacci outputs disagree with the OEIS b-files; 'inconclusive' if the control family contains no system exceeding the thresholds (the complexity measure would then be too weak to distinguish nested from more complicated behaviour).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates every neighbour-independent substitution system in the two pre-registered families (225 + 2197 systems), iterates each from every single colour (7041 runs) until the string has at least 2^15 symbols, dies, becomes bounded or exceeds 40000 steps, and computes the subword complexity p(n) for n = 1..20 of the first <= 2^17 symbols of every growing run (5109 runs; 24 slow linear-growth runs are analysed at the ~20000 symbols they reached). The same statistics are computed for the pre-registered neighbour-dependent control family (1296 systems, 2592 runs, <= 2000 steps) and, exploratorily, for 1500 random three-context systems. The Thue-Morse and Fibonacci systems are compared with the OEIS b-files, and a random 2^15-bit string gives the complexity reference. Run time about 9 minutes (the slow linear-growth systems dominate).

claims.label: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity
claims.statement: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.
claims.quote: allowing elements to have three or four colors rather than just two immediately makes much more complicated behavior possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Text-editor-like search-and-replace rules can generate great complexity
claims.statement: Sequential substitution systems, which repeatedly apply the first matching search-and-replace rule like a text editor, give only simple behavior with two replacements and two elements, but with three replacements about one in 10,000 random rules produces seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: just by using the simple operations available even in a very basic text editor, it is still ultimately possible to produce behavior of great complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
claims.statement: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.
claims.quote: if only one element is removed at each step, then a tag system always effectively acts just like a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system of the kind we discussed on page 83.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. (1) Equivalence: for all 225 one-deletion two-colour tag systems with blocks of length 0-3, all 62 initial sequences of length 1-5, and 4 consecutive passes, the sequence after each pass of |s| steps equals the substitution-system iterate exactly (100% of cases). (2) Simplicity: for every one-deletion rule started from the sequences 1, 11 and 10 and run for up to 400 passes, either the state space is finite (the sequence empties or an exact state recurs, i.e. repetitive) or the sequence reaches >= 2000 symbols and its factor complexity p(10) (number of distinct length-10 subwords) is <= 60 (nested, linear complexity). (3) Complexity with two deletions: at least one of the 50625 two-deletion two-colour tag systems with blocks of length 0-3, started from the pair 11, runs 50000 steps without emptying and without any exact state recurrence, and the lzma-compressed size of its length-difference series over steps 10000-50000 is at least 60% of the median compressed size of 5 random shuffles of the same series. 'Supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if (1) fails in any case, or if any one-deletion rule reaches >= 2000 symbols with p(10) > 200, or if no two-deletion rule meets (3). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py (1) runs every one-deletion rule for |s| steps from every sequence s of length 1-5 and compares with the substitution image, over 4 passes; (2) iterates every one-deletion rule from 1, 11 and 10 as a substitution system until the state recurs or empties (finite state space) or the sequence reaches 2000 symbols, where the number of distinct length-10 subwords p(10) is computed; (3) runs all 50625 two-deletion rules from 11 for 2000 steps, classifies them as emptied, recurrent or running, then runs the 400 running rules with the smallest length (and NKS p. 94 case (a)) for 50000 steps with exact state-recurrence detection and compares the lzma size of the length-difference series over steps 10000-50000 with that of its shuffles.

claims.label: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
claims.statement: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.
claims.quote: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: all 225 cyclic tag systems with two blocks, each block a binary string of length 0-3 (15 choices per block), initial sequence {1}, Wolfram's update (remove first element; if it was 1 append the current block; blocks alternate every step). Stage 1: run each system 100,000 steps; a system is 'growing' if the sequence never empties and its final length is >= 1000. Stage 2: run each growing system 1,000,000 steps and compute (i) linear fit of length L(t) vs t: R^2 >= 0.999 and local growth rates over 10 equal windows all within 25% of the global slope ('steady growth'); (ii) Hurst exponent H of the detrended residual r(t) = L(t) - (a + b t), estimated as half the log-log slope of Var[r(t+tau) - r(t)] over tau = 2^0..2^13, in [0.35, 0.65] ('random-walk-like fluctuations'); (iii) lzma (preset 9 | EXTREME) compressed size of the packed leading-element bit sequence >= 0.25 bits per symbol ('incompressible driver'). The claim PASSES if at least one system satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Secondary, reported but not decisive: whether the book's own examples (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} and (e) {{1,1,1},{0}} pass.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no system in the 225-member family satisfies all of (i)-(iii): i.e. every growing system has either unsteady growth, bounded or non-diffusive fluctuations (H outside [0.35, 0.65]), or a leading-element sequence that compresses below 0.25 bits per symbol (periodic or nested).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates the 225 rules, stores each history as one growing tape (sequence at step t is tape[t:]), screens all rules for 100,000 steps, then runs the 80 growing rules for 1,000,000 steps. For each it fits L(t) linearly, computes local growth rates in 10 windows, estimates the Hurst exponent of the detrended residual from the variance of increments at lags 1..8192, and lzma-compresses the packed leading-element bit sequence. Two seeded control sequences (i.i.d. Bernoulli(3/4); first-order Markov with no '00' and P(1)=3/4, the local statistics Wolfram reports for example (d)) calibrate the compression measure. Per-rule results are in derived/systems.csv.

claims.label: Register machines need eight instructions to show complex behavior
claims.statement: Among two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions, all programs of up to four instructions behave repetitively, only two five-instruction programs give nesting, none up to seven instructions is substantially more complicated, and 126 of the 11,019,960,576 eight-instruction programs show complex behavior.
claims.quote: But with eight instructions, 126 out of the 11,019,960,576 possible programs finally do show more complicated behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
claims.statement: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: searching through many millions of short programs typically yields at least a few that exhibit complex and seemingly random behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Combinator-like symbolic rewriting systems can behave randomly
claims.statement: Symbolic systems that repeatedly apply a single rewrite rule of the form e[x_][y_] → (expression in x and y) to nested expressions can, like other simple programs, produce behavior that is complex and seemingly random rather than stabilizing.
claims.quote: But often—just as in so many other kinds of systems—the behavior is instead complex and seemingly quite random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata
claims.statement: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.quote: So this suggests that in fact the phenomenon of complexity is quite universal—and quite independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
claims.statement: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.
claims.quote: The remarkable discovery that we have made, however, is that this threshold is typically extremely low.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures dominate everywhere
claims.statement: The four themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures are the dominant types of behavior across a vast range of systems, and these overall behavior types are almost independent of the details of the underlying rules.
claims.quote: the basic themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures that we already saw in specific cellular automata in the previous chapter are actually very general, and in fact represent the dominant themes in the behavior of a vast range of different systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details
claims.statement: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.
claims.quote: even if we do not know all the details of what is inside some specific system in nature, we can still potentially make fundamental statements about its overall behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance
claims.statement: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.
claims.quote: And the great advantage of such an experimental approach is that it does not require one to know in advance exactly what kinds of behavior can occur.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system
claims.statement: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.
claims.quote: in my experience the single most common mistake in doing computer experiments is to look at systems that are vastly more complicated than is necessary.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
claims.statement: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.
claims.quote: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
claims.statement: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: all pairs (m, b) with multiplier m in 2..9 and base b in 2..9, iterating x_{t+1} = m x_t from x_0 = 1 for t = 1..T = 3000 (i.e. the digits of m^t). For each pair build the digit array of rows m^t written in base b; take the interior window of each row consisting of digit positions between 25% and 75% of that row's length (least significant digit = position 0), concatenate all interior digits in row order into one byte string (one digit per byte). Measure (i) bits per digit = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size / number of digits; (ii) maximum absolute deviation of any digit-value frequency from 1/b. A pair is 'complex' if (i) >= 0.8 * log2(b) and (ii) <= 0.02; a pair is 'simple' if (i) < 0.1 * log2(b). The claim PASSES if at least one pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' AND every pair with m a power of b (m = b^j, j >= 1, e.g. (2,2), (4,2), (8,2), (9,3), (3,3), ...) is 'simple' (validity check that the measure separates trivially regular digit arrays). Reported, not decisive: how many of the 64 pairs are complex, and whether the pairs with m and b sharing all prime factors (e.g. (6,2), (4,8), (2,4)) behave differently.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' (every such digit array compresses below 0.8 log2(b) bits per digit or has digit frequencies deviating from uniform by more than 0.02). If any trivial pair (m a power of b) is not 'simple', the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py iterates x -> m x from 1 for 3000 steps for each of the 64 (m, b) pairs using Python integers, converts each power to base-b digits, keeps the interior 25%-75% of digit positions per row, concatenates (one byte per digit) and lzma-compresses; it also computes digit-value frequencies in the window. Per-pair results are in derived/pairs.csv. Runtime about 4 minutes.

claims.label: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claims.statement: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.
claims.quote: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
claims.statement: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.
claims.quote: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
claims.statement: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.
claims.quote: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
claims.statement: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.
claims.quote: But despite fundamental differences like this in underlying rules, the overall behavior produced by systems based on numbers is still very similar to what one sees for example in cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
claims.statement: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.
claims.quote: Localized structures are visible, but the overall pattern never seems to take on any kind of simple repetitive form.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
claims.statement: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.
claims.quote: even though the rules ultimately involve only addition and subtraction, they nevertheless correspond to programs that are capable of producing behavior of great complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Rules (all with f[1]=f[2]=1, from NKS pp. 129-130): (c) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-1]] (OEIS A004001); (d) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (e) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]] (OEIS A005185); (f) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]-1]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (g) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (h) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-2f[n-1]+1]. Compute f[n] for n <= N = 2^20 (stop a rule if an index < 1 occurs). Residual r[n] = f[n] - n/2 for (c)-(g); for (h) r[n] = f[n] - a n^b with (a,b) a least-squares power-law fit in log-log. Statistics: (i) bits per symbol = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size of the increment-sign sequence sign(r[n]-r[n-1]) in {-1,0,1} stored as one byte each, divided by N-1; (ii) sign balance |P(increment>0) - P(increment<0)|; (iii) dyadic self-similarity corr(r[n], r[2n]) for n in [N/4, N/2) (reported). A rule is 'complex/random-like' if it is well defined up to N, (i) >= 0.5 bits/symbol and (ii) <= 0.05. The claim PASSES if at least one of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like AND the nested controls (c) and (d) both have (i) < 0.15 bits/symbol (validity of the measure). Calibration from controls outside the family: binary digit sum s2(n) gives 0.002 bits/symbol, its partial sums 0.005, a symmetric random walk 1.10.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if none of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like (every one is undefined before N, or compresses below 0.5 bits/symbol, or is sign-unbalanced by more than 0.05). If the nested controls (c) or (d) do not compress below 0.15 bits/symbol the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable). If computed terms disagree with the OEIS b-files for A005185 or A004001, the verdict is inconclusive (other) until the implementation is fixed.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py computes each of the six recurrences for n <= 2^20 with memoised integer arithmetic, verifies rules (e) and (c) term-by-term against the 10,000-term OEIS b-files of A005185 and A004001 (all terms match), detrends by n/2 (rules c-g) or by a log-log power-law fit for n >= 16 (rule h), lzma-compresses the increment-sign sequence of the residual, and measures sign balance and the dyadic correlation corr(r[n], r[2n]).

claims.label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
claims.statement: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
claims.quote: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
claims.statement: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
claims.quote: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
claims.statement: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
claims.quote: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: All 20 p-values from the fixed battery on 10^6 decimal and 10^6 hexadecimal digits of pi are consistent with uniform i.i.d. digits: none below 1e-4 and at most 2 below 0.01.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: A p-value below 1e-6, or 4 or more of the 20 below 0.01, i.e. a detectable regularity in the digits.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Digits of pi from a published digit file whose every digit is checked against an independent exact computation and against an independent tabulation (OEIS); random references from a seeded standard PRNG. Digits must start right after the point and be contiguous.
test_contract.inference_method: Ten classical randomness tests per base (chi-square frequency, pair, triple, poker, gap; serial correlation lags 1-3; maximum periodogram; lzma size against 20 PRNG references), p-values counted against the pre-registered thresholds at alpha = 0.01 with the binomial multiplicity rule above.

claims.label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
claims.statement: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
claims.quote: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
claims.statement: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.quote: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
claims.statement: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
claims.quote: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: (1) for bases 2, 3 and 10 and all denominators q = 1..20000, the digit expansion of 1/q (and of p/q for all 1 <= p < q when q <= 300) has period <= q - 1 and preperiod + period <= q, with zero violations, and the base-10 periods of 1/q agree with OEIS A007732 for every n covered by its b-file; (2) 100% of 20000 random eventually periodic digit patterns (random preperiod of length 0..20, random non-trivial period block of length 1..30, bases 2, 3, 10) are reproduced exactly when the rational number reconstructed from them is re-expanded by long division; (3) none of the first 10000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi (OEIS b-files) is eventually periodic in the sense that, for some period p <= N/3, the last 2p digits already repeat with period p.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: any rational whose expansion has minimal period > q - 1 or does not become periodic within q digits; any disagreement with A007732; any eventually periodic pattern whose reconstructed rational re-expands differently; or an irrational constant's published digits exhibiting at least two full agreeing periods for some p <= N/3.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Planned datasets: rational-expansions-bases-2-3-10-q-le-20000, oeis-a007732-bfile, random-eventually-periodic-patterns, oeis-a002193-bfile, oeis-a001113-bfile, oeis-a000796-bfile
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py (1) runs long division for 1/q, q = 1..20000, and for all p/q with q <= 300, in bases 2, 3 and 10 (64,850 expansions per base), recording preperiod and period from the first repeated remainder and counting violations of period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q; base-10 periods of 1/n are compared with the 10,000-term OEIS A007732 b-file. (2) It draws 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns (base in {2,3,10}, preperiod 0-20 digits, block 1-30 digits, all-(b-1) blocks rejected), reconstructs the exact rational with Python Fractions and re-expands it, counting patterns not reproduced digit for digit. (3) It downloads the first 10,000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi from OEIS and, for every p <= N/3, finds the smallest index after which the digit sequence agrees with its shift by p, flagging any p for which two full periods already agree. Run time about 9 s including downloads.

claims.label: Roots never have nested digit sequences
claims.statement: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
claims.quote: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
claims.statement: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
claims.quote: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
claims.statement: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
claims.quote: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations are often in some intrinsic sense complex, independent of the particular representation that one uses to look at them.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claims.statement: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
claims.quote: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Test set: a in {sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt7, (1+sqrt5)/2, 1+sqrt2, 2+sqrt3} (quadratic irrationals), {pi, e, 2^(1/3), ln 10} and 20 pseudo-random a uniform in [1.05, 12] from numpy seed 20261031 (31 values). For each a: (1) take the first N = 20000 positive zeros of f(x) = sin x + sin(a x), each verified numerically (|f(x)| <= 1e-8), labelled A if it is a zero of sin((1+a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(1+a)) and B if it is a zero of cos((1-a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(a-1)); (2) build the substitution word s_1 = A^{c_1} B, s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} (equivalently the composition tau_{c_1} ... tau_{c_n}(A)) to length >= 200000 from the continued fraction theta = [0; c_1, c_2, ...]. PASS (supports) if for every a and every n in 1..24 the set of length-n factors of the crossing word equals the set of length-n factors of the substitution word and has exactly n + 1 elements, and if for every quadratic-irrational a the continued fraction of theta is eventually periodic within 60 terms and the composite substitution over one period has the substitution word's tail as a fixed point (applying it to the first 2000 symbols of the tail reproduces a prefix of the tail).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if for any a there is some n <= 24 at which the factor sets differ, after excluding near-coincident zeros (two zeros closer than 1e-9 times the A spacing, which would make the ordering numerically undefined); or if any quadratic-irrational case has a non-eventually-periodic continued fraction or a tail that is not a fixed point of the period substitution. Partial agreement (factor sets equal only for some a, or only up to a smaller n without a numerical explanation) is 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py lists the first 20000 positive zeros of sin x + sin(a x) analytically from the two factor families, verifies |f| <= 2.9e-11 at each, and forms the A/B label word. It computes the continued fraction of theta = (a-1)/(a+1) (exactly, with period detection, for the seven quadratic surds; from the double's exact rational value for the others, keeping terms while the convergent denominator is below 200000), builds the substitution word s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} to 200000 symbols (checked against the composition tau_{c_1}...tau_{c_n}(A)), and compares the sets of factors of length 1..24. For the quadratic cases it also checks that the composite substitution over one continued-fraction period fixes the tail word and that the preperiod substitutions map the tail onto the full word. Runtime about 12 s.

claims.label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
claims.statement: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
claims.quote: in no real sense is any randomness actually being generated by the evolution of this system. Instead, it is just that randomness that was inserted in the digit sequence of the original number shows up in the results one gets.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered, all of: (1) transcription identity: for 2000 random reduced fractions p/q with odd q in [3, 10^5], the itinerary of the exact rational orbit (Python Fractions) for 2000 steps agrees bit for bit with the binary digits d_1..d_2000 of p/q computed independently by long division (0 mismatches of 4,000,000), and for three seeds whose binary digits are taken from OEIS b-files truncated to N = 10000 digits (A004539 binary digits of sqrt(2), A010060 Thue-Morse, A030190 binary Champernowne) the exact itinerary agrees with the published digits for all t < N (0 mismatches), with A004539 additionally cross-checked against digits computed with integer isqrt (0 mismatches); (2) periodic seeds stay periodic: for every odd q in 3..2000 and p = 1, the itinerary of p/q, found by exact cycle detection, is purely periodic with minimal period equal to the multiplicative order of 2 modulo q (0 exceptions), and every seed p/2^k (k <= 60) reaches the fixed point 0 within k steps; (3) randomness is inherited, not created: for every seed class the lzma compression ratio of the 10000-bit itinerary differs from the ratio of the seed's own first 10000 digits by less than 0.01, the itinerary of a periodic seed (1/q, q <= 2000) has ratio below 0.10, the Thue-Morse itinerary has ratio below the 1st percentile of 200 random-bit references, and the itinerary of a random-bit seed has ratio within the central 98% of the random references; (4) control with discriminating power: the itinerary of x -> 3x mod 1 started at the seed 1/2^60 (whose binary digits are a single 1 followed by zeros, ratio below 0.05) for 10000 steps has compression ratio above 0.8 times the median random reference and passes an 8-bit block chi-square test at p > 0.001, i.e. it does produce randomness its seed did not have.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: any itinerary bit that differs from the corresponding seed digit in part (1); any odd-q seed whose itinerary period differs from the multiplicative order of 2, or any dyadic seed not reaching 0 within k steps; any seed class whose shift-map itinerary is more than 0.01 less compressible than the seed digits, or a periodic/Thue-Morse itinerary as incompressible as random bits (ratio within the central 98% of the random references). Failure of the control (4) alone does not refute the claim but would be reported as reducing the discriminating power of the test (verdict stays 'supports' with lower confidence if (1)-(3) pass). If (1) fails the verdict is 'refutes'; if (1) passes but (2) or (3) fails the verdict is 'mixed'.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Planned datasets: shift-map-exact-orbits, oeis-a004539-bfile, oeis-a010060-bfile, oeis-a030190-bfile, control-3x-mod-1-orbit
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py computes exact orbits of the doubling map with Python Fractions. (1) For 2000 random reduced fractions p/q (odd q <= 10^5) the 2000-step itinerary is compared bit for bit with the binary digits of p/q from long division; for seeds whose digits are OEIS b-files (A004539 sqrt(2), A010060 Thue-Morse, A030190 Champernowne) truncated to a dyadic rational, the itinerary is compared with the published digits, and the A004539 digits are cross-checked against math.isqrt. (2) For every odd q in 3..2000 the exact orbit of 1/q is walked until it repeats and its period and preperiod are compared with the multiplicative order of 2 mod q; 1/2^k is iterated for k <= 60. (3) lzma compression ratios of seed digits and of the 10000-bit itinerary are compared for Thue-Morse, Champernowne, sqrt(2), random bits, 1/1999 and 1/7, against 200 random-bit references; the NIST serial test (m = 8) is applied to each itinerary. (4) Control: the exact orbit of 3x mod 1 from 1/2^60 for 10000 steps, with compression ratio, pair frequencies and serial test. Run time about 15 s including downloads.

claims.label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claims.statement: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
claims.quote: a crucial discovery in this book is that systems like (a) and (b) on pages 150 and 151 can show behavior that seems in many respects random even when their initial conditions show no sign of randomness and are in fact extremely simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
claims.statement: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
claims.quote: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
claims.quote: despite the presence of continuous gray levels, the behavior that is produced exhibits the same kind of complexity that we have seen in many ordinary cellular automata and other systems with discrete underlying elements.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
claims.statement: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
claims.quote: it is certainly not that nature fundamentally follows these abstractions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
claims.statement: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
claims.quote: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
claims.statement: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
claims.quote: we now know that the same kind of behavior can also occur in completely continuous systems such as partial differential equations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
claims.statement: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.
claims.quote: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
claims.statement: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.quote: I suspect that essentially all of the various phenomena that we have observed in discrete systems in the past several chapters can in fact also be found even in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
claims.statement: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
claims.quote: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
claims.statement: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
claims.quote: if one looks at the evolution of a one-dimensional slice through each two-dimensional pattern the results one gets are strikingly similar to what we have seen in ordinary one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
claims.statement: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
claims.quote: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Run code 746 (a white cell becomes black iff exactly 3 of its 8 neighbours are black; a black cell stays black iff it has 0-4 black neighbours and becomes white with 5 or more; Wolfram's outer-totalistic numbering, bit index 2*s + c) from a horizontal row of 7 black cells for T = 400 and T = 1200 steps on a grid large enough that the pattern never touches the edge. Take the centroid of all black cells as centre, bin all black cells by polar angle into 360 one-degree bins and let r(theta) be the largest centre distance in each bin (outer boundary profile). Compute CV = std(r)/mean(r) and the anisotropy ratio A = mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four axis directions divided by the mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four diagonal directions (a square gives A = 0.707, a diamond 1.414, a circle 1). 'supports' if at T = 1200 both CV <= 0.03 and |A - 1| <= 0.03, and at T = 400 both CV <= 0.05 and |A - 1| <= 0.05. Measurement validation (not part of the verdict): the same statistics for the control rule 'a cell becomes black if any of its 8 neighbours is black' (which grows a square) must give A < 0.8 and CV > 0.06, otherwise the method is declared broken and the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at T = 1200 CV >= 0.06 or |A - 1| >= 0.06 (the outline is at least as far from a circle as a regular octagon is from its circumscribed circle in CV terms, or shows a clear square or diamond bias). Any intermediate outcome -> 'mixed'. Growth rate: the mean radius divided by T is reported and compared with Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t', but does not enter the verdict.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves Wolfram's 8-neighbour outer totalistic code 746 from a row of 7 black cells on a 500x500 (T = 400) and 1100x1100 (T = 1200) grid with numpy, asserting that the pattern never reaches the grid edge. All black cells are binned by polar angle about the centroid into 360 one-degree bins and the largest radius per bin forms the outer profile r(theta); CV = std/mean of that profile and A = mean radius within 5 degrees of the lattice axes over the mean radius within 5 degrees of the diagonals. A control rule in which any black neighbour makes a cell black (which grows a square) was run with the same initial condition to validate that the statistics detect lattice anisotropy.

claims.label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
claims.statement: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
claims.quote: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Run the rule for T = 1000 steps from a row of 11 black cells. Let rho_t(theta) be the outer radius of the occupied set from the pattern centroid in 360 angular bins, normalised by its mean, and D(t1,t2) the mean absolute difference between rho_t1 and rho_t2. PASS (supports) if all three hold: (a) growth continues: mean radius R(1000) >= 1.5 * R(500) and the population is larger at step 1000 than at step 500; (b) the outline keeps changing: D(500,1000) >= 0.05 and D(750,1000) >= 0.03, while both control rules (8-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a square, and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a diamond) give D(500,1000) <= 0.02; (c) the outline at step 1000 is not a simple form: the minimum over the reference family {circle, axis-aligned square, 45-degree square, regular octagon at 0 and 22.5 degrees} of the mean absolute difference between rho_1000 and the reference profile is >= 0.05, while for each control rule the same minimum is <= 0.03.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if growth stops (population unchanged over steps 900-1000) or if the outline converges to a simple form: D(500,1000) < 0.02 and the minimum simple-shape distance at step 1000 is < 0.03. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. shape still changing but growth slowing, or controls not behaving as expected, which would mean the descriptor is not discriminating).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves NKS code 174826 (B3/S012345678) from a row of 11 black cells for 1000 steps on a dynamically padded numpy grid, and at 8 checkpoints records population, mean radius, convex-hull solidity and the normalised outer-radius profile rho_t(theta) in 360 angular bins about the pattern centroid. It computes D(t1,t2) = mean |rho_t1 - rho_t2| between checkpoints and the distance from rho_1000 to five reference profiles (circle, two squares, two octagons). The same pipeline is run on two simple-growth controls (8-neighbour and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black') and on code 175850 from a row of 7 for comparison. Runtime about 20 s.

claims.label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
claims.statement: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
claims.quote: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
claims.statement: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).
claims.quote: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
claims.statement: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.
claims.quote: with this kind of setup, it is ultimately inevitable that all the patterns produced must have a completely regular nested structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

test_contract.expected_observation: Every enumerated or sampled neighbour-independent substitution rule yields a pattern that exactly decomposes into single-cell patterns at every scale and whose number of distinct 4 x 4 and 8 x 8 blocks stays below s^4 b^2 k^2, while some neighbour-dependent rules and a random image violate these.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: A neighbour-independent rule whose pattern breaks the scale decomposition or exceeds the quadratic block-complexity bound.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Patterns generated exactly by committed code from fully specified substitution rules (all two-colour 2 x 2 rules, seeded samples of larger rule spaces); controls generated by the same code.
test_contract.inference_method: Exact array equality for the nesting identity at every scale j; exact (or 64-bit-hashed) counts of distinct k x k windows compared with the bound s^4 b^2 k^2; validity requires the neighbour-dependent controls and a random image to be flagged.

claims.label: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
claims.statement: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.
claims.quote: in traditional fractal geometry the idea of interaction between elements is not considered—so that all patterns that are produced have a purely nested form.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
