morpholib.label: Murray (1981) Thomas substrate-inhibition reaction-diffusion pre-pattern, conical tail spot-to-ring transition & P1 surface-FEM felid body faithfully reproduces African leopard (Panthera pardus) coat rosettes and tapered tail markings morphology
morpholib.organism: African leopard (Panthera pardus) coat rosettes and tapered tail markings

morpholib.note: Short-range melanophore-xanthophore repulsion with long-range support is a local-activation / longer-range-inhibition rule producing zebrafish stripes and the leopard spot-to-stripe morphospace.
morpholib.label: Nakamasu et al. (2009) 3-variable zebrafish pigment-cell reaction-diffusion network + Volkening-Sandstede iridophore S/L agents on a growing flank, laser-ablation polarity & leopard (cx41.8) spot-to-stripe morphospace faithfully reproduces Zebrafish (Danio rerio) melanophore-xanthophore-iridophore flank stripes, juvenile (stage PB) to adult morphology
morpholib.organism: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) melanophore-xanthophore-iridophore flank stripes, juvenile (stage PB) to adult

morpholib.note: The Kondo-Asai activator-inhibitor kinetics are a local-activation, longer-range-inhibition rule producing animal stripe pigmentation, which is the mechanism this claim proposes for coat patterns.
morpholib.label: Painter, Maini & Othmer (1999) Pomacanthus Turing-chemotaxis stripe doubling on a growing curved flank & Keller-Segel rippling with slime-trail tensor faithfully reproduces Pomacanthus semicirculatus juvenile pigment stripes (model target) & Myxococcus xanthus rippling cell populations (specimen) morphology
morpholib.organism: Pomacanthus semicirculatus juvenile pigment stripes (model target) & Myxococcus xanthus rippling cell populations (specimen)

morpholib.note: Reaction-diffusion with local activation and longer-range inhibition is the mechanism the claim proposes for animal spots and stripes, simulated here for fish skin.
morpholib.label: Turing (1952), Pearson (1993) & Kondo-Asai (1995) reaction-diffusion morphogenesis faithfully reproduces Marine angelfish (Pomacanthus imperator) skin stripes, spotted boxfish (Ostracion meleagris) spots & Gray-Scott chemical patterns morphology
morpholib.organism: Marine angelfish (Pomacanthus imperator) skin stripes, spotted boxfish (Ostracion meleagris) spots & Gray-Scott chemical patterns

morpholib.note: Holstein coat spotting is checked against the activator-inhibitor coat-pattern mechanism Wolfram says produces animal spots, and the hypothesis is reported as not supported.
morpholib.label: Turing RD claim for Holstein coat spotting (tested negative hypothesis) faithfully reproduces Bos taurus (Holstein-Friesian, 10 specimens) morphology
morpholib.organism: Bos taurus (Holstein-Friesian, 10 specimens)

claims.label: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics
claims.statement: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.
claims.quote: particularly on short timescales much of the randomness that one sees is purely a consequence of internal dynamics in the market, and has little if anything to do with the nature or value of what is being traded.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
claims.statement: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.
claims.quote: as soon as the underlying rule for the cellular automaton is such that information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others—in effect a minimal version of an efficient market hypothesis—it is essentially inevitable that running totals of numbers of cells will exhibit significant randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules (Wolfram numbering), two colours, nearest neighbours. Propagation test (per rule): 20 trials; lattice of 1601 cells (non-wrapping: cells outside are fixed to the random background and the lattice is wide enough that the perturbation cannot reach the edge in 400 steps), random initial condition with density 1/2 from a fixed seed, second copy with the centre cell flipped; after 400 steps the damage width w = (rightmost differing cell - leftmost differing cell + 1) is recorded (0 if no cell differs); a rule is 'propagating' if w >= 100 (= 0.25 x 400, i.e. the damaged region grows linearly rather than staying bounded or merely moving) in at least 10 of 20 trials. Price-series test (per rule): ring of N = 400 cells, random initial condition density 1/2 from a fixed seed, discard 1000 transient steps, record d(t) = (#black - #white) for W = 4096 further steps; d(t) is 'significantly random' if (R1) it is not exactly periodic with any period p <= W/2 within the window and (R2) the first differences D(t) = d(t+1) - d(t), stored as int16, have plug-in marginal entropy H >= 1 bit and lzma (preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size >= 0.5 x H bits per sample. Calibration on controls: i.i.d. binomial counts give ratio 1.35, an AR(1) series 1.40, a period-97 series 0.09, a noiseless sinusoid 0.47. The claim PASSES if at least 90% of propagating rules are significantly random. Reported, not decisive: the fraction of non-propagating rules that are significantly random, and the list of propagating-but-not-random rules.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 75% of propagating rules are significantly random (several counterexamples to 'essentially inevitable' inside the stated family). Between 75% and 90% the verdict is 'mixed'. If fewer than 5 rules are propagating under the definition the test is underpowered (inconclusive).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evaluates all 256 rules. Damage spreading: 20 seeded random initial conditions on a 1601-cell open lattice, centre cell flipped in a copy, damage width after 400 steps; propagating if width >= 100 in >= 10 trials. Price series: ring of 400 cells, seeded random initial condition, 1000 transient steps, d(t) = #black - #white for 4096 steps; exact-periodicity scan over periods <= 2048; lzma compression of the int16 first differences compared with their plug-in marginal entropy. Per-rule values in derived/rules.csv; runtime about 1 minute.

claims.label: A very simple program may underlie all of physics
claims.statement: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.
claims.quote: Underneath the laws of physics as we know them today it could be that there lies a very simple program from which all the known laws—and ultimately all the complexity we see in the universe—emerges.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata
claims.statement: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.
claims.quote: There are a total of 7,625,597,484,987 cellular automata with three colors and nearest-neighbor rules, and searching through these one finds just 1800 that are reversible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. An exhaustive enumeration with an exact injectivity test (pair graph of the de Bruijn graph: a rule is injective iff the pair graph has no cycle through an off-diagonal node and no diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes; used both as a sound pruning condition during depth-first assignment of the rule table and as the exact test at the leaves) yields exactly 6 reversible rules for k = 2, r = 1 and exactly 1800 for k = 3, r = 1. As a check of the method, the same program must give 62 for k = 2, r = 2 (NKS note 'Numbers of reversible rules'), and the 6 elementary rules must be {15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240}. Also, every rule found must pass Wolfram's finite test (distinct successors for all periodic configurations of period <= 9, as his note says suffices for k = 3) and every rule not found that is sampled (10000 random balanced k = 3 rules) must fail it. 'Supports' requires the counts 6 and 1800 and the consistency checks.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the exhaustive enumeration completes and gives a count other than 6 for k = 2, r = 1 or other than 1800 for k = 3, r = 1 (with the k = 2, r = 2 check giving 62, so the method is validated). If the k = 3 enumeration cannot be completed within the compute budget (about 1 hour), the verdict is 'mixed' or 'inconclusive' (reason: other) with the k = 2 result and a lower bound on the k = 3 count reported.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py compiles revca.c and runs the exhaustive depth-first enumeration of rule tables for (k,r) = (2,1), (2,2) and (3,1). Table entries are assigned in order of the period of their neighbourhood word; after each assignment the pair graph of the de Bruijn graph is built from definite edges (both labels assigned and equal) and the branch is cut if an off-diagonal cycle or a diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes exists (both are sound: they witness two distinct configurations with the same image); the balance condition (each colour exactly k^(2r) times) also prunes. At a leaf the same test is exact. The 1800 rules found for k = 3 are then checked in Python with Wolfram's ReversibleQ (distinct successors of all cyclic configurations of length <= 9), 10000 random balanced k = 3 tables not in the list are checked to fail it, all 256 elementary rules are classified by both methods, and the k = 3 rules are grouped into symmetry families under colour permutations and reflection.

claims.label: Reversible systems can behave as complexly as any other
claims.statement: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.
claims.quote: So in the end it seems that even though only a very small fraction of possible systems have the property of being reversible, such systems can still exhibit behavior just as complex as one sees anywhere else.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: The consequence of this is that no reasonable experiment can ever involve setting up the kind of initial conditions that will lead to decreases in randomness, and that therefore all practical experiments will tend to show only increases in randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
claims.statement: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.
claims.quote: There is, I believe, no choice but to conclude that for practical purposes rule 37R simply does not obey the Second Law.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
claims.statement: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.
claims.quote: This basic mechanism may well be the main one at work in many biological systems: each cell or each organism becomes separated from others, and while it survives, it can exhibit organized behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.
claims.quote: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
claims.statement: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.
claims.quote: And much as in physical systems like fluids, what ultimately leads to this is the presence of small-scale apparent randomness that washes out details of individual cells or molecules—as well as of conserved quantities that force certain overall features not to change too quickly.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
claims.statement: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
claims.quote: my guess is that the only realistic way to find the rule in the first place will be to start from some very straightforward representation, and then just to search through large numbers of possible rules in this representation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
claims.statement: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
claims.quote: so also I suspect that properties such as the existence of seemingly continuous space, as well as certain features of gravitation and quantum mechanics, will emerge with many different possible underlying rules for the universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
claims.statement: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
claims.statement: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
claims.quote: Particle physics experiments have shown that space acts as a continuum down to distances of around 10^(-20) meters—or a hundred thousandth the radius of a proton. But there is absolutely no reason to think that discrete elements will not be found at still smaller distances.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
claims.statement: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: But if the ultimate model for the universe is to be as simple as possible, then it seems much more plausible that both space and its contents should somehow be made of the same stuff—so that in a sense space becomes the only thing in the universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
claims.statement: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
claims.quote: And with this in mind I believe that what is by far the most likely is that at the lowest level space is in effect a giant network of nodes.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
claims.statement: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
claims.quote: in general the condition for a network to correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space is precisely that the total number of nodes that appear in it out to distance r grows in some limiting sense like r^d
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Primary (necessity and the tree/random clause): for the hypercubic lattices Z^1, Z^2, Z^3, Z^4 the growth exponent, estimated as the ordinary-least-squares slope of log N(r) against log r over r in [R/2, R] (R = 32 for d <= 3, R = 20 for d = 4), lies within 0.15 of d; for the infinite 3-regular tree (R = 13) and for a random 4-regular graph on n = 300000 nodes (R = largest radius with N(R) <= n/10) the same slope estimated over r in [R/2, R] exceeds 5, and log N(r) is better fit (higher R^2) by a straight line in r than in log r. If every one of these six conditions holds the primary test passes. Secondary (sufficiency / 'precisely'): the Cayley graph of the discrete Heisenberg group with generators x, y and inverses is known not to be quasi-isometric to any Z^d (Pansu 1983), yet has polynomial growth of degree 4 (Bass 1972 / Guivarc'h 1973). If its measured slope over r in [12, 24] lies in [3.5, 4.5], then a network with r^d growth exists that does not correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space in the strict sense. Verdict rule: primary passes and secondary slope in [3.5, 4.5] -> 'mixed' (the necessity direction and the tree/random clause hold; the sufficiency direction holds only if 'corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is read as 'has growth dimension d'); primary passes and secondary slope outside [3.5, 4.5] -> 'supports'.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any lattice exponent differs from d by more than 0.5, or if either the tree or the random 4-regular graph has a slope below 3 over the stated range (i.e. appears to have a small finite dimension), or if log N(r) for the tree or random graph is better fit by a straight line in log r than in r. Any other outcome (e.g. a lattice exponent off by between 0.15 and 0.5) -> 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py generates each graph implicitly (lattices, tree, Heisenberg Cayley graph) or explicitly (configuration-model random 4-regular graph, n = 300000, numpy seed 20261031) and counts the closed ball N(r) around the origin by breadth-first search. The growth exponent is the OLS slope of log N(r) on log r over r in [R/2, R] with R = 32 (Z^1..Z^3), 20 (Z^4), 13 (tree), 8 (random graph; largest r with N(r) <= n/10) and 24 (Heisenberg). For the tree and random graph the fit of log N(r) linear in r is compared with the log-log fit by R^2. Exact closed-form ball sizes of Z^d were used post hoc to check the BFS counts and to show how the slope estimator converges.

claims.label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
claims.statement: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
claims.quote: The most they will be able to tell is that a certain network of causal relationships exists—and their perception of time must therefore derive purely from the properties of this network.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
claims.statement: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
claims.quote: And any substitution system whose rules specify replacements only for blocks such as these is guaranteed to yield the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are performed.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: among all enumerated (rule set, initial string) pairs whose rule set is syntactically non-overlapping and which admit at least two distinct complete evolutions, 100% have exactly one causal-network isomorphism class (and one final string) over all complete evolutions; and at least 10% of the overlapping rule sets exhibit at least two non-isomorphic causal networks for some initial string (otherwise the test has no discriminating power and the verdict is 'inconclusive', reason 'not-operationalizable').
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: at least one non-overlapping (rule set, initial string) pair whose complete evolutions produce two or more non-isomorphic causal networks.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates all 2305 one- and two-rule systems over {A,B} with lhs length 1-3 and strictly shorter rhs, classifies each syntactically as non-overlapping (37 systems; lhs sets {A}, {B}, {A,B}, {AB}, {BA}, {AAB}, {ABB}, {BAA}, {BBA}) or overlapping (2268), and for each of the 62 initial strings of length 1-5 generates every complete evolution by depth-first search over all possible replacement choices, tracking element identities so that each event is identified by (rule, consumed elements) and the causal network by its identity-labelled edges. Networks from different orders are compared first for identity and then, if they differ, up to isomorphism by brute force over event permutations. A supplementary (not pre-registered) run covers all 127 non-overlapping systems with lhs length up to 4 (which includes genuinely non-overlapping pairs such as {AAB, BBBA} and {AABB, BBAA}) from all 126 initial strings of length 1-6. Run time about 3 s.

claims.label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
claims.statement: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
claims.quote: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
claims.statement: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
claims.quote: my expectation is that they will give rise to networks that on a small scale look largely random. But this very randomness will most likely be what for example allows a definite and robust value of 3 to emerge for the dimensionality of space
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
claims.statement: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.
claims.quote: One may guess that this elementary distance is around 10^(-35) meters, and that the elementary time interval is around 10^(-43) seconds. But whatever these values are, a crucial point is that their ratio must be a fixed speed, and we can identify this with the speed of light.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Causal invariance yields special relativity
claims.statement: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
claims.quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
claims.statement: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.
claims.quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
claims.statement: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
claims.statement: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.
claims.quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by r^(d + 1).
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Random geometric graphs with identical node density (3183 per unit area in d = 2, 7600 per unit volume in d = 3) and connection radius (geodesic epsilon = 0.045 in d = 2, 0.086 in d = 3, mean degree about 20) on: flat torus (R = 0), unit 2-sphere (R = 2), 2-sphere of radius 1.5 (R = 8/9), hyperbolic plane of curvature -1 (R = -2; sampled within hyperbolic radius 1.8, sources within 0.2 of the centre), flat 3-torus (R = 0) and unit 3-sphere (R = 6); 3 independent graphs per geometry, 500 BFS sources per graph. Let S_g(r) be the mean number of nodes at hop distance r, s(r) the mean geodesic distance of hop-r nodes measured in the flat graph of the same dimension, and Q_g(r) = S_g(r)/S_flat(r) - 1. Fit range: hops r with 0.25 <= s(r) <= 0.7. (a) Sign: Q_g(r) < 0 for every r in the fit range for the three positively curved geometries and > 0 for the hyperbolic plane. (b) Exponent: the least-squares slope of log|S_g(r) - S_flat(r)| against log r over the fit range lies within d+1 +/- 0.6 for every curved geometry. (c) Proportionality to R: the coefficient k_g of the through-origin fit Q_g(r) = k_g s(r)^2 over the fit range satisfies 0.7 <= k_g / (-R_g/(6d)) <= 1.3 for every curved geometry, and k(unit sphere)/k(sphere 1.5) is within 30% of 2.25. 'Supports' requires (a), (b) and (c).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the sign in (a) is wrong for any geometry over the fit range, or if any exponent in (b) lies outside [d, d+2], or if any ratio in (c) lies outside [0.4, 2.5] (the correction is not proportional to the Ricci scalar with the continuum coefficient). Other combinations (e.g. correct sign and exponent but coefficient off by 30-60%) are 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py builds, for 3 seeds each, random geometric graphs with density 3183 and epsilon 0.045 on the flat 2-torus (40000 nodes), unit 2-sphere (40000), 2-sphere of radius 1.5 (90000) and hyperbolic plane (curvature -1, disk of hyperbolic radius 2.2, 71356 nodes), and with density 7600 and epsilon 0.086 on the flat 3-torus and unit 3-sphere (150018 nodes each); runs BFS from 500 sources per graph (hyperbolic: sources within hyperbolic radius 1.0 of the centre), averages the shell counts S(r), measures on the flat graphs the mean geodesic radius s(r) of hop-r nodes, and over hops with 0.25 <= s(r) <= 0.7 computes the relative correction Q(r) = S_curved/S_flat - 1, its sign, the log-log slope of S_curved - S_flat against r, and the through-origin coefficient k in Q = k s(r)^2 compared with the continuum value -R/(6d).

claims.label: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
claims.statement: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.
claims.quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
claims.statement: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.
claims.quote: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
claims.statement: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.
claims.quote: And the basic reason for this is that if the universe is a network then it can in a sense easily contain threads that continue to connect particles even when the particles get far apart in terms of ordinary space.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claims.statement: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
claims.quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claims.statement: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
claims.quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claims.statement: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
claims.quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claims.statement: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
claims.quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claims.statement: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
claims.quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claims.statement: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
claims.quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claims.statement: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
claims.quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

test_contract.expected_observation: Across all six methods, uniform and repetitive windows compress to a small fraction of a density-matched random window, nested windows compress at least partly, and rule 30 and rule 45 windows compress by at most 15 %.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Any generic method compressing a rule 30 or rule 45 window to less than 60 % of a density-matched random window, or the methods failing to compress both repetitive and nested patterns.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Patterns generated exactly from elementary CA rules by committed code, analysed in a window inside the light cone; generic compressors not tuned to any rule; density-matched seeded random references.
test_contract.inference_method: Compressed size ratio r against a density-matched Bernoulli pattern for each (rule, method), compared with the pre-registered per-class thresholds.

claims.label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claims.statement: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
claims.quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claims.statement: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claims.statement: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
claims.quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claims.statement: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
claims.quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claims.statement: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
claims.quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claims.statement: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
claims.quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: (1) LFSR (taps {2,11} as in NKS p. 594, period 2047, and a 20-bit register with period 2^20 - 1): over one full period every block of length L <= r - 1 (r = register length) occurs a number of times within 1 of the uniform expectation (N - L + 1)/2^L; Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity equals r (a random sequence of the same length has about N/2); and the chi-square statistic of its block counts for each L in 4..8 lies below the 1st percentile of 200 random sequences of the same length (the 'abnormally small spread'). (2) Binary Champernowne sequence, N = 2^20 bits: for every L <= 8 the maximum relative deviation of any block frequency from 2^-L decreases from the first N/4 bits to the first N/2 bits to all N bits and is <= 0.5 at N (coarse accuracy: every block within a factor 1.5 of uniform); its lzma compression ratio is <= 0.5 while that of the random reference is >= 0.95 (detectable regularity); and its bits agree with OEIS A030190 for every term in the b-file. Verdict 'supports' if (1) and (2) both hold; 'mixed' if (1) holds but (2) fails; 'refutes' if (1) fails.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: the LFSR block counts deviate by more than 1 from uniform for some L <= r - 1, or its chi-square spread is not below the 1st percentile of random sequences for some L in 4..8, or its linear complexity is not r; for Champernowne, a block frequency deviation that does not decrease with N or exceeds 0.5 at L <= 8, or a compression ratio above 0.9 (no regularity detected by compression).
test_contract.admissible_datasets: Planned datasets: lfsr-taps-2-11-full-period, lfsr-taps-3-20-full-period, binary-champernowne-2pow20, oeis-a030190-bfile, random-reference-pcg64
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py generates the two LFSR sequences over one full period (periods verified maximal: 2047 and 1,048,575), the first 2^20 bits of the binary Champernowne word (checked bit for bit against the 10,000 terms of OEIS A030190 after accounting for its leading n = 0 term) and seeded random references. For each sequence it counts all overlapping blocks of lengths 1..8 (1..r-1 for the LFSRs), reports the maximum absolute and relative deviation from uniform, the chi-square spread of block counts against the empirical distribution over 200 random sequences of the same length, the Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity of the first 4000 bits, and the lzma compression ratio of the packed bits. For Champernowne the maximum relative deviation is also computed on the first N/4 and N/2 bits. Run time about 17 s.

claims.label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claims.statement: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
claims.quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

test_contract.expected_observation: Both sequences give block-frequency p-values consistent with uniformity (none < 1e-4, at most 2 of 24 < 0.01) and elementary-CA output statistics within 5 standard deviations of those for random input, while the CA analysis flags the Champernowne and Thue-Morse sequences.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: A block-frequency p-value below 1e-6, 4 or more below 0.01, or an elementary CA whose output density or compressibility on either sequence is more than 6 standard deviations from its value on random input.
test_contract.admissible_datasets: The exact rule 30 centre column and binary digits of pi, generated by committed code and cross-checked against independent tabulations (OEIS); random references from a seeded standard PRNG; known non-random positive controls.
test_contract.inference_method: NIST serial-test increments del-psi^2_L for L = 1..12 with chi-square p-values; z-scores of CA output density and zlib size against 100 random inputs for all 88 inequivalent elementary rules; thresholds and controls as pre-registered.

morpholib.note: Runs block-frequency statistics on the Rule 30 center column, the quantity this claim asserts is statistically random.
morpholib.label: Wolfram (1984) Rule 30 & Meinhardt–Klingler (1987) Conus textile Pigmentation faithfully reproduces Conus textile Linnaeus, 1758 (textile cone snail) morphology
morpholib.organism: Conus textile Linnaeus, 1758 (textile cone snail)

claims.label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claims.statement: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.statement: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
claims.quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claims.statement: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
claims.quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claims.statement: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
claims.quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claims.statement: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
claims.quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claims.statement: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claims.statement: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
claims.quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claims.statement: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
claims.quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Generate six byte strings of 4096 bytes (32768 bits) each: (1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (2) a linear congruential generator modulo 2^32 (a = 1664525, c = 1013904223, seed 1), 32-bit words little-endian; (3) xorshift32 (shifts 13, 17, 5, seed 2463534242), 32-bit words; (4) binary digits of pi after the binary point (Machin formula, exact integer arithmetic); (5) Thue-Morse sequence bits (positive control, obviously regular); (6) os.urandom bytes (baseline, no short description assumed). Generating source for (1)-(5) must be under 400 bytes each (recorded). A method 'recognizes' a string if: for a compressor, its output is at most 0.97 times the compressed size of the urandom baseline of the same length (3% gain); for Berlekamp-Massey, the linear complexity of the bit sequence is below one quarter of its length; for the affine recognizer, the recurrence x_{i+1} = a x_i + c mod 2^32 solved from the first three words holds for every remaining word. 'Supports' if ALL of the following hold: (a) each of the three compressors fails to recognize at least two of the four simple-description strings (1)-(4); (b) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by a specialized method but by none of the three compressors; (c) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by none of the five methods; (d) controls: all three compressors recognize (5) with output below 0.2 of the urandom size, and no method recognizes (6).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim is a theorem (uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity) and cannot be refuted by a finite computation; this test checks whether its concrete content is exhibited by actual methods. 'Mixed' if any compressor recognizes all four simple-description strings (the chosen simple descriptions are all perceptible to a standard method) or if any method recognizes the urandom baseline (false alarm, so 'recognition' is not meaningful at this length). 'Inconclusive' with reason 'construction-failed' if (b) or (c) fails, i.e. the chosen generators do not exhibit a regularity that some method misses while another catches, or none that every method misses.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py holds the five generating programs as Python source strings (94-207 bytes each, all under the pre-registered 400), executes them to produce 4096-byte strings, draws 4096 bytes from os.urandom, and applies zlib level 9, bz2 level 9 and lzma preset 9 extreme (recognition = compressed size <= 0.97 x the compressed size of the urandom string), the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm over GF(2) on the 32768-bit sequence (recognition = linear complexity < 8192), and an affine-recurrence fit modulo 2^32 solved from the first three 32-bit words and verified on the remaining 1021 (recognition = exact fit). Sanity checks: the pi string starts with the known hex expansion 243F6A88..., Berlekamp-Massey returns 4 for a degree-4 LFSR, and the rule 30 column matches OEIS A051023 (checked by hand on the first 32 bits).

claims.label: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
claims.statement: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.
claims.quote: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
claims.statement: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.
claims.quote: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science
claims.statement: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.
claims.quote: And in many respects the single most important idea that underlies this new science is the notion of computation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Any system can be viewed as performing a computation
claims.statement: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.quote: At some level, any cellular automaton—or for that matter, any system whatsoever—can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems
claims.statement: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this chapter and the next is that in fact universality is for example quite crucial in finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity we see in natural systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior
claims.statement: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.quote: So knowing that a particular system is universal thus immediately implies that the system can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. analysis.py re-uses the published rule list (derived/uca_rule.txt copied from the ch11-06 test, or fetched live) and runs the universal automaton on a cyclic array of N = 128 encoded blocks for S = 128 emulated steps (128 x 53 = 6784 universal steps) from a single black cell, for targets: elementary rules 250 (uniform growth), 90 (nested), 110 (localised structures), 30 (random), and one random two-colour range-1 rule drawn with seed 20261104 from rules with f(000) = 0. For each target: rho_dec = 8 * lzma bytes / cells of the decoded S x N binary pattern; rho_ref = the same measure for the directly computed target pattern; rho_raw = 8 * lzma bytes / (cells * log2 19) of the universal automaton's raw S x 20N checkpoint array (rows at multiples of 53 steps). 'supports' if (i) rho_dec equals rho_ref for every target (the universal system's decoded behaviour is exactly as complex as the emulated system's) and (ii) rho_raw(250) < rho_raw(90) < rho_raw(30) with rho_raw(30) >= 2 * rho_raw(250), i.e. the universal system's own pattern spans a wide range of complexity set only by the initial condition. Thresholds fixed before running.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if some decoded pattern differs from the target pattern (then the universal system does not reproduce the emulated behaviour and (i) fails). 'mixed' if (i) holds but (ii) fails, meaning the emulated complexity is visible only after decoding and the universal system's own pattern is dominated by its fixed scaffolding. 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable' if the rule text is unavailable.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py imports the parser, lookup-table builder, encoder and stepper from the ch11-06 test, fetches the published rule list (same page, SHA-256 recorded), and runs the fixed 19-colour rule on a cyclic array of 128 encoded blocks (2560 cells) for 128 emulated steps (6784 universal steps) from a single black cell, with the encoded target being rule 250, 90, 110, 30 or the seed-drawn rule 10. At each 53-step checkpoint the decoded colour cells were compared with the directly computed target, and lzma compressibility was measured for the decoded 128 x 128 pattern (rho_dec), the direct target pattern (rho_ref) and the raw 128 x 2560 universal-automaton checkpoint array (rho_raw, normalised by log2 19). All decoded patterns equal the targets (0 mismatches), so rho_dec = rho_ref exactly: 0.10 (250), 0.15 (90), 0.52 (110), 0.97 (30), 0.06 (10). Raw: 0.0022 (250) < 0.0029 (90) < 0.0172 (110) < 0.0208 (30); ratio 30/250 = 9.32, above the pre-registered 2.

claims.label: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature
claims.statement: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.
claims.quote: But one of the results of this chapter is that in fact universality is a much more widespread phenomenon. And in the next chapter I will argue that for example it also occurs in a wide range of important systems that we see in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton
claims.statement: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.
claims.quote: And the conclusion is therefore that the universal cellular automaton can ultimately emulate a cellular automaton with absolutely any set of rules, regardless of how many neighbors and how many colors they may involve.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. analysis.py fetches the NKS online note 'Universal cellular automaton' (https://www.wolframscience.com/nks/notes-11-4--universal-cellular-automaton/), records byte size and SHA-256 of the page, and parses the published rule list (Mathematica replacement rules on 5-cell neighbourhoods, first matching rule applies; the arrow glyphs are lost in the HTML text, so each rule is read as 'pattern in braces' followed by 'output expression') and the published block encoding Flatten[{Transpose[{Join[{4, 18(1-a), 6}, Table[9, {2^(2r+1)-3}]], 10 - 3 rtab}], Table[{9, 1}, {r}], 9, 13}] with rtab in Wolfram's standard order (outcome for all-ones neighbourhood first). The universal automaton is run on a cyclic array of N blocks (N cells of the target automaton with cyclic boundaries) for S * P steps, where P = (3r+2) 2^(2r+1) + 3r^2 + 7r + 3 is the published period (53 for r = 1, 285 for r = 2). After each P steps, each block must equal the encoding of the directly computed target configuration (strict block-level check, which also verifies the decoded colours). Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules, N = 16, S = 8, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261106); (b) 30 random two-colour range-2 rules (32-entry tables), N = 10, S = 4, one random initial condition each. 'supports' if the total number of mismatching universal-automaton cells over all checks is 0.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if, with the rule list and encoding exactly as published, some target rule's evolution is not reproduced (one or more mismatching cells at a checkpoint). If mismatches occur, the first action is to re-check the transcription of the published text (lost arrows, exponent formatting); a correction that makes the parse agree with the published text is a harness fix and is disclosed in caveats; any remaining mismatch is a refutation. 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable' if the note cannot be retrieved and no verifiable copy is at hand; 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the cyclic-boundary set-up turns out to be incompatible with the construction in a way that cannot be resolved from the published description (for example if the construction requires a special terminator block that the note does not specify).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py fetched the NKS online note (86,136 bytes), extracted the published rule list (65 replacement rules on 5-cell neighbourhoods, arrow glyphs decoded from the HTML entity, first matching rule applies) and the block encoding, compiled the rules into a complete 19^5-entry lookup table (every neighbourhood covered), and ran the universal automaton on a cyclic array of encoded blocks. For all 256 elementary rules (16 cells, 2 random initial conditions, 8 emulated steps of 53 universal steps each) and 30 random two-colour range-2 rules (10 cells, 4 emulated steps of 285 universal steps each; 70-cell blocks), the array after each period was compared cell-for-cell with the encoding of the directly computed cyclic target configuration: 0 mismatches in 1,394,720 cells. Checks that the harness is not vacuous: encoding rule 30 but comparing against rule 110 gives 309 mismatches in 6 steps; within one 53-step period up to 208 of 320 cells differ from the resting form before the array returns to it with exactly the colour cells changed; the decoded rule-30 evolution from one black cell shows the rule-30 pattern.

claims.label: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
claims.statement: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this section is that in fact this is not the case, and that in the end cellular automata can actually be made to emulate almost every single type of system that we have discussed in this book.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Five system types are tested with the rule lists given in the NKS notes, transcribed into analysis.py (first matching rule wins, as in Mathematica). (1) Mobile automata (MAToCA, 4 colours, range 2): all 65536 two-colour mobile automata in Wolfram's {colours, displacements} numbering, from the all-white initial condition and from one seeded random initial condition each; 60 steps; exact if at every step the CA colours mod 2 equal the mobile automaton's cells and the unique dark cell sits at the active position. (2) Turing machines (TMToCA, k(s+1) colours, range 1): all 4096 machines with s = 2, k = 2 and 4096 seeded random machines for each of (s,k) = (3,2), (2,3), (4,2), (3,3), each from a blank tape and from a seeded random tape; 60 steps; exact if tape, head position and head state agree at every step. (3) Substitution systems (SSToCA, 12 colours): all 36 neighbour-independent systems on {0,1} whose two blocks have length 1 or 2, from initial strings {0} and {1}; the CA is run until it has produced 8 'sweep-start' configurations (exactly one r cell, no p or m[0|1] cells), whose decoded strings must equal the substitution system's strings at steps 0..7; a run exceeding 3000 CA steps or reaching the array edge counts as not exact. (4) Register machines (RMToCA, m+7 colours): 300 seeded random programs with m = 2..6 instructions over two registers (i[r], d[r,q]) and initial registers a, b in 0..3, keeping only programs that run at least 20 steps without halting (the construction has no colour for a program counter past the end); the sequence of distinct decoded CA states (program-counter colour, r1 = #(m+2) + 2#(m+3), r2 = #(m+5) + 2#(m+6)) must equal the register machine's trajectory for up to 40 steps. Both the published construction and a one-rule repair described below are run. (5) Logic circuits (the 5-colour rule of p. 1112): 400 seeded random And/Or/Not expressions of depth <= 4 over constants, encoded with the published initial-condition rule and run for the published number of steps; exact if the final configuration has a single non-zero cell equal to 2 for false and 4 for true. The measured value is the number of system types (out of 5) for which 100% of tested instances are emulated exactly, using for register machines the repaired construction. The claim PASSES if the value is 5 and additionally at least 4 of the 5 published constructions are exact as printed.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. If some system type has fewer than 95% exact instances even with the repaired construction the verdict is 'inconclusive' (a failing construction does not show that no construction exists, so an existence claim cannot be refuted this way; reason: construction-failure). If every type is >= 95% but not all are 100%, or if two or more of the published constructions are not exact as printed, the verdict is 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py transcribes the five rule lists into a generic ordered-pattern compiler (first matching rule wins) that produces full lookup tables, then runs the CA and an independent direct simulator of each emulated system side by side. Mobile automata (65536 rules) and Turing machines (4096 + 4 x 4096 rules) are run fully vectorised in numpy; substitution systems, register machines and logic circuits are run one instance at a time. Decodings: MA colour mod 2 and the unique dark cell; TM colour mod k and the unique cell >= k (state = colour div k); SS string read at the start of each replacement sweep; RM (program-counter colour, #(m+2) + 2#(m+3), #(m+5) + 2#(m+6)) with consecutive duplicates removed; logic circuit single surviving cell 2/4. Per-instance tables in derived/*.csv, full summary in derived/summary.json; runtime about 1 minute.

claims.label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
claims.statement: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
claims.quote: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. (A) Light-cone bound: for all 128 elementary rules with quiescent background (000 -> 0), 10 random finite seeds of 20 cells each, 300 steps on a lattice wide enough never to reach the edge, the width of the non-zero region (rightmost minus leftmost black cell plus one) never increases by more than 2 in one step; likewise never by more than 4 for 50 random radius-2 two-colour rules with quiescent background (seeds 0-49), 5 seeds each, 200 steps. (B) Multiplicative growth: among all 225 two-colour neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, at least 50% have Perron root lambda > 1 of their 2x2 growth matrix, and for every system the lengths L_t for t <= 12 from a single black cell equal the matrix prediction exactly. (C) Growing cost: for every system with lambda > 1, the number of radius-1 cellular-automaton steps needed to contain L_12 cells starting from L_0 = 1, ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2), exceeds 12 (more than one CA step per substitution step on average), and the per-step requirement c_t = ceil((L_t - L_{t-1})/2) at t = 12 is at least 4 times c_t at t = 4 (progressively more steps). (D) Contrast with Turing machines: a radius-1 cellular automaton with k(s+1) colours (cell = tape colour x {no head, head state}) built mechanically from the Turing-machine rule reproduces the tape and head of 20 random 2-colour, 2-4-state Turing machines exactly at every one of 200 steps. 'Supports' requires A-D.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A is violated for any rule, seed and step (the fixed-growth premise is false), or if any system with lambda > 1 has ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2) <= 12 (one CA step per substitution step is not excluded by the bound), or if D fails for any machine (Turing machines cannot be emulated step for step either, so the contrast is false). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py: (A) evolves every quiescent elementary rule (128) from 10 random 20-cell seeds for 300 steps and 50 random quiescent radius-2 rules from 5 seeds for 200 steps on zero-padded lattices, recording the largest one-step increase of the non-zero region's width; (B) enumerates the 225 two-colour substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, iterates each 12 times from a single black cell, compares the lengths with the growth-matrix prediction and computes the Perron root; (C) for growing systems computes the minimal number of radius-1 CA steps needed to accommodate the length, ceil((L_t - L_s)/2), over the whole run and over early and late windows; (D) builds, for 20 random 2-colour Turing machines, the radius-1 CA on 2(m+1) colours whose table is generated mechanically from the machine's rule, and compares the CA configuration with the machine's tape and head after each of 200 steps.

claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
claims.statement: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
claims.quote: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if any neighbour-independent rule in the family has p(14) >= 2000 (rule-30-like complexity), or if the neighbour-dependent construction does not reproduce rule 90 or rule 30. If some neighbour-independent rule has 225 < p(14) < 2000 the result is 'mixed' and the rule is reported with its complexity profile.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates all 196 two-colour (blocks 1-3) and 1728 three-colour (blocks 1-2) neighbour-independent substitution rules, iterates each from a single cell of colour 1 until the word has 131072 symbols (or 60 steps), and counts distinct factors of length 1..14 with a sorted rolling-code method. It generates rule 30 from a single black cell with big-integer bit operations, taking the central 40001 cells of row 20000 and the first 65536 centre-column cells, and applies the same count. It also measures what share of the centre column's length-14 factors appear in any binary substitution word, and runs the one-cell-per-cell neighbour-dependent substitution systems for rules 90 and 30 against the direct CA for 1000 steps. Runtime about 19 s.

claims.label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
claims.statement: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.
claims.quote: And as soon as one knows that any particular type of system is capable of emulating any cellular automaton, it immediately follows that there must be examples of that type of system that are universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. analysis.py builds, for a given (k, r, rule table), a Turing machine whose tape holds the cellular-automaton configuration on W cells between two end-marker symbols, and whose head performs one left-to-right sweep (reading each old cell value once, carrying the last 2r old values in its state, stepping back r cells to write the new value) followed by a return to the left end, so that one round trip equals one cellular-automaton step with fixed white (0) boundaries. The machine must be a genuine finite table: every (state, symbol) pair reachable in the runs has exactly one transition writing one symbol and moving one cell. Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules (k = 2, r = 1), W = 48, 40 steps, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261110); (b) 100 random 3-colour radius-1 rules (k = 3, r = 1), same W and steps; (c) 50 random 2-colour radius-2 rules (k = 2, r = 2); (d) 20 random 4-colour radius-1 rules and 10 random 3-colour radius-2 rules. After every round trip the tape between the markers is compared cell-for-cell with the directly computed cellular-automaton configuration (fixed-0 boundary). 'supports' if the total number of mismatching cells over all runs is 0 and the rule-110 machine is produced with a finite, fully specified state table (its state count and transition count reported).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered.
