'refutes' if any run produces a mismatch (one or more cells differing from the direct evolution) that cannot be traced to a bug in the harness rather than the construction; since the construction is uniform in (k, r, rule), a single irreparable mismatch shows the uniform construction does not emulate every cellular automaton. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the harness cannot complete the runs within the time budget.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py builds, from any (k, r, rule table), an explicit finite Turing-machine transition table: states ('scan', B, j) carry the last 2r old cell values B during a left-to-right sweep, step back r cells to write each new value, finish the last r cells at the right end-marker with virtual zero reads, and return to the left marker, so one round trip is one cellular-automaton step with fixed-0 boundaries. The machine for each rule was run on W = 48 cells for 40 steps from two random initial conditions (seed 20261110) and the tape compared cell-for-cell with direct evolution after every step: all 256 elementary rules, 100 random k=3 r=1 rules, 50 random k=2 r=2 rules, 20 random k=4 r=1 rules and 10 random k=3 r=2 rules (436 rules, 1,674,240 cell comparisons). A mutation check (machine for rule 110 compared with rule 124) produced 225 mismatches in 10 steps, confirming the harness detects disagreement.

claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
claims.statement: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
claims.quote: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. analysis.py compiles each register machine into the remainder-selected arithmetic map, then runs machine and map side by side. Test set: (a) all 200 register machines drawn with numpy seed 20261111 from the family with L = 5 and two registers (instruction type, register and jump target uniform), each from the state (1, 0, 0) and from one random state with registers in [0, 20], for 10000 steps; (b) three hand-written programs with L in {3, 5, 7} that move or copy register contents so that the registers grow without bound, 20000 steps each. 'supports' if at every step of every run the decoded (i, a, b) equals the directly simulated register-machine state (0 mismatches out of all compared steps) and, as a check that the comparison can fail, a deliberately perturbed map (one branch's additive constant changed by 1) produces a mismatch within 10000 steps on at least one of the hand-written programs. Universality of the arithmetic systems then follows from the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not tested.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run of the correctly compiled map disagrees with the register machine at any step. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the perturbation check fails to produce a mismatch (the comparison would then be too weak to count).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py compiles each two-register machine (program length L) into a table of 6L branches (p, q, s), one per residue n mod 6L, of the form n -> (p*n + q)/s with p, s in {1, 2, 3}: increments multiply the 2^a 3^b part by 2 or 3, decrements of a nonzero register divide it by 2 or 3 (the residue mod 6L tells whether the register is nonzero), and the additive constant moves the program position. Register machine and arithmetic map were run side by side in exact Python integers: 200 random L = 5 programs (numpy seed 20261111) from two starting states each for 10000 steps, and three hand-written growth programs (L = 3, 5, 7; moduli 18, 30, 42) for 20000 steps. At every step the integer n was compared with the encoding i + L * 2^a * 3^b of the simulated machine state (equivalent to decoding, since the encoding is injective). A perturbed map with one additive constant changed by one was run as a check that the comparison can fail.

claims.label: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
claims.statement: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.
claims.quote: In a sense its most important consequence is that it implies that from a computational point of view a very wide variety of systems, with very different underlying structures, are at some level fundamentally equivalent.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
claims.statement: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.
claims.quote: But the phenomenon of universality implies that this is not the case, and that as soon as one has passed the threshold of universality, nothing more can in a sense ever be gained.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
claims.statement: Rule 110, a two-color nearest-neighbor elementary cellular automaton, is universal: by arranging its naturally occurring localized structures as components, it can be made to emulate any cyclic tag system, and hence any Turing machine.
claims.quote: And indeed in the case of rule 110 it took several years of work to develop the necessary ideas and tools. But finally it has turned out to be possible to show that the rule 110 cellular automaton is in fact universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered: simulate rule 110 on rings of 1200 cells from 60 uniformly random initial rows (numpy default_rng seed 20261031) for 4000 steps. Ether cells are those whose 7 x 14 neighbourhood is invariant under the lattice translation (t, x) -> (t + 1, x - 4). In rows t = 3000..3900 (every 100 steps), maximal runs of non-ether cells of width <= 60 are 'structures'. For each structure, search for the smallest temporal period P <= 100 and shift |s| <= 50 such that the window (structure plus 14 cells of ether on each side) reappears exactly at (t + P, x + s). Component premise confirmed if: (1) the ether, i.e. the (3,2)/(4,-2) lattice, covers more than 50% of the cells at t >= 3000 in every run; (2) at least 90% of structures resolve to a period, and every resolved period (P, s) is a positive integer combination of Cook's A and B periods that coincides with one of Cook's tabulated glider periods (allowing the period to be a positive integer multiple of a tabulated one, for packets such as A^n); (3) the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar are each observed at least once. Because the test replays only the glider inventory and not the cyclic-tag-system emulation, the verdict when all three conditions hold is pre-declared as 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable' (universality is settled by proof, not by this computation), with the component results reported as supporting evidence.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the standard ether does not form (condition 1 fails in a majority of runs), or if the A, C or E-bar classes (the data carriers of Cook's construction) are never observed in 60 random runs, or if resolved structures have space-time periods incompatible with Cook's table (a period that is not an integer combination of (3, 2) and (4, -2) would contradict his lattice argument). Such results would undermine the published construction that the claim cites and would be reported as 'refutes' of the component premise with confidence <= 0.6, since a construction could in principle use rarer gliders.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py runs rule 110 from 60 random rows on 1200-cell rings for 4208 steps. In rows 3000..3900 (every 100 steps) it marks ether cells by invariance of their 7 x 14 neighbourhood under the ether lattice translation (t, x) -> (t+1, x-4), extracts maximal non-ether runs (structures) of width <= 60, keeps those with 14 cells of ether on each side (isolated), and for each searches the smallest space-time period (P <= 100, |s| <= min(50, P)) at which the structure and its margins recur twice. Each minimal period is compared with the (time, displacement) periods of Cook's Figure 5 (exact match, or an integer multiple for packets) and checked to be a non-negative integer combination of the A period (3, 2) and the B period (4, -2). Two refinements were added after a trial run: |s| <= P (matches with faster-than-light displacement are neighbouring identical gliders, not periods) and recurrence at two consecutive periods. Run time about 15 s including the PDF download.

claims.label: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules
claims.statement: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.quote: But knowing that a system like rule 110 is universal, the whole picture changes, and now it seems likely that instead universality should actually be seen in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules
claims.statement: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.
claims.quote: So what this means is that if one looks at a sequence of systems with progressively more complicated rules, one should expect that the overall behavior they produce will become more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: All class 4 cellular automata are expected to be universal
claims.statement: Any cellular automaton showing class 4 behavior (localized structures moving and interacting in complicated ways) will, like rule 110, turn out to be universal, because such rules eventually yield localized structures rich enough to support universality.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is true in general that any cellular automaton which shows overall class 4 behavior will turn out—like rule 110—to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.
claims.quote: Among the 256 so-called elementary cellular automata that allow only two possible colors for each cell and depend only on nearest neighbors, the only clear immediate example is rule 110—together with rules 124, 137 and 193 obtained by trivially reversing left and right or black and white.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.statement: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.
claims.quote: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules. For each rule, 10 trials: ring of N = 800 cells, random initial condition with density 1/2 (numpy default_rng seed 20261033), evolve 1000 steps to configuration C; the trial is 'settled' if C recurs within the next 64 steps (temporal period <= 64, which includes uniform and shifted-periodic states). A rule is 'operational class 1/2' if >= 9 of 10 trials settle. In every settled trial, flip one cell of C (the cell at index 400) and evolve both copies 400 further steps on the ring (N = 800 > 2 x 400, so the damage cannot wrap); record the damage width w = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1 (0 if none). A rule is 'bounded' if w <= 20 in all of its settled trials, 'spreading' if the median w over settled trials >= 100 (linear growth), otherwise 'intermediate'. The claim PASSES if 100% of operational class 1/2 rules are 'bounded'. Validation (reported, not decisive): the rules Wikipedia cites as Wolfram's class 1 and 2 examples (0, 32, 160, 232; 4, 108, 218, 250) must be operational class 1/2 and the class 3 and 4 examples (22, 30, 126, 150, 182; 110, 54) must not be; and the fraction of non-settled rules that are 'spreading' is reported.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if any operational class 1/2 rule is 'spreading' (a settled rule that nevertheless transmits a perturbation over a linearly growing region). If some class 1/2 rules are 'intermediate' but none 'spreading', the verdict is 'mixed'. If the Wikipedia example rules are misclassified by the operational definition, that is reported as a caveat on the mapping to Wolfram's phenomenological classes but does not change the verdict.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py runs all 256 rules: 10 seeded random initial conditions on an 800-cell ring, 1000 steps, period detection up to 64 steps, then a single-cell flip of the settled configuration and 400 further steps for both copies; damage width = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1. Operational class 1/2 = >= 9/10 trials settled; bounded = max width <= 20; spreading = median width >= 100. The Wikipedia page is fetched for its checksum and the example rules per class are checked against the operational classification. Per-rule values in derived/rules.csv (including a post-hoc width at step 200), fetch record in derived/wikipedia.json; runtime about 50 s.

claims.label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
claims.quote: And since there are many kinds of behavior that do not return to such predictable forms after any limited number of steps, one must conclude that additive rules cannot be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. (a) For each of the eight linear rules, each cyclic lattice size N in {1023, 2048}, 20 seeded random initial conditions of density 1/2 plus the single-cell initial condition, and each k = 0..10, the configuration after 2^k steps equals bit-for-bit the XOR of the initial condition shifted by d*2^k over the offsets d in the rule's support (the support is read off the rule table as the cells on which the one-step response to a single 1 is nonzero). (b) An additivity screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) on 200 seeded random pairs at N = 256 identifies exactly the eight linear rules, and the affine screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) xor T(0) exactly the eight linear plus the eight complementary rules (255, 195, 165, 153, 105, 85, 51, 15). (c) For each of the eight control rules 18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122 and each k = 0..8, the 2^k-step map fails additivity on at least one of 50 seeded random pairs at N = 256 (so the state after 2^k steps is not a superposition of shifted copies of the initial condition for generic initial conditions). (d) The number of nonzero cells in row t of the single-cell pattern of rule 90 (t = 0..T) equals term t of OEIS A001316 and that of rule 150 equals term t of A071053, for every term available in the OEIS b-files up to t = 4095 (the b-files are fetched and their sha256 recorded). PASS (supports the claim's checkable premise) if (a), (b), (c) and (d) all hold. The non-universality conclusion itself is a proof-type statement (a map that is linear over GF(2) at every power-of-two step cannot emulate the non-linear behaviour an arbitrary computation requires under the encodings the book considers) and is not decided by this test; its evidential weight is recorded in the confidence.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes the premise) if (a) fails for any linear rule, k, lattice size or initial condition (the stated superposition property is false), or if (d) fails for rule 90 or rule 150 (the single-cell patterns are not the nested patterns the claim describes). MIXED if (a) and (d) hold but (b) or (c) fails (the superposition property is true of rules 90 and 150 but does not cleanly separate additive from complex rules as the book's argument requires). INCONCLUSIVE with reason data-unavailable only for part (d) if the OEIS b-files cannot be retrieved; (a)-(c) are then still reported and the verdict rests on them with reduced confidence.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py implements elementary CA rules on cyclic lattices. (a) For each of the eight GF(2)-linear rules it reads the support offsets off the rule table and checks, for N = 1023 and 2048, 20 seeded random initial conditions plus a single cell, and k = 0..10, that the configuration after 2^k steps equals the XOR of the initial condition shifted by d*2^k over the support (462 checks per rule). (b) It screens all 256 rules for additivity T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) and affinity on 200 random pairs at N = 256. (c) For the eight class-3/4 control rules it counts, for k = 0..8, how many of 50 random pairs violate additivity of the 2^k-step map. (d) It computes the row populations of the single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 for 4096 rows and compares them term by term with the OEIS b-files of A001316 and A071053 fetched over HTTPS (sha256 recorded). Runtime 15 s.

claims.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
claims.statement: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
claims.quote: And as one continues one sees various other repetitive and nested forms. But at least up to the hundred millionth initial condition one sees nothing that is fundamentally any more complicated.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: initial conditions n = 1..65536 (16 bits), cell values = binary digits of n placed on an infinite white background (validated against the figure: n = 1 single cell, n = 3 two cells, n = 291 nested); rule 54 run for T = 256 steps on a lattice wide enough that the light cone never reaches the edge. Classifier (frozen before the census): the number D of distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles whose top-left corner lies in rows 128..250 and inside the light cone (plus 2 cells) of the pattern. Calibration on controls outside the family, disclosed: repetitive and nested rules give D <= 1007 (rule 90 single cell 115, random 14-bit seeds 267-395; rule 150 single 316, random seeds 804-1007; rule 22 single 119; rule 18 random 309-602; rules 250, 108, 184, 62, 41 random 1-178), while class 3/4 controls give D >= 1094 (rule 110 random 14- and 30-bit seeds 1094-1553; rule 30 6801-7166; rule 45 6338-6401), with a few class-3 rules from narrow seeds in between (rule 106: 462 and 2912; rule 126: 130-402; rule 146: 371-413; rule 73: 64-774). The eight rule-54 patterns shown in the book's figure (n = 1, 3, 75, 259, 291, 787, 803, 56549) give D = 10, 37, 315, 315, 286, 391, 391, 370, and a batch of 256 random 14-bit seeds gave max 391. Threshold: D > 1050 (geometric midpoint of 1007 and 1094) = 'more complicated'. Also recorded per initial condition: exact temporal periodicity (period <= 16) of the pattern's core over steps 128..256 ('repetitive'). The claim PASSES if 0 of the 65536 initial conditions has D > 1050. Reported, not decisive: the distribution of D, the fraction that is exactly periodic, the number with D > 700 (a stricter threshold that still clears all rule-54 book examples), and for any initial condition above threshold a re-run with T = 512.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if at least one initial condition n <= 65536 has D > 1050 and the T = 512 re-run also gives D > 1050 (sustained local complexity comparable to the class 3/4 controls). If some exceed 1050 at T = 256 but not at T = 512 the verdict is 'mixed' (transient complexity). The census is 1/1526 of the book's 10^8 initial conditions; a pass is consistent with the claim but far from exhausting it.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves rule 54 for 256 steps from every initial condition n = 1..65535 (binary digits of n on white; batches of 512 vectorised in numpy on a lattice wide enough that the light cone never reaches the edge), encodes every 6 x 6 space-time tile with top-left in rows 128..250 inside the light cone as a 36-bit integer and counts distinct tiles D; patterns with D <= 400 are also tested for exact temporal periodicity (period <= 16) of the light-cone core over steps 128..256. The 20 initial conditions with the largest D are re-run for 512 steps. Per-initial-condition values in derived/census.csv.xz; runtime about 3 minutes.

claims.label: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal
claims.statement: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.
claims.quote: As I will discuss in the next chapter, my general expectation is that more or less any system whose behavior is not somehow fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs
claims.statement: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.
claims.quote: And this kind of uncontrolled transmission of information makes it very difficult to identify pieces that could be used as definite components in a construction.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal
claims.statement: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.
claims.quote: So although this means that the particular type of approach we used to demonstrate the universality of rule 110 cannot immediately be used for rule 30 or rule 45, it certainly does not mean that these rules are not in the end universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
claims.statement: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbitrarily sophisticated computations.
claims.quote: But for underlying rules that have more complex behavior—like rules 22, 30, or 110—it turns out that in the end it is always possible to emulate all 256 elementary rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Scheme: the initial condition is periodic with period w+1: one input cell x[i] in {0,1} followed by a fixed background block B in {0,1}^w. The underlying rule f is run for t steps with w+1 <= t <= 2w+2 and the output for cell i is read at offset d in 0..w to the right of x[i]'s position. For each (w, B, t, d) the output is computed for all 32 assignments of (x[i-2], ..., x[i+2]) in a window padded on both sides with t+2 further background cells (input positions in the padding set to 0; they lie outside the light cone). If the output depends only on (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) (the 4 assignments of the outer inputs agree for each of the 8 inner triples), the induced 3-input truth table is an elementary rule g that f emulates for one step at width w. E(f, W) = the set of g realised for some w <= W. Widths searched: W = 1..6. 'supports' if |E(f, 6)| = 256 for each f in {22, 30, 110} and |E(f, 6)| <= 32 for each f in {90, 184}.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if |E(90, 6)| >= 128 or |E(184, 6)| >= 128 (a 'simple' rule emulates at least half of all elementary rules), or if min over f in {22, 30, 110} of |E(f, 6)| is smaller than max over f in {90, 184} of |E(f, 6)| (the contrast is reversed). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if neither condition holds, e.g. because 22, 30 or 110 do not reach 256 within W = 6 under this scheme: Wolfram's figure uses a scheme whose exact readout and width conventions are not fully recoverable from the online text, so a shortfall under the reconstructed scheme does not refute the claim. In every case the counts for all 256 underlying rules at W = 6 are reported.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py builds, for each underlying rule f, each background width w = 1..6 and each of the 2^w background blocks, a periodic initial condition with one input cell per period, runs f for t = w+1..2w+2 steps on all 32 assignments of five consecutive inputs (numpy, vectorised over assignments), reads the output at each offset d = 0..w below the central input, and records the induced 3-input truth table whenever the output is independent of the two outer inputs. The cumulative number of distinct elementary rules so obtained was computed for all 256 underlying rules (25 s). After seeing that the counts were still rising at w = 6, the same search was continued post hoc to w = 12 for rules 22, 30, 45, 90, 110 and 184 (a further 2 minutes).

claims.label: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal
claims.statement: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.
claims.quote: And this suggests that such cellular automata will in the end turn out to be universal—with the result that out of the 256 elementary rules one expects that perhaps as many as 27 will in fact be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
claims.statement: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.
claims.quote: And in fact, by using the universality of rule 110 it turns out to be possible to come up with the vastly simpler universal Turing machine shown below—with just 2 states and 5 possible colors.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Using the rule table transcribed from the p. 707 figure (10 cases; the transcription is recorded in derived/tm25-rule.json), for the single-cell initial list and for 40 random binary lists of length 10-60 (numpy default_rng seeds 0..39), with a fixed integer offset c determined once from the single-cell run and then held fixed, the k-th new-rightmost snapshot decoded as above equals rule-110 iterate k-c of the initial list for every k from c to c+199, on every cell of the window spanning the full rule-110 pattern (100% of 41 x 200 snapshot comparisons). 'Supports' if this holds.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if for any initial list some snapshot differs from the corresponding rule-110 iterate, or if no fixed offset makes the single-cell run match; 'inconclusive / not-operationalizable' if the rule table cannot be read unambiguously from the published figure.
test_contract.inference_method: The 10 rule icons of the p. 707 figure were transcribed by grey level and arrow geometry (derived/tm25-rule.json). analysis.py simulates the machine on a tape of colour-1 cells, a 0, the rule-110 list encoded as 4*list, and 0's, with the head on the first 0 right of the data in state 1 (as in the figure), records the tape each time the head reaches a new rightmost position, decodes colour 4 as black, and compares snapshot k with rule-110 iterate k of the list (time offset and spatial shift fixed once from the single-cell run: both 0). This is done for the single-cell list and 40 random lists of length 10-60, 200 snapshots each. The pre-registration's guessed start (head on the prepended 0) is also run and reported.

claims.label: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
claims.statement: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.
claims.quote: If one looks at the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors it is fairly easy to see that their behavior is in all cases too simple to support universality.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. For each of the 4096 machines and each initial condition in the set I = {every binary tape string of length 1-7 with the head on each of its cells, in each of the 2 states} (1284 initial conditions per machine) plus 100 random tapes of length 16-32 per machine (seeded), simulate on an infinite blank (0) tape for up to 10000 steps and classify the evolution exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation: the head-relative configuration (state, tape between the outermost non-zero cells, head offset) recurs exactly, which implies periodic evolution forever; or (B) escaping: the head is beyond all non-zero cells, moving outward over blank cells, and the same state occurs twice during that outward run, which implies it moves outward forever. 'Supports' if 100% of the (machine, initial condition) pairs are classified as (A) or (B) within 10000 steps, and the largest period found is at most 1000 steps. The symmetry-reduced count of distinct machines (state relabelling, colour swap, reflection) is also computed and compared with Wolfram's 560 as a consistency check on the enumeration.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The test cannot establish universality, so 'refutes' is not reachable by this computation alone. 'Mixed' if any (machine, initial condition) pair is unclassified after 10000 steps (unbounded non-periodic behaviour within the tested inputs, which would be at least consistent with the complexity universality needs) or if periods above 1000 steps occur. 'Supports' otherwise.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py writes the random initial tapes, compiles tm22.c with gcc and runs it over all 4096 machines x 3176 initial conditions (13,008,896 runs, 10000-step limit). Each run is classified exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation (the head-relative configuration recurs) or (B) escaping, with two exact escape tests: B1 as pre-registered (head beyond all non-zero cells moving outward with a repeated state) and B2 (two successive new-extreme head positions with identical state and identical non-zero tape, the head farther from the tape than the time between them, so the motion repeats verbatim on blank tape). Runs that are neither are put through three post-hoc heuristic classes added after the first full run showed 16% of runs growing their tape: (C) regular linear growth, where the last 16 events at which the head reaches a new extreme position (sampled with stride 1-3) have constant second time differences, constant state and tape contents S_{n+1} = P + S_n[:o] + B + S_n[o:] + Q with fixed P, B, Q, o; (D) the same with event gaps obeying g_{n+1} = a g_n + b, a >= 2 (binary-counter growth); (E) a counter certificate for runs whose tape never grows: at >= 8 returns of the head to one end of its range, in a fixed state, the tape read as a binary number changes by the same non-zero amount. C/D stop the run early once 16 events fit; as a check the program is also run without early stopping (full 10000 steps) on machines 256-319 and 2048-2111 and the class counts compared. Symmetry-distinct machines are counted under state relabelling, colour swap and reflection.

claims.label: Complex behavior is rare but present in small Turing machine spaces
claims.statement: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.
claims.quote: Among such 2-state 4-color Turing machines perhaps one in 50,000 shows complex behavior when started from a blank tape.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A complex 2-state 3-color Turing machine is likely the simplest universal one
claims.statement: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.
claims.quote: And although it will no doubt be very difficult to prove, it seems likely that this Turing machine will in the end turn out to be universal. And if so, then presumably it will by most measures be the very simplest Turing machine that is universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: All 3-state 2-color Turing machines behave simply from blank tape
claims.statement: With blank initial conditions all 2,985,984 Turing machines with 3 states and 2 colors quickly produce simple repetitive or nested behavior, and even with more complicated initial conditions their behavior eventually seems to resolve into a simple form.
claims.quote: With 3 states and 2 colors it turns out that with blank initial conditions all of the 2,985,984 possible Turing machines of this type quickly evolve to produce simple repetitive or nested behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
claims.statement: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.
claims.quote: But from pictures like the ones on the facing page it is rather clear that despite their fairly simple underlying rules, the behavior of combinators can be highly complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. (A) Growth: evolve s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps, each step = one ReplaceAll pass of {s[x][y][z] -> x[z][y[z]], k[x][y] -> x} (outermost subexpression first, no re-scan of replaced parts, heads and arguments visited); PASS-A if no fixed point is reached and a least-squares fit of log2(LeafCount) against step over steps 10..40 has slope in [0.45, 0.55] (book: growth like 2^(t/2)) with R^2 >= 0.99. (B) Census (reported, not decisive): evolve all 109,824 size-8 S/K expressions for up to 60 steps or until LeafCount > 20,000; record how many reach a fixed point, how many exceed 20,000 leaves (unbounded/exponential candidates), and the remainder; the book reports 49 with exponential growth. (C) Emulation: implement ToC bracket abstraction, p, num, inc, cr and w exactly as printed in the note; encode every binary list of length 3, 4 and 5 (56 lists) with p[num[Length]][Fold[p[Nest[s,k,#2]][#1]&, p[k][k], list]] fully normalised; apply w once, twice and three times (full normalisation by iterated ReplaceAll after each application); decode by applying the pair selectors (p[a][b][s[k]] -> a, p[a][b][k] -> b) and normalising; PASS-C if for all 56 lists and all t in 1..3 the decoded list equals t steps of rule 110 applied to the list padded with one 0 on each side per step (length n + 2t). The claim PASSES if PASS-A and PASS-C both hold (the growth and the emulation components, which are what the book presents as evidence); the census (B) and any descriptive statistics of internal structure are reported only.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if the size-7 expression reaches a fixed point or its growth is not exponential (slope outside [0.45, 0.55] or R^2 < 0.99), or if the published w combinator does not reproduce rule 110 for every tested list and step count. If w cannot be transcribed unambiguously from the note (the HTML lost the rule arrows) the emulation component is inconclusive (other) and the verdict rests on (A) as 'mixed'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py implements hash-consed S/K terms with a memoised one-pass ReplaceAll step (whole expression first, then head and argument, replaced parts not re-scanned) and full normalisation by iterating passes to a fixed point. It (A) evolves s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps and fits log2 LeafCount on steps 10-40; (C) implements ToC bracket abstraction, p, inc, num, cr, the rule-110 cell combinator f (size 62, book: 61) and the step combinator w (size 674) from the note, encodes all 56 binary lists of length 3-5, applies w up to three times and decodes with the pair selectors; (B) runs the exhaustive census of the 109,824 size-8 expressions (60 steps or LeafCount > 20,000) and, as validation of the rewrite semantics, the 16,896 size-7 expressions, comparing with the counts printed in the note 'Combinator properties'. Full output in derived/census.json; runtime about 8 s.

claims.label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
claims.statement: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
claims.quote: all processes, whether they are produced by human effort or occur spontaneously in nature, can be viewed as computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
claims.statement: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
claims.quote: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
claims.statement: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
claims.quote: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
claims.statement: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
claims.quote: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
claims.statement: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
claims.quote: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
claims.statement: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
claims.quote: So far as I can tell, all possible blocks eventually appear, potentially letting the pattern serve as a kind of directory of all possible computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
claims.statement: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
claims.quote: while in simple cases complicated molecules may for example arrange themselves in configurations that minimize energy, the evidence is that in more complicated cases they typically do not.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
claims.statement: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.
claims.quote: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claims.statement: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
claims.statement: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.
claims.quote: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
claims.statement: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.
claims.quote: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
claims.statement: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
claims.statement: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
claims.statement: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.
claims.quote: this, I believe, is the fundamental reason that traditional theoretical science has never managed to get far in studying most types of systems whose behavior is not ultimately quite simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
claims.statement: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.
claims.quote: there are many common systems whose behavior cannot in the end be determined at all except by something like an explicit simulation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
claims.statement: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.
claims.quote: In general, to find the color of a cell after t steps of rule 188 or rule 60 evolution takes about Log[2, t] steps.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered, for each of rules 60 and 188: (i) the number of distinct 2-kernel elements A(2^k t + r, 2^k x + s), compared on a 64 x 64 window, saturates: the cumulative count over levels k <= 5 equals the cumulative count over all levels k <= K - 6 of a 2^K x 2^K pattern with K = 11 (i.e. no new element appears beyond level 5), and that count is at most 64; (ii) the finite automaton whose states are those kernel elements and whose transitions on a digit pair (dt, dx) go from element (k, r, s) to (k+1, r + 2^k dt, s + 2^k dx) is consistent (every representative of a state yields the same target state for each digit pair) and, run on the least-significant-first binary digits of (t, x), reproduces 100% of the cells of an independently evolved 2^12 x 2^12 pattern (t < 4096), three quarters of which lie outside the K = 11 construction range; (iii) the number of automaton steps for a cell at time t equals the number of binary digits of t, i.e. floor(log2 t) + 1.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered: for rule 60 or rule 188 the kernel count keeps growing beyond level 5 (no saturation) or exceeds 64, or the automaton is inconsistent, or any cell of the 2^12 x 2^12 pattern disagrees with the automaton's output. Control rules 30 and 110 (not nested) are expected to fail (i) and (ii); if they passed, the test would be too weak and the verdict would be 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable'.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py evolves each rule from a single black cell to a 4096 x 4096 array A(t, x). (i) For levels k = 0..7 it extracts every 2-kernel element A(2^k t + r, 2^k x + s) on a 32 x 32 window and counts cumulative distinct elements. (ii) From the 2048 x 2048 sub-pattern it builds the automaton whose states are the distinct 64 x 64 kernel windows (levels k <= 5), with transition (k, r, s) -> (k+1, r + 2^k dt, s + 2^k dx) on digit pair (dt, dx), checks that no state has conflicting or undefined transitions, then runs the automaton on the least-significant-first binary digits of (t, x) for all 16,777,216 cells of the 4096 x 4096 array (12 digit pairs) and compares with A; it also stops the automaton after bitlen(t) digit pairs and compares on the 8,390,656 cells with x <= t. Controls 30, 110 (mirrored), 90 and 150 (right halves) are treated identically. Run time about 30 s.

claims.label: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
claims.statement: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
claims.statement: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
claims.quote: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
claims.statement: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.
claims.quote: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
claims.statement: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.
claims.quote: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
claims.statement: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that even with just three pairs there is already computational irreducibility
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
claims.statement: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.
claims.quote: it turns out that the only rates of growth that one ever sees are linear, square and exponential.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Conventions from NKS pp. 761 and 1143: tape cells i = 1, 2, ... hold the binary digits of x with the least significant digit at i = 1 (x = 0 is the single digit 0), all other cells 0; head starts at i = 1 in state 1; a step applies the rule (new state, new colour, displacement d) and moves the head to i - d; the computation is complete at the first step t at which i = 0; the output f(x) is the tape read as a binary number. Machines are numbered with the NKS scheme (p. 888). Inputs x = 0..1023 (lengths n = 1..10). Non-halting is established by (i) a cycle of states that keeps moving left on blank cells once the head is left of every visited cell, (ii) exact repetition of the configuration (Brent's algorithm), or (iii) a cutoff of 20000 steps. For each machine and each distinct (f, t) pair over x = 0..1023, T(n) = max t(x) over halting x of length n. Growth class on n = 3..10, requiring halting inputs at >= 5 of these lengths (otherwise 'insufficient'): exact fit (max residual < 1e-9) tried in the order constant, linear a+bn (b>0), quadratic a+bn+cn^2 (c>0), exponential a*2^n+b (a>0); if none is exact, the lowest-complexity of linear, quadratic, exponential (a*c^n+b, c in {2,3,4}) whose relative RMS residual over n = 3..10 is <= 0.15; else 'other'. PASS (supports) if (a) no (f, t) pair with sufficient data is classed 'other', and (b) for every exponential pair the same function f (as a map on x = 0..1023 including where it is undefined) is computed by at least one machine whose pair is classed constant. The book's census numbers (748 never halt / 3348 sometimes / 1683 always; 351 functions, 149 total; 492 (f,t) pairs; 164 constant, 295 linear, 27 quadratic, 6 exponential; machines 378, 1953, 2289 exponential with total functions; the formulas for machines 3279, 1285, 3333, 261, 1447, 1953, 1969, 3517, 3246, 3374) are recorded as cross-checks of the implementation and do not decide the verdict.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if some (f, t) pair with sufficient data has a growth class other than constant, linear, quadratic or exponential and this is confirmed when the machine is rerun on x up to 2^14 - 1 with cutoff 2^20 steps (e.g. a cubic or super-exponential fit is best), or if some exponential pair has no constant-time partner computing the same function. MIXED if 'other' pairs exist but on the extended inputs fit one of the four classes within tolerance, or if the cross-check numbers disagree with the book in a way that indicates a convention mismatch.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates all 4096 two-state two-colour machines with the NKS numbering (p. 888) and runs each on x = 0..1023 under the one-sided convention of pp. 761/1143 (binary digits of x on cells 1, 2, ... with the least significant digit at cell 1, head starting at cell 1 in state 1, halting when the head reaches cell 0, output read from the tape); non-halting is established by a left-runaway state cycle, Brent cycle detection on full configurations, or a 20000-step cutoff. The runner is vectorised over (machine, input) pairs and is checked against a scalar reference on 32 machines x 256 inputs. For every machine and every distinct (function, halting-time) pair it takes T(n) = max halting time over inputs of length n = 3..10 and classifies growth by the pre-registered exact-then-approximate fits; the 61 machines classed 'other' are rerun on x = 0..16383 (n <= 14) with cutoff 2^17 (the pre-registered 2^20 was reduced for memory and time; the longest halting time seen is 303). Supplementary, non-pre-registered analyses: a parity-aware classifier (odd and even n fitted separately, first two lengths dropped), and for exponential pairs computing partial functions a search for machines agreeing with them on every input where they halt. Book census numbers are recorded as cross-checks. Runtime about 10 minutes.

claims.label: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort
claims.statement: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.
claims.quote: there are indeed Turing machine computations that cannot actually be carried out except by spending an amount of computational effort that can increase exponentially with the length of input.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
claims.statement: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.
claims.quote: almost all the very varied systems in this book can actually be made to emulate each other in a quite comparable number of steps.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: P is likely different from NP
claims.statement: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.
claims.quote: And although it has never been established for certain it seems by now likely that in most meaningful senses there is not.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
claims.statement: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.
claims.quote: my expectation is that asking about possible outcomes of t steps of evolution will already be NP-complete even for the rule 30 cellular automaton
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact
claims.statement: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that even if this is formally the case, it will still not turn out to be a true representation of ultimate physical reality
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution
claims.statement: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.
claims.quote: there really can in some fundamental sense be an almost exponential difference in the amount of computational effort needed to find the behavior of a system with given particular initial conditions, and to solve the inverse problem of determining which if any initial conditions yield particular behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable
claims.statement: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.
claims.quote: But I suspect that ultimately there is almost always computational irreducibility, and this makes it essentially inevitable that there will be short theorems that only allow long proofs.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
claims.statement: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.
claims.quote: So the result of this is that if the evolution of a multiway system is computationally irreducible—so that questions about its ultimate behavior are undecidable—the system cannot be both complete and consistent.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Every axiom system used in current mathematical research is universal
claims.statement: Basic logic and pure predicate logic are not universal, but adding a function or relation with more than one argument gives universality; arithmetic, set theory, group theory and ring theory are universal, and every axiom system actually used in current mathematical research is known to be universal, while heavily constrained systems such as commutative group theory and simplified real algebra and geometry are not.
claims.quote: But of the axiom systems actually used in current mathematics research every single one is now known to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Beyond a low threshold almost every axiom system should be universal
claims.statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that, beyond a low threshold of complexity, almost any axiom system (including very simple ones) should be universal, and so should exhibit undecidability and have no general upper limit on proof length.
claims.quote: And indeed the Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that beyond some low threshold almost any axiom system should be expected to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
claims.statement: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: And with the cellular automaton being a universal one such as rule 110 this implies that the axioms of arithmetic can support universality.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable
claims.statement: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.
claims.quote: so that in fact there are in the end rather simple integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the normal axioms of arithmetic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms
claims.statement: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.
claims.quote: And it is my strong suspicion that in fact of all the current unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory a fair fraction will in the end turn out to be questions that cannot ever be answered using the normal axioms of arithmetic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: And indeed from the Principle of Computational Equivalence I strongly believe that in general undecidability and unprovability will start to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond the level of questions that are always easy to answer.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Mathematics avoids undecidability by choosing questions its methods can answer
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability have seemed rare in mathematics because mathematics, shaped by its history, has defined itself around the questions and systems that proof-based methods can address, concentrating on limited patches of computational reducibility; so present-day mathematics is a small and uncharacteristic sample of what is possible.
claims.quote: it is that like most other fields of human inquiry mathematics has tended to define itself to be concerned with just those questions that its methods can successfully address.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
claims.statement: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.
claims.quote: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Part 1 (sets): for length n = 3, enumerate all 764 involutions of the 8 strings and all 256 subsets S; for n = 4, take 300 pseudo-random involutions of the 16 strings (numpy seed 20261031, including the complement map, reversal and the identity-on-some-strings cases) and all 65536 subsets. For each (involution, S) record complete, consistent, |S| versus half. Part 2 (multiway systems): enumerate all multiway systems over {A,B} with one or two rules lhs -> rhs, |lhs| in {1,2}, |rhs| in {|lhs|, |lhs|+1} (length-non-decreasing so that the set of generated strings of each length <= 6 stabilises and can be computed exactly), started from the string 'A' taken to represent true; for each system and each length n = 2..6 record the exactly generated set, under negation = complement and under negation = reversal. PASS (supports) if in Part 1 and Part 2 there is no counterexample to either direction of the biconditional (complete and consistent <=> exactly half) for any involution.
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the biconditional fails in both directions, or if either of the book's two directional arguments (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete) has a counterexample. MIXED if the three implications the book argues for (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete; hence complete and consistent => exactly half) hold without exception but the converse (exactly half => complete and consistent) has counterexamples both among arbitrary sets and among stabilised generated sets of actual multiway systems. The number of counterexamples and the role of involution fixed points are reported.
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates all 764 involutions of the 8 binary strings of length 3 against all 256 subsets, and for length 4 the complement, reversal and identity maps plus 300 seeded random involutions against all 65536 subsets, recording for each (involution, set) whether the set is complete, consistent and of size exactly half. It then enumerates all 1485 multiway systems with one or two length-non-decreasing rules (|lhs| 1-2, |rhs| = |lhs| or |lhs|+1) over {A,B}, computes the exact closure of 'A' restricted to strings of length <= 6, and evaluates the same quantities at each length 2-6 under complement and reversal negation. Runtime 2 s.

claims.label: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete
claims.statement: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.
claims.quote: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms
claims.statement: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.
claims.quote: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Family: all single-equation axiom systems lhs == rhs where lhs and rhs are terms built from one binary operator and variables, with a total of n = 1..4 operator occurrences in the equation, variables named canonically in order of first occurrence (a, b, c, ...) reading lhs then rhs, excluding equations with lhs identical to rhs, and identifying an equation with its side-swapped twin (so each unordered pair of sides is counted once). For each axiom system and each k in {2, 3}, enumerate all k^(k^2) operator tables (16 and 19,683), keep those satisfying the equation for every assignment of the variables, and count the models up to isomorphism (relabelling of the k elements by any permutation): m2 and m3. Definitions: 'many forms' = m3 >= 3; 'single form' = m2 <= 1 and m3 <= 1 and m2 + m3 >= 1; 'no non-trivial form' = m2 = m3 = 0 (only the one-element model). The claim PASSES if the fraction of axiom systems with 'many forms' is >= 0.80 and the fraction with 'single form' is <= 0.05. Reported, not decisive: the same fractions restricted to n = 4; the list of 'single form' systems; the systems whose k = 2 model set is exactly {Nand, Nor} (operators 7 and 1 in Wolfram's numbering) or {Xor, Xnor} (6 and 9); and, as a validation of the model-finding code against the note 'Properties of operators from axioms' (p. 1171), the k = 2 model sets of all lhs == a systems with up to 6 operators under this canonical labelling, listing how many allow only {6, 9} and only {1, 7} (the note reports 32,004 and 964 for its family of 274,499 systems; the family definition in the note is not fully specified, so this is a plausibility check, not a decisive comparison).
test_contract.disconfirming_observation: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 50% of the axiom systems have 'many forms', or if more than 20% force a 'single form'. Between those bounds and the pass thresholds the verdict is 'mixed'. If the enumeration cannot be completed for k = 3 within the run-time budget the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).
test_contract.inference_method: analysis.py enumerates all binary-tree term shapes with up to 4 operator occurrences split between the two sides, labels variables canonically (restricted-growth strings over the leaves of lhs then rhs), drops lhs == rhs and side-swapped duplicates (4692 systems), and for k = 2 and 3 evaluates every one of the 16 and 19,683 operator tables on every variable assignment with numpy, keeping the models and counting isomorphism classes via the canonical (minimal) table number over all permutations of the k elements. Validation family (lhs == a, up to 6 operators, k = 2 only) and the supplementary runs S1 (Wolfram's lhs == a family over {a, b} with up to 3 operators, k = 2, 3 exact plus a capped 4-element search) and S2 (capped 4-element search for the 2792 main-family systems not already 'many forms' at k = 3; --k4 flag, about 25 minutes) are described in interpretation and caveats. Default run about 2 minutes; derived/axioms.csv.gz (gzip, without the k2 model-set column) and derived/supplementary.json are from the --k4 run.

claims.label: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
claims.statement: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.
claims.quote: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

test_contract.expected_observation: Pre-registered. Enumerate all Nand expression trees X with k Nands (k+1 leaves) over variables a, b, c and consider (I) single axioms {X = a} for k <= 6 (34488 systems for k <= 5, 288684 for k = 6, plus the 16896 two-variable systems for k = 6) and (II) two-axiom systems {X = a, a.b = b.a} with k = 4 (3402 systems, 6 Nands in total). Screen each system against all 16 binary operations on {0,1}, all 19683 on {0,1,2} and, by backtracking search, all operations on {0,1,2,3}; a system 'works up to n values' if its models on each domain of size <= n are exactly the operation tables isomorphic to the Nand (or, on 2 elements, Nand or Nor) of a Boolean algebra of that size, i.e. {Nand, Nor} on 2, none on 3, the 12 tables isomorphic to Nand_4 on 4. PASS (supports) if (a) the published axiom works up to 4 values; (b) no single axiom {X = a} with k <= 5 over <= 3 variables works up to 3 values; (c) at least one system of family (II) works up to 4 values, and the number of systems of forms (I) and (II) with at most 6 Nands in total that precede it in the enumeration (fewer Nands first) is below 10000. The book's counts (0 of 16896 two-variable six-Nand systems up to 3 values; 296 of 288684 up to 3 values and 100 up to 4 values; 32 of 3402 in family II) are recorded as cross-checks and do not decide the verdict. If the 4-value search over all 3-value survivors of (I) exceeds 20 minutes it is applied only to the published axiom and to family (II), and the 100-count cross-check is dropped and reported.
