claims.statement: The camel carries its young for twelve months and never bears more than one at a time.
claims.quote: Its period of gestation is twelve months; and it is never delivered of more than one foal at a time.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 14

claims.label: Elephant gestation lasts two years with a single calf
claims.statement: The female elephant carries her young for two years and bears only one at a time.
claims.quote: The period of gestation with the female is two years; and only one young animal is produced at a time, in other words it is uniparous.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 14

claims.label: The murex lives about six years, with yearly growth marked on its shell
claims.statement: The purple murex lives about six years, and each year's growth is marked by a distinct interval in the spiral of its shell.
claims.quote: The murex lives for about six years; and the yearly increase is indicated by a distinct interval in the spiral convolution of the shell.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 15

claims.label: The pinna dies if deprived of its pinna-guard crab or shrimp
claims.statement: The pinna (fan mussel) houses a small shrimp or crab, the pinna-guard, and if it loses this companion it soon dies.
claims.quote: these creatures have inside them a parasite nicknamed the pinna-guard, in some cases a small carid and in other cases a little crab; if the pinna be deprived of this pinna-guard it soon dies
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 15

claims.label: All testaceans are spontaneously generated in mud, according to the material
claims.statement: As a general rule all testaceans (shelled molluscs and the like) arise by spontaneous generation in mud, and differ according to the material: oysters in slime, cockles on sandy bottoms, ascidians, barnacles and limpets in rock hollows.
claims.quote: As a general rule, then, all testaceans grow by spontaneous generation in mud, differing from one another according to the differences of the material
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 15

claims.label: Eggs of crustaceans, molluscs and oviparous fishes grow after laying
claims.statement: In crustaceans, molluscs and oviparous fishes the egg continues to grow after it has been laid.
claims.quote: This same phenomenon is observable in molluscs also, and in such fishes as are oviparous; for in all these cases the egg continues to grow.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 17

claims.label: Squid, cuttlefish and octopus rarely live beyond a year
claims.statement: The squid and the cuttlefish are short-lived and with few exceptions do not live out a year, and the same is true of the octopus.
claims.quote: The calamary and the cuttle-fish are short-lived, as, with few exceptions, they never see the year out; and the same statement is applicable to the octopus.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 18

claims.label: The whole insect grub develops into the animal, not part of it
claims.statement: All insects produce grubs (except one kind of butterfly that lays a hard egg), and the young insect develops from the whole grub, not from a part of it as an animal develops from part of an egg.
claims.quote: But from the grub, the young animal does not grow out of a mere portion of it, as a young animal grows from a portion only of an egg, but the grub entire grows and the animal becomes differentiated out of it.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 19

claims.label: Intestinal worms do not reproduce their kind
claims.statement: Intestinal worms, of which there are three kinds (flat-worm, round-worm and ascarid), never propagate their kind, although the flat-worm lays something like a melon seed.
claims.quote: These intestinal worms do not in any case propagate their kind.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 19

claims.label: Caterpillars feed and excrete; chrysalises do neither
claims.statement: The butterfly caterpillar feeds and voids excrement, but once it becomes a chrysalis it neither feeds nor voids excrement; the same holds for all insects that develop from a grub, such as bees and wasps.
claims.quote: At first, when it is a caterpillar, it feeds and ejects excrement; but when it turns into the chrysalis it neither feeds nor ejects excrement.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 19

claims.label: Generation of grubs is due primarily to the sun's heat or wind
claims.statement: In all grubs and all animals that emerge from the grub state, generation is caused primarily by the heat of the sun or by wind.
claims.quote: With all grubs and all animals that break out from the grub state, generation is due primarily to the heat of the sun or to wind.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 19

claims.label: A winged animal in Cyprus is generated in copper-smelting fires
claims.statement: In Cyprus, where copper ore is smelted, a winged animal somewhat larger than a bluebottle fly is generated in the fire, can hop or crawl through it, and perishes when kept away from the fire.
claims.quote: In Cyprus, in places where copper-ore is smelted, with heaps of the ore piled on day after day, an animal is engendered in the fire, somewhat larger than a blue bottle fly, furnished with wings, which can hop or crawl through the fire.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 19

claims.label: Ichneumon wasps provision mud-sealed holes with dead spiders
claims.statement: The wasps called ichneumons, smaller than ordinary wasps, kill spiders, carry them to a hole in a wall, seal it with mud and lay their grubs inside, and from the grubs come new ichneumons.
claims.quote: kill spiders and carry off the dead bodies to a wall or some such place with a hole in it; this hole they smear over with mud and lay their grubs inside it, and from the grubs come the hunter-wasps
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 20

claims.label: Bees make wax from flowers but gather honey from the air
claims.statement: The bee makes wax from flowers but does not make honey; it merely gathers honey that is deposited out of the atmosphere as dew.
claims.quote: The bee, then, makes the wax from flowers. The honey, however, it does not make, but merely gathers what is deposited out of the atmosphere
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 22

claims.label: A bee lives six years, at most seven
claims.statement: The bee lives six years as a rule and seven at most.
claims.quote: The bee lives for six years as a rule, as an exception for seven years.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 22

claims.label: Young scorpions and spiders kill their parent after hatching
claims.statement: When the land-scorpion's brood has hatched, the young eject and kill the parent, as also happens with the spider.
claims.quote: When the hatching is completed, the parent animal, as happens with the parent spider, is ejected and put to death by the young ones
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 26

claims.label: Grasshoppers lay eggs at summer's end and then die
claims.statement: The grasshopper lays its eggs at the close of summer and dies after laying them, the males dying about the same time.
claims.quote: The grasshopper lays its eggs at the close of summer, and dies after laying them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 28

claims.label: Only male cicadas sing
claims.statement: In both the large and small cicadas it is the male that sings and the female is silent.
claims.quote: In both species, the larger and the smaller, it is the male that sings, and the female that is unvocal.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 30

claims.label: Lice, fleas and bugs produce nits that generate nothing
claims.statement: Insects that live on the juices of living flesh, such as lice, fleas and bugs, all produce nits, and these nits produce nothing further.
claims.quote: all, without exception, generate what are called 'nits', and these nits generate nothing
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 31

claims.label: The ass alone among hairy animals has neither lice nor ticks
claims.statement: All feathered and hair-coated animals are infested with lice, with the single exception of the ass, which has neither lice nor ticks.
claims.quote: All other winged animals that are furnished with feathers are similarly infested, and all hair-coated creatures also, with the single exception of the ass, which is infested neither with lice nor with ticks.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 31

claims.label: Fig-wasps from wild figs enter cultivated figs and keep them from dropping
claims.statement: The fig-wasp develops in the fruit of the wild fig, then flies into the fruit of the cultivated fig through its opening and makes the fruit stay on the tree, which is why farmers hang wild figs on fig trees.
claims.quote: the psen leaves the husk behind it and flies away, and enters into the fruit of the fig-tree through its orifice, and causes the fruit not to drop off
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 32

claims.label: The viper is internally oviparous and externally viviparous
claims.statement: The viper produces eggs internally but gives birth to live young, all in one day, about twenty in number and one at a time, whereas other serpents lay eggs.
claims.quote: the viper is externally viviparous, having been previously oviparous internally
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book V, Part 34

claims.label: Birds of prey lay few eggs, the kestrel excepted
claims.statement: All birds of prey (birds with crooked talons) are unprolific, except the kestrel, which is the most prolific of them and lays four or occasionally more eggs.
claims.quote: All birds of prey, or birds with crooked talons, are unprolific, except the kestrel: this bird is the most prolific of birds of prey; as many as four eggs have been observed in the nest, and occasionally it lays even more.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 1

claims.label: Waterbird eggs have more yolk and less white than landbird eggs
claims.statement: The eggs of birds that frequent rivers and marshes have proportionally more yolk and less white than the eggs of land birds.
claims.quote: the eggs of waterbirds have comparatively more of the yellow or yolk and less of the white
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 2

claims.label: Long pointed eggs hatch females, rounded eggs hatch males
claims.statement: Long, pointed eggs produce females, while round eggs, or eggs more rounded at the narrow end, produce males.
claims.quote: Long and pointed eggs are female; those that are round, or more rounded at the narrow end, are male.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 2

claims.label: Hens and geese lay wind-eggs without ever copulating
claims.statement: Wind-eggs (infertile eggs) are not residues of earlier copulation: hens and geese that have never copulated lay them.
claims.quote: we have cases well authenticated where chickens of the common hen and goose have laid wind-eggs without ever having been subjected to copulation
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 2

claims.label: Egg and incubation periods in birds increase with body size
claims.statement: The time for an egg to form after copulation and for the chick to hatch differs between birds according to the size of the parents.
claims.quote: The generation of the egg after copulation and the generation of the chick from the subsequent hatching of the egg are not brought about within equal periods for all birds, but differ as to time according to the size of the parent-birds.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 2

claims.label: The heart is the first organ, a beating speck of blood
claims.statement: The heart appears in the developing egg as a speck of blood that beats and moves as though alive, and two blood vessels lead from it.
claims.quote: and the heart appears, like a speck of blood, in the white of the egg. This point beats and moves as though endowed with life, and from it two vein-ducts with blood in them trend in a convoluted course
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 3

claims.label: The chick forms from the white and is nourished by the yolk
claims.statement: The principle of life of the chick lies in the white of the egg, while its nutriment comes from the yolk through a navel-string.
claims.quote: The life-element of the chick is in the white of the egg, and the nutriment comes through the navel-string out of the yolk.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 3

claims.label: Very few birds breed in their first year
claims.statement: Very few birds breed within their first year.
claims.quote: Very few birds propagate within their first year.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 4

claims.label: Blinded swallow chicks recover their sight
claims.statement: If the eyes of young swallow chicks are pricked out, the birds recover and later see again.
claims.quote: If you prick out the eyes of swallow chicks while they are yet young, the birds will get well again and will see by and by.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 5

claims.label: The eagle usually rears two young and expels one from the nest
claims.statement: The eagle usually lays three eggs and hatches two (occasionally three), and as the young grow the mother, wearied of feeding them, expels one from the nest; she broods for about thirty days.
claims.quote: This is the case in most instances, though occasionally a brood of three has been observed. As the young ones grow, the mother becomes wearied with feeding them and extrudes one of the pair from the nest.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 6

claims.label: The cuckoo is not a transformed hawk
claims.statement: The cuckoo is not a transformed hawk: it lacks the hawk's crooked talons, resembles the pigeon in head and claws, and is preyed on by hawks, which never happens between birds of one kind.
claims.quote: The cuckoo has been seen to be preyed on by the hawk; and this never happens between birds of the same species.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 7

claims.label: The cuckoo builds no nest and lays in other birds' nests
claims.statement: The cuckoo builds no nest but lays its egg, usually one, in the nest of a smaller bird, after devouring that bird's eggs, and the host bird hatches and rears the young cuckoo.
claims.quote: The bird eggs, but does not build a nest. Sometimes it lays its eggs in the nest of a smaller bird after first devouring the eggs of this bird
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 7

claims.label: Bird testes enlarge in the breeding season, most in salacious birds
claims.statement: In male birds the testicles are visibly larger at pairing time than at other times, most conspicuously in the more salacious birds such as the cock and the cock partridge.
claims.quote: With male birds about pairing time the testicles are obviously larger than at other times, and this is conspicuously the case with the more salacious birds, such as the barn-door cock and the cock partridge
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 9

claims.label: Cartilaginous fishes are viviparous after internal eggs
claims.statement: Cartilaginous fishes (selachians) are viviparous and all other fishes are oviparous; selachians first produce eggs internally and then bear live young, the fishing-frog excepted.
claims.quote: Fishes of the cartilaginous genus are viviparous; the rest are oviparous. And cartilaginous fishes are first oviparous internally and subsequently viviparous; they rear the embryos internally, the batrachus or fishing-frog being an exception.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 10

claims.label: The smooth shark's embryo is nourished by a cord attached to the womb
claims.statement: In the smooth shark the young develop with a navel-string attached to the womb, so that once the yolk is used up the embryo is sustained as in quadrupeds, with a chorion and membranes.
claims.quote: the young develop with the navel-string attached to the womb, so that, as the egg-substance gets used up, the embryo is sustained to all appearance just as in the case of quadrupeds
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 10

claims.label: Selachians come inshore to give birth, for warmth and protection
claims.statement: Cartilaginous fishes move from the open and deep sea towards the shore to bear their young, for the sake of warmth and of protection for the young.
claims.quote: Cartilaginous fishes come out from the main seas and deep waters towards the shore and there bring forth their young, and they do so for the sake of warmth and by way of protection for their young.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 11

claims.label: Fishes of different kinds do not interbreed
claims.statement: As a general rule no kind of fish pairs with another kind.
claims.quote: Observations would lead to the general rule that no one variety of fish pairs with another variety.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 11

claims.label: All cetaceans are viviparous, never carrying eggs
claims.statement: The dolphin, the whale and all other cetaceans (animals with a blow-hole instead of gills) are viviparous, carrying an embryo rather than eggs, as do humans and viviparous quadrupeds.
claims.quote: The dolphin, the whale, and all the rest of the Cetacea, all, that is to say, that are provided with a blow-hole instead of gills, are viviparous.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 12

claims.label: Dolphins and porpoises suckle their young
claims.statement: The dolphin and the porpoise have milk and suckle their young.
claims.quote: The dolphin and the porpoise are provided with milk, and suckle their young.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 12

claims.label: All scaly fishes are oviparous
claims.statement: All scaly fishes are oviparous, as are all smooth or slippery fishes except the eel.
claims.quote: all scaly fish are oviparous, as the basse, the mullet, the grey mullet, and the etelis, and all the so-called white-fish, and all the smooth or slippery fish except the eel
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 13

claims.label: Erythrinus and channa are always caught full of eggs
claims.statement: Fishes are mostly divided into males and females, but specimens of the erythrinus and the channa are never caught except full of eggs.
claims.quote: Fishes for the most part are divided into males and females, but one is puzzled to account for the erythrinus and the channa, for specimens of these species are never caught except in a condition of pregnancy.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 13

claims.label: Only fish eggs sprinkled with milt after laying develop
claims.statement: In oviparous fishes the female lays her eggs and the male then sheds milt over them; only the eggs so sprinkled produce young, the rest being lost.
claims.quote: The greater number of these eggs so deposited are not productive, but only those over which the male sheds the milt or sperm; for when the female has laid her eggs, the male follows and sheds its sperm over them
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 13

claims.label: Fishes spawn inshore for warmth, food and protection from predators
claims.statement: Fishes in general lay their eggs close to shore, because inshore water is warmer, richer in food, and protects the spawn from larger fishes.
claims.quote: for the water close in to shore is warm and is better supplied with food than the outer sea, and serves as a protection to the spawn against the voracity of the larger fish
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 13

claims.label: In fish embryos the large eyes are the first organs visible
claims.statement: In oviparous fishes the embryo forms at the upper end of the egg within a membrane and its large spherical eyes are the first organs visible, so fishes do not develop like grubs, which form the lower end first.
claims.quote: the embryo comes at the upper end of the egg and is enveloped in a membrane, and the eyes, large and spherical, are the first organs visible
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 13

claims.label: The male sheat-fish guards the spawn for forty to fifty days
claims.statement: In the sheat-fish the eggs develop exceptionally slowly and the male guards the spawn for forty or fifty days against small fishes, while the female leaves after spawning.
claims.quote: In the case of the sheat-fish the growth from the egg is exceptionally slow, and, in consequence, the male has to keep watch for forty or fifty days to prevent the-spawn being devoured by such little fishes as chance to come by.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 14

claims.label: Eels go down from rivers to the sea while mullet go up
claims.statement: The mullet migrates up from the sea into marshes and rivers, while eels migrate down from marshes and rivers to the sea.
claims.quote: The mullet goes up from the sea to marshes and rivers; the eels, on the contrary, make their way down from the marshes and rivers to the sea.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 14

claims.label: Some fishes arise spontaneously from mud and sand
claims.statement: Certain fishes come into existence spontaneously, not from eggs or copulation, arising from mud or from sand and decaying matter; such fry cannot grow or reproduce.
claims.quote: From the facts above enumerated it is quite proved that certain fishes come spontaneously into existence, not being derived from eggs or from copulation.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 15

claims.label: Eels have no milt, spawn or reproductive passages
claims.statement: Eels are neither born from pairing nor oviparous: no eel has ever been found with milt or spawn, nor with passages for spawn or eggs.
claims.quote: nor was an eel ever found supplied with either milt or spawn, nor are they when cut open found to have within them passages for spawn or for eggs
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 16

claims.label: Eels arise from 'earth's guts' in mud and wet ground
claims.statement: Eels arise from the so-called 'earth's guts', worms that grow spontaneously in mud and humid ground where sun heat causes putrefaction.
claims.quote: Eels are derived from the so-called 'earth's guts' that grow spontaneously in mud and in humid ground
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 16

claims.label: Fish gestation always lasts a number of days divisible by seven
claims.statement: In fishes gestation lasts thirty days or less, but always a number of days divisible by seven.
claims.quote: With some fishes the time of gestation is not longer than thirty days, with others it is a lesser period; but with all it extends over a number of days divisible by seven.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 17

claims.label: Viviparous selachians are less fecund but their young survive better
claims.statement: Cartilaginous fishes as a rule are less prolific than other fishes because they are viviparous, and their young, being large, have a better chance of escaping destruction.
claims.quote: As a rule, cartilaginous fish are less prolific than other fish owing to their being viviparous; and their young by reason of their size have a better chance of escaping destruction.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 17

claims.label: Females are fiercest after giving birth, males in the rut
claims.statement: Female animals are most bad-tempered just after giving birth and males during the pairing season.
claims.quote: The female is most cross-tempered just after parturition, the male during the time of pairing
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 18

claims.label: Breeding seasons are timed so the young are reared at a good season
claims.statement: Sexual appetite is keenest in spring, but the pairing season differs between animals and is adapted so that the young are reared at a convenient season.
claims.quote: In general the sexual appetites of animals are keenest in spring-time; the time of pairing, however, is not the same for all, but is adapted so as to ensure the rearing of the young at a convenient season.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 18

claims.label: North winds at mating give male lambs, south winds female
claims.statement: Sheep and goats mated when north winds blow tend to bear males, and when south winds blow, females.
claims.quote: And if they submit to the male when north winds are blowing, they are apt to bear males; if when south winds are blowing, females.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 19

claims.label: Male horses die sooner because of the cost of sexual service
claims.statement: The male horse is shorter-lived than the female because of the sexual service it renders, and stable-reared horses live longer than those reared in troops.
claims.quote: The male is less long-lived than the female by reason of the sexual service he is called on to render; and horses that are reared in a private stable live longer than such as are reared in troops.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 22

claims.label: Hybrid gestation follows the sire; the foal resembles the mother
claims.statement: In a cross between horse and ass, gestation lasts as long as it would for the sire's own species, while in size, looks and vigour the foal tends to resemble the mother more than the sire.
claims.quote: The period for gestation in the case of a cross depends on the male, and is just what it would have been if the male had had commerce with a female of his own kind. In regard to size, looks, and vigour, the foal is more apt to resemble the mother than the sire.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 23

claims.label: Female mules can conceive but never carry to birth
claims.statement: A female mule has been known to be impregnated, but without giving birth.
claims.quote: A female mule has been known to be impregnated, but without the impregnation being followed up by parturition.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 24

claims.label: Short gestation and fast growth argue against long deer lifespans
claims.statement: The short gestation and rapid growth of the fawn indicate that the deer is not extremely long-lived, contrary to fabulous stories.
claims.quote: the brevity of the period of gestation and the rapidity of growth in the fawn would not lead one to attribute extreme longevity to this creature
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 29

claims.label: Bear cubs are the smallest newborns relative to the mother
claims.statement: Of all animals the newborn bear cub is the smallest relative to its mother, larger than a mouse but smaller than a weasel, and is born hairless, blind and with its limbs and organs unformed.
claims.quote: Of all animals the newly born cub of the she bear is the smallest in proportion to the size of the mother; that is to say, it is larger than a mouse but smaller than a weasel.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 30

claims.label: Hyenas are not hermaphrodites
claims.statement: It is untrue that every hyena has the organs of both sexes: the male has a male organ like the dog's and a blind female-like part under the tail, and the female has a blind male-like part and a true female organ.
claims.quote: What is recounted concerning its genital organs, to the effect that every hyena is furnished with the organ both of the male and the female, is untrue.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 32

claims.label: Hares breed year-round, superfoetate and bear every month
claims.statement: Hares breed and bear at all seasons, superfoetate during pregnancy, bear young every month, and can conceive again immediately after giving birth while suckling.
claims.quote: They breed and bear at all seasons, superfoetate during pregnancy, and bear young every month.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 33

claims.label: Mice are the most prolific animals in litter size and frequency
claims.statement: The mouse is the most astonishing of animals in generation, both for the number of its young and for how quickly births recur.
claims.quote: The phenomena of generation in regard to the mouse are the most astonishing both for the number of the young and for the rapidity of recurrence in the births.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VI, Part 37

claims.label: Male puberty begins at about fourteen with seed and pubic hair
claims.statement: In most cases a boy begins to produce seed at about fourteen years of age, and pubic hair appears at the same time.
claims.quote: When twice seven years old, in the most of cases, the male begins to engender seed; and at the same time hair appears upon the pubes
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 1

claims.label: Menstruation and breast growth begin at about fourteen in girls
claims.statement: In girls, at about fourteen years of age (the same age as male puberty), the breasts swell and menstruation begins.
claims.quote: At the same age in the female, the breasts swell and the so-called catamenia commence to flow
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 1

claims.label: Semen is infertile until twenty-one and young parents have small, imperfect offspring
claims.statement: Until about the age of twenty-one a man's seed is infertile; after that it becomes fertile, but very young men and women produce undersized and imperfect offspring, as do young animals generally.
claims.quote: At the outset and till the age of one and twenty the spermatic discharge is devoid of fecundity; afterwards it becomes fertile, but young men and women produce undersized and imperfect progeny, as is the case also with the common run of animals.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 1

claims.label: Thick, granular semen tends to produce males and thin semen females
claims.statement: Thin seed is infertile; granular seed is fertile and likely to produce male children, while thin, unclotted seed tends to produce female children.
claims.quote: When the spermatic fluid is of a thin consistency it is infertile; when granular it is fertile and likely to produce male children, but when thin and unclotted it is apt to produce female offspring.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 1

claims.label: In non-viviparous animals the menstrual residue becomes body, scales and feathers
claims.statement: Animals that do not bear live young have no menstrual discharge, because the corresponding residue is turned into bodily substance, scutes, scales or feathers; in viviparous quadrupeds it becomes hair, flesh and urine, and only in women is it discharged.
claims.quote: In creatures that do not bring forth their young alive nothing of the sort manifests itself, this particular superfluity being converted into bodily substance
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 2

claims.label: A male foetus first moves at about forty days, a female at about ninety
claims.statement: A male foetus usually first moves on the right side of the womb at about the fortieth day, a female on the left side at about the ninetieth day, though there are many exceptions.
claims.quote: In the case of male children the first movement usually occurs on the right-hand side of the womb and about the fortieth day, but if the child be a female then on the left-hand side and about the ninetieth day.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 3

claims.label: An aborted male embryo at forty days is ant-sized with limbs and eyes visible
claims.statement: A male human embryo aborted at the fortieth day is about the size of a large ant, with all the limbs, the penis and the disproportionately large eyes plainly visible.
claims.quote: If the membrane be pulled to bits the embryo is revealed, as big as one of the large kind of ants; and all the limbs are plain to see, including the penis, and the eyes also, which as in other animals are of great size.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 3

claims.label: Female embryos develop more slowly in the womb than male embryos
claims.statement: In the womb a female embryo completes the development of its parts more slowly than a male, and more often than a male takes ten months to reach full term.
claims.quote: In short, while within the womb, the female infant accomplishes the whole development of its parts more slowly than the male, and more frequently than the man-child takes ten months to come to perfection.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 3

claims.label: Humans alone have a variable term of pregnancy, from seven to eleven months
claims.statement: Every other animal has a single fixed term of pregnancy, but in humans alone it varies, lasting seven, eight, nine or, most commonly, ten months, and occasionally into the eleventh.
claims.quote: But in the case of mankind alone of all animals the times are diverse; for pregnancy may be of seven months' duration, or of eight months or of nine, and still more commonly of ten months, while some few women go even into the eleventh month.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 4

claims.label: Children born before seven months never survive
claims.statement: Children born before the seventh month of pregnancy can never survive; seven-month children are the earliest viable, and most of them are weakly.
claims.quote: Children that come into the world before seven months can under no circumstances survive. The seven-months' children are the earliest that are capable of life, and most of them are weakly
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 4

claims.label: Eight-month children mostly die in Greece but survive in Egypt
claims.statement: Children born in the eighth month are reared successfully in Egypt and some other places, but in Greece only a few survive and most perish.
claims.quote: in these places the eight-months' children live and are brought up, but in Greece it is only a few of them that survive while most perish.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 4

claims.label: The most children a woman has borne at one birth is five
claims.statement: The largest number of children ever born to a woman at one birth is five, which has been observed several times.
claims.quote: The largest number ever brought forth is five, and such an occurrence has been witnessed on several occasions.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 4

claims.label: Women and mares, unlike other animals, accept the male during pregnancy
claims.statement: Of all animals the woman and the mare are most inclined to accept mating during pregnancy; all other animals avoid the male when pregnant, except those that show superfoetation, such as the hare.
claims.quote: Of all animals the woman and the mare are most inclined to receive the commerce of the male during pregnancy; while all other animals when they are pregnant avoid the male, save those in which the phenomenon of superfoetation occurs, such as the hare.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 4

claims.label: Menstruation ceases at about forty, at the latest fifty, ending childbearing
claims.statement: In most women menstruation ceases at about forty; in some it lasts until fifty, and women of that age have borne children, but none beyond it.
claims.quote: the menstrual discharges ceases in most women about their fortieth year; but with those in whom it goes on longer it lasts even to the fiftieth year, and women of that age have been known to bear children. But beyond that age there is no case on record.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 5

claims.label: Men remain fertile to sixty and sometimes seventy
claims.statement: Men in most cases remain sexually competent until sixty, and some until seventy; men have fathered children at seventy.
claims.quote: Men in most cases continue to be sexually competent until they are sixty years old, and if that limit be overpassed then until seventy years; and men have been actually known to procreate children at seventy years of age.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 6

claims.label: Children often inherit their parents' deformities and acquired marks
claims.statement: Deformed parents produce deformed children (lame from lame, blind from blind), and children often inherit their parents' peculiarities, including marks such as pimples or scars.
claims.quote: From deformed parents come deformed children, lame from lame and blind from blind, and, speaking generally, children often inherit anything that is peculiar in their parents and are born with similar marks, such as pimples or scars.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 6

claims.label: Resemblance can skip a generation and reappear in grandchildren
claims.statement: Children usually resemble their parents or ancestors, but resemblance can be passed on after several generations, appearing in a grandchild but not in the child.
claims.quote: While children mostly resemble their parents or their ancestors, it sometimes happens that no such resemblance is to be traced. But parents may pass on resemblance after several generations
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 6

claims.label: All animals develop in the same way, differing in where the navel attaches
claims.statement: All animals, whether flying, swimming or walking, viviparous or oviparous, develop in the same way, except that in viviparous animals the navel is attached to the womb, in others to the egg, and in certain fishes to both.
claims.quote: All animals whatsoever, whether they fly or swim or walk upon dry land, whether they bring forth their young alive or in the egg, develop in the same way: save only that some have the navel attached to the womb, namely the viviparous animals, and some have it attached to the egg, and some to both parts alike, as in a certain sort of fishes.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 7

claims.label: All animals are born head first in the natural course
claims.statement: All animals are at first head-upward in the womb but turn downward near term, and in the natural course birth in all animals is head first.
claims.quote: birth in the natural course of things takes place in all animals head foremost
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 8

claims.label: The navel-string has four vessels in oxen, two in smaller animals, one in fowls
claims.statement: The navel-string contains four blood vessels in large animals such as oxen, two in smaller animals, and only one in very small ones such as fowls.
claims.quote: In the larger animals, such as the embryos of oxen, the vessels are four in number, and in smaller animals two; in the very little ones, such as fowls, one vessel only.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 8

claims.label: Children cut their first teeth in the seventh month, front teeth first
claims.statement: Children begin cutting teeth in the seventh month, the front teeth first, upper or lower; teeth come sooner the warmer the nurse's milk.
claims.quote: children begin to cut their teeth in the seventh month; and the front teeth are the first to come through, sometimes the upper and sometimes the lower ones.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 10

claims.label: Menstruation is suppressed while milk flows
claims.statement: As a general rule menstruation does not occur while a woman is producing milk, because moisture is not directed in several directions at once.
claims.quote: So long as there is a flow of milk the menstrual purgations do not take place, at least as a general rule, though the discharge has been known to occur during the period of suckling.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VII, Part 11

claims.label: Most animals show traces of the psychical qualities found in man
claims.statement: Most animals show traces of psychical qualities such as gentleness, fierceness, courage, timidity and something like sagacity, which differ from man's either in degree or by analogy.
claims.quote: In the great majority of animals there are traces of psychical qualities or attitudes, which qualities are more markedly differentiated in the case of human beings.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 1

claims.label: Nature passes by degrees from lifeless things to animals with no sharp boundary
claims.statement: Nature proceeds little by little from lifeless things through plants to animals, so that no exact boundary can be drawn and intermediate forms cannot be assigned to one side or the other.
claims.quote: Nature proceeds little by little from things lifeless to animal life in such a way that it is impossible to determine the exact line of demarcation, nor on which side thereof an intermediate form should lie.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 1

claims.label: More intelligent animals with memory stay longer with their young
claims.statement: Some animals simply breed at definite seasons, others also feed their young and then leave them, while the more intelligent animals with memory live with their offspring for longer and more socially.
claims.quote: other animals are more intelligent and endowed with memory, and they live with their offspring for a longer period and on a more social footing.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 1

claims.label: Air-breathing aquatic animals drown unless they surface to breathe
claims.statement: Some air-breathing animals that live in water, such as the sea-turtle, crocodile, hippopotamus, seal, freshwater tortoise and frog, choke or drown unless they breathe air from time to time, and they breed on or near land.
claims.quote: now all these animals choke or drown if they do not from time to time breathe atmospheric air: they breed and rear their young on dry land, or near the land, but they pass their lives in water.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: The dolphin breathes air with lungs and suffocates when caught in nets
claims.statement: The dolphin breathes air into lungs, suffocates quickly when caught in nets, can live a considerable time out of water, and sleeps with its nose above water in order to breathe.
claims.quote: he also inhales air into his lungs; for, by the way, the creature is furnished with this organ and respires thereby, and accordingly, when caught in the nets, he is quickly suffocated for lack of air.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: Aquatic animals take in water to cool the blood, as land animals take in air
claims.statement: Some aquatic animals take in water and discharge it for the same reason that air-breathers inhale air, to cool the blood; blooded animals that do this have gills, while those that take in water while catching prey have a blow-hole.
claims.quote: some aquatic animals take in water and discharge it again, for the same reason that leads air-breathing animals to inhale air: in other words, with the object of cooling the blood.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: The cordylus (water-newt) has gills instead of lungs yet walks on land
claims.statement: The cordylus or water-newt is the only known animal that takes in water through gills, having no lungs, yet is a four-footed animal that walks on land and gets its living there.
claims.quote: this creature is furnished not with lungs but with gills, but for all that it is a quadruped and fitted for walking on dry land.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: A small change in a minute organ can change an animal's whole form
claims.statement: A change in a minute organ can cause an immense change in an animal's overall form; castration, mutilating one small organ, turns a male towards the female form, and a slight change in size of an essential organ in the embryo decides whether it becomes male or female.
claims.quote: The fact is that animals, if they be subjected to a modification in minute organs, are liable to immense modifications in their general configuration. This phenomenon may be observed in the case of gelded animals: only a minute organ of the animal is mutilated, and the creature passes from the male to the female form.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: An empty wax vessel lowered into the sea fills with fresh water within a day
claims.statement: Sea water contains fresh water that can be strained from it: an empty thin vessel of moulded wax let down into the sea will within twenty-four hours contain fresh, drinkable water.
claims.quote: Take a thin vessel of moulded wax, attach a cord to it, and let it down quite empty into the sea: in twenty-four hours it will be found to contain a quantity of water, and the water will be fresh and drinkable.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: All fishes eat their own species except the mullet
claims.statement: All fishes eat members of their own species, with the single exception of the mullet; the conger is especially given to it.
claims.quote: All fishes devour their own species, with the single exception of the cestreus or mullet; and the conger is especially ravenous in this respect.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: Fishes have the stomach next to the mouth and no gullet
claims.statement: Fishes have their stomachs close to the mouth and have no gullet, which is why some cast up their stomachs while chasing prey.
claims.quote: fishes have their stomachs close to the mouth, and are not furnished with a gullet.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: The parrot-fish is the only fish that chews the cud
claims.statement: Of all fishes the scarus (parrot-fish) is the only one known to chew the cud like a quadruped.
claims.quote: Of all fishes the so-called scarus, or parrot, wrasse, is the only one known to chew the cud like a quadruped.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: Eels can live seven or eight years
claims.statement: The eel lives in some cases for seven or eight years.
claims.quote: The eel in some cases lives for seven or eight years.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 2

claims.label: Birds with crooked talons are all carnivorous and cannot swallow grain
claims.statement: Birds with crooked talons are carnivorous without exception and cannot swallow grain or bread even if it is put into their bills.
claims.quote: Of birds, such as have crooked talons are carnivorous without exception, and cannot swallow corn or bread-food even if it be put into their bills in tit-bits
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 3

claims.label: Birds of prey almost never drink
claims.statement: Birds as a rule drink very little, and birds of prey never drink at all apart from a very few that drink very rarely, such as the kestrel and the kite.
claims.quote: In fact birds of prey never drink at all, excepting a very few, and these drink very rarely
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 3

claims.label: Oviparous animals have a spongy, bloodless lung and drink little
claims.statement: Scaly (tessellated) animals are spare drinkers, as are all animals with a spongy lung, and such a lung, poorly supplied with blood, is found in all oviparous animals.
claims.quote: Tessellated animals are spare drinkers, as are also all such animals as have a spongy lung, and such a lung, scantily supplied with blood, is found in all oviparous animals.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 4

claims.label: Carnivores eat grass only when sick, to purge themselves
claims.statement: Fierce, jag-toothed viviparous quadrupeds are all carnivorous and never eat grass except when sick, as dogs eat grass to make themselves vomit.
claims.quote: These carnivorous animals never eat grass except when they are sick, just as dogs bring on a vomit by eating grass and thereby purge themselves.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 5

claims.label: A pig's carcass weighs five-sixths of its live weight
claims.statement: A pig fattens faster for its size than any other animal, and after slaughter its flesh weighs five-sixths of its live weight, the hair, blood and the rest making up the other sixth.
claims.quote: If a pig be weighed when living, you may calculate that after death its flesh will weigh five-sixths of that weight, and the hair, the blood, and the rest will weigh the other sixth.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 6

claims.label: Camels live about thirty years and occasionally to a hundred
claims.statement: Camels live for about thirty years; some live much longer, and some have been known to reach a hundred.
claims.quote: Camels live for about thirty years; in some exceptional cases they live much longer, and instances have been known of their living to the age of a hundred.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 9

claims.label: The bee is the only insect that always avoids rotten food
claims.statement: The bee is the only insect that invariably avoids anything rotten and touches no food without a sweet juice.
claims.quote: The bee is the only insect that invariably eschews whatever is rotten
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 11

claims.label: Cranes migrate from Scythia to the marshes at the source of the Nile
claims.statement: Cranes migrate from the steppes of Scythia to the marshlands south of Egypt where the Nile rises.
claims.quote: for these birds migrate from the steppes of Scythia to the marshlands south of Egypt where the Nile has its source.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 12

claims.label: Migrants are fatter leaving cold for warm lands than on the return
claims.statement: All animals are fatter when migrating from cold to warm regions than when migrating from warm to cold; the quail is fatter when it leaves in autumn than when it arrives in spring.
claims.quote: All creatures are fatter in migrating from cold to heat than in migrating from heat to cold; thus the quail is fatter when he emigrates in autumn than when he arrives in spring.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 12

claims.label: Birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued and mimics
claims.statement: As a general rule all birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued and given to mimicry, as is the parrot.
claims.quote: As a general rule all birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued, and disposed to mimicry.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 12

claims.label: The trichia leaves the Black Sea up the Danube into the Adriatic
claims.statement: The trichia is caught entering but never leaving the Black Sea because it alone swims north into the Danube and, where the river divides, down into the Adriatic.
claims.quote: The way of accounting for this phenomenon is that this fish, and this one only, swims northwards into the Danube, and then at the point of its bifurcation swims down southwards into the Adriatic.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 13

claims.label: Animals hide away against extreme heat as well as extreme cold
claims.statement: Animals go into concealment (dormancy) as a refuge against extreme heat as well as extreme cold; shellfish all do so, snails in winter and the purple murex and scallop in the hottest season.
claims.quote: animals go into concealment by way of refuge against extreme heat, as well as against extreme cold.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 13

claims.label: Snakes and lizards hide for four months in winter and eat nothing
claims.statement: Scaly animals such as the serpent, lizard, gecko and river crocodile go into hiding for four months in the depth of winter and eat nothing during that time.
claims.quote: all of which go into hiding for four months in the depth of winter, and during that time eat nothing.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 15

claims.label: Many birds hide in winter rather than migrate, including swallows
claims.statement: Many birds do not migrate to warmer countries but hide where they are in winter; swallows have often been found in holes without feathers, and the kite, stork, turtle-dove, lark and others go into hiding.
claims.quote: A great number of birds also go into hiding; they do not all migrate, as is generally supposed, to warmer countries.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 16

claims.label: The she-bear gives birth during winter concealment and emerges in spring
claims.statement: The she-bear gives birth while in winter concealment and stays hidden until she brings the cubs out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice; bears eat nothing while hidden.
claims.quote: The female brings forth her young at this time, and remains in concealment until it is time to bring the cubs out; and she brings them out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 17

claims.label: Crustaceans moult not once but repeatedly
claims.statement: Crabs, crawfish and lobsters slough their shells, becoming soft all over, and they do so not once for all but over and over again.
claims.quote: These animals also do not cast their skins once and for all, but over and over again.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 17

claims.label: Fishes have no pestilential diseases like those of man and livestock
claims.statement: No pestilential (epidemic) disease is known to attack fishes as such diseases attack man, horses and oxen, although individual fishes do appear to fall sick.
claims.quote: We know of no pestilential malady attacking fishes, such as those which attack man, and horses and oxen among the quadrupedal vivipara
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 19

claims.label: The purple murex dies within a day of tasting fresh water
claims.statement: Shellfish generally benefit from rain, but the purple murex is an exception: placed near a river mouth, it dies within a day of tasting fresh water.
claims.quote: if it be placed on a shore near to where a river discharges, it will die within a day after tasting the fresh water.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 20

claims.label: The pig is the only animal known to get measles
claims.statement: The pig is the only animal known to suffer from 'measles' (pimples in the flesh, seen especially under the tongue), and pigs never get it while still sucklings.
claims.quote: The pig is the only animal known to be subject to measles.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 21

claims.label: Rabies passes to every animal bitten by a mad dog except man
claims.statement: Rabies drives dogs mad and is fatal to them, and any animal bitten by a rabid dog catches it and dies, with the exception of man.
claims.quote: ary animal whatever, excepting man, will take the disease if bitten by a dog so afflicted; the disease is fatal to the dog itself, and to any animal it may bite, man excepted.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 22

claims.label: The ass tolerates cold least and is absent from Scythia
claims.statement: Of all animals of its kind the ass is least able to endure extreme cold, which is why it is not found on the shores of the Black Sea or in Scythia.
claims.quote: Of all animals on its of its kind it is the least capable of enduring extreme cold, which circumstance will account for the fact that the animal is not found on the shores of the Euxine, nor in Scythia.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 25

claims.label: All insects die when smeared with oil
claims.statement: All insects without exception die if smeared with oil, and die faster if the head is smeared and they are laid in the sun.
claims.quote: All insects, without exception, die if they be smeared over with oil; and they die all the more rapidly if you smear their head with the oil and lay them out in the sun.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 27

claims.label: The leopard is absent from Europe while lions live in part of Greece
claims.statement: Lions are more numerous in Libya and in the part of Europe between the Achelous and the Nessus rivers; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor and is not found in Europe at all.
claims.quote: lions are more numerous in Libya, and in that district of Europe that lies between the Achelous and the Nessus; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor, and is not found in Europe at all.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: Different species breed together if similar in size and gestation length
claims.statement: In Libya animals of different species meet at watering places and pair, and such pairs often breed if they are nearly the same size and have gestation periods of the same length.
claims.quote: such pairs will often breed if they be nearly of the same size and have periods of gestation of the same length.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: Wolves and dogs interbreed, and the Laconian hound is a fox–dog cross
claims.statement: Animals of different kinds produce hybrids: in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch couple and breed, and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
claims.quote: Elsewhere also bastard-animals are born to heterogeneous pairs; thus in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch will couple and breed; and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: A scaly fish's age can be told from the size and hardness of its scales
claims.statement: The age of a scaly fish can be told from the size and hardness of its scales.
claims.quote: The age of a scaly fish may be told by the size and the hardness of its scales.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 30

claims.label: Females are less spirited than males, except in the bear and leopard
claims.statement: In all animals with separate sexes the female is less spirited (less courageous) than the male, except in the bear and the leopard, where the female is the more courageous.
claims.quote: In all cases, excepting those of the bear and leopard, the female is less spirited than the male; in regard to the two exceptional cases, the superiority in courage rests with the female.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: Animals sharing a locality or food are enemies
claims.statement: Animals that live in the same localities or feed on the same food are enemies, and when food runs short animals of the same kind fight one another.
claims.quote: There is enmity between such animals as dwell in the same localities or subsist on the food. If the means of subsistence run short, creatures of like kind will fight together.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: With unlimited food, wild animals would be tame to man and each other
claims.statement: If there were no shortage of food, animals that are now wild or afraid of man would become tame towards man and peaceable towards one another, as fed animals in Egypt show.
claims.quote: One may go so far as to say that if there were no lack or stint of food, then those animals that are now afraid of man or are wild by nature would be tame and familiar with him, and in like manner with one another.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: Stag antler points increase yearly until about six years old
claims.statement: Stags grow no horns in their first year, unbranched spikes in their second, two-pointed antlers in the third and three-pointed in the fourth, increasing in complexity until about six years old, after which antlers no longer indicate age.
claims.quote: In the third year the antlers are bifurcate; in the fourth year they grow trifurcate; and so they go on increasing in complexity until the creature is six years old: after this they grow their horns without any specific differentiation, so that you cannot by observation of them tell the animal's age.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 5

claims.label: Hinds swallow the afterbirth immediately after giving birth
claims.statement: After giving birth, the hind (female deer) at once swallows the afterbirth, catching it before it falls to the ground.
claims.quote: The hinds after parturition at once swallow the afterbirth, and it is impossible to secure it, for the hind catches it before it falls to the ground
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 5

claims.label: Sick animals treat themselves, e.g. dogs eat grass to vomit
claims.statement: Many quadrupeds treat their own ailments: dogs, when ill, eat a kind of grass that makes them vomit.
claims.quote: Many other quadrupeds help themselves in clever ways. Wild goats in Crete are said, when wounded by arrows, to go in search of dittany, which is supposed to have the property of ejecting arrows in the body. Dogs, when they are ill, eat some kind of grass and produce vomiting.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 6

claims.label: The trochilus cleans the crocodile's teeth
claims.statement: When the crocodile gapes, a small bird, the trochilus, enters its mouth and cleans its teeth, feeding itself thereby, and the crocodile does not harm it.
claims.quote: When the crocodile yawns, the trochilus flies into his mouth and cleans his teeth. The trochilus gets his food thereby, and the crocodile gets ease and comfort; it makes no attempt to injure its little friend
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 6

claims.label: Pigeons pair for life
claims.statement: Pigeons pair with the same mate until one of the pair dies, though occasionally a female mates with a bird other than her mate.
claims.quote: In pairing the same male and the same female keep together; and the union is only broken by the death of one of the two parties.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 7

claims.label: Heavy-bodied birds like quails and partridges build no nests
claims.statement: Heavy-bodied birds such as quails and partridges build no nests but lay in a scraped hollow on level ground, since nest building would be of no use to birds that cannot fly well.
claims.quote: Birds of a heavy build, such as quails, partridges, and the like, build no nests; indeed, where they are incapable of flight, it would be of no use if they could do so.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 8

claims.label: Partridge hens feign lameness to lure intruders from the brood
claims.statement: When a man comes upon a partridge brood, the hen rolls in front of him pretending to be lame, drawing him away until the young have escaped, then returns and calls them back.
claims.quote: When a man comes by chance upon a young brood, and tries to catch them, the hen-bird rolls in front of the hunter, pretending to be lame: the man every moment thinks he is on the point of catching her, and so she draws him on and on, until every one of her brood has had time to escape
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 8

claims.label: Web-footed birds all live near water
claims.statement: All web-footed birds live near the sea, rivers or pools, because they resort to places suited to their structure.
claims.quote: Web-footed birds without exception live near the sea or rivers or pools, as they naturally resort to places adapted to their structure.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 12

claims.label: Swans sing chiefly as they approach death
claims.statement: Swans are musical and sing chiefly at the approach of death, flying out to sea at that time.
claims.quote: They are musical, and sing chiefly at the approach of death; at this time they fly out to sea, and men, when sailing past the coast of Libya, have fallen in with many of them out at sea singing in mournful strains
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 12

claims.label: The cuckoo lays a single egg in another bird's nest and does not hatch it
claims.statement: The cuckoo builds no nest, lays only one egg in the nest of another bird, and leaves the foster mother to hatch and rear it.
claims.quote: it lays only one egg and does not hatch it itself, but the mother-bird in whose nest it has deposited it hatches and rears it
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 29

claims.label: Cuckoos lay in others' nests because of their own cowardice
claims.statement: The cuckoo places its young in another bird's nest because it is the most cowardly of birds and could not defend its young in an emergency.
claims.quote: The cuckoo shows great sagacity in the disposal of its progeny; the fact is, the mother cuckoo is quite conscious of her own cowardice and of the fact that she could never help her young one in an emergency
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 29

claims.label: A pair of eagles needs a large territory and drives other birds away
claims.statement: A pair of eagles needs an extensive area to maintain itself, so it expels its fledged young from the neighbourhood and does not allow other birds to settle nearby.
claims.quote: The fact is that a pair of eagles demands an extensive space for its maintenance, and consequently cannot allow other birds to quarter themselves in close neighbourhood.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 32

claims.label: The sea-eagle makes its young stare at the sun and kills those that cannot
claims.statement: Before its young are fledged the sea-eagle makes them stare at the sun, beats any that refuse, and kills one whose eyes water.
claims.quote: the sea-eagle is very keen-sighted, and before its young are fledged tries to make them stare at the sun, and beats the one that refuses to do so, and twists him back in the sun's direction; and if one of them gets watery eyes in the process, it kills him, and rears the other.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 34

claims.label: The fishing-frog lures prey with filaments in front of its eyes
claims.statement: The fishing-frog (angler) has long thin filaments with rounded tips in front of its eyes which it raises as bait while hidden in sand and mud, drawing small fish that touch them into its mouth.
claims.quote: The fishing-frog has a set of filaments that project in front of its eyes; they are long and thin like hairs, and are round at the tips; they lie on either side, and are used as baits.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The torpedo stuns its prey with a shock from its body
claims.statement: The torpedo (electric ray) catches its prey by numbing it with a shock residing in its body, and can numb humans too.
claims.quote: The torpedo narcotizes the creatures that it wants to catch, overpowering them by the power of shock that is resident in its body, and feeds upon them
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The male sheat-fish guards the spawn for forty to fifty days
claims.statement: In the sheat-fish the female leaves after spawning while the male guards the spawn and fry, driving off small fish, for forty or fifty days until the young can escape on their own.
claims.quote: contenting himself with keeping off all other little fishes that might steal the spawn or fry, and this he does for forty or fifty days, until the young are sufficiently grown to make away from the other fishes for themselves.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: All fish are carnivorous except a few, and carnivorous fish wander most
claims.statement: All fish are carnivorous except a few such as the grey mullet, the saupe, the red mullet and the chalcis, and the carnivorous fish wander most.
claims.quote: Carnivorous fish wander most; and all fish are carnivorous with the exception of a few, such as the mullet, the saupe, the red mullet, and the chalcis.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: Only the sepia uses its ink for concealment; octopus and squid ink from fear
claims.statement: Among cephalopods the sepia (cuttlefish) alone discharges its ink for concealment as well as from fear, while the octopus and calamary (squid) discharge it only from fear.
claims.quote: Of molluscs the sepia is the most cunning, and is the only species that employs its dark liquid for the sake of concealment as well as from fear: the octopus and calamary make the discharge solely from fear.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The octopus changes colour to match nearby stones
claims.statement: The octopus hunts by changing its colour to match the adjacent stones, and does so also when alarmed.
claims.quote: It seeks its prey by so changing its colour as to render it like the colour of the stones adjacent to it; it does so also when alarmed.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The octopus as a rule does not live beyond one year
claims.statement: The octopus as a rule does not live a full year, and after spawning the female in particular becomes weak, stupid and wastes away.
claims.quote: The octopus as a rule does not live the year out.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The argonaut uses its web as a sail and arms as oars
claims.statement: The nautilus (argonaut) rises to the surface and, when a breeze blows, uses a thin web between its arms as a sail and lets down some arms as rudder-oars.
claims.quote: It uses this structure, when a breeze is blowing, for a sail, and lets down some of its feelers alongside as rudder-oars.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: Spiders spin from the surface of the body, not from an excretion
claims.statement: Spiders can spin from birth, and their thread comes off the body like bark rather than from inside as a superfluity or excretion, contrary to Democritus.
claims.quote: Spiders can spin webs from the time of their birth, not from their interior as a superfluity or excretion, as Democritus avers, but off their body as a kind of tree-bark
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 39

claims.label: On each trip a bee visits flowers of only one kind
claims.statement: On each foraging trip a bee goes from flower to flower of one kind only and does not visit another kind until it has returned to the hive.
claims.quote: On each expedition the bee does not fly from a flower of one kind to a flower of another, but flies from one violet, say, to another violet, and never meddles with another flower until it has got back to the hive
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Bees kill most of their kings to prevent the hive splitting
claims.statement: Worker bees kill most of their kings, especially inferior ones, to prevent a multiplicity of kings from splitting the hive, and destroy royal cells when no swarm is intended.
claims.quote: These bees also kill without mercy most of their kings, and especially kings of the inferior sort; and this they do for fear a multiplicity of kings should lead to a dismemberment of the hive.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: A bee that stings dies because it loses its gut with the sting
claims.statement: A bee that stings dies because it cannot withdraw its sting without tearing out its intestines; once it loses its sting it must die.
claims.quote: Bees that sting die from their inability to extract the sting without at the same time extracting their intestines.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Older bees work indoors, younger bees forage outside
claims.statement: Older bees do the work inside the hive and are rough and hairy from staying indoors, while young bees do the carrying outside and are comparatively smooth.
claims.quote: The elder bees do the indoor work, and are rough and hairy from staying indoors; the young bees do the outer carrying, and are comparatively smooth.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Bees carry a stone as ballast in high wind
claims.statement: In a high wind bees carry a stone as ballast to steady their flight.
claims.quote: In a high wind they carry a stone by way of ballast to steady them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Worker wasps all die in winter; only the mother-wasps overwinter
claims.statement: Worker wasps do not survive into a second year but all die as winter comes on, while the larger mother-wasps survive the winter in holes underground.
claims.quote: The workers do not live over into a second year, but all die when winter comes on; and this can be proved, for at the commencement of winter the workers become drowsy, and about the time of the winter solstice they are never seen at all.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 41

claims.label: Lions attack humans when old and their teeth are diseased
claims.statement: Lions invade cattle-folds and attack humans when old age and diseased teeth prevent them from catching their usual prey.
claims.quote: They invade the cattle-folds and attack human beings when they are grown old and so by reason of old age and the diseased condition of their teeth are unable to pursue their wonted prey.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 44

claims.label: The elephant breathes through its trunk to cross water
claims.statement: The elephant can make its way through water as long as the tip of its trunk is above the surface, because it breathes through its trunk.
claims.quote: he can make his way through water, as long as the tip of his trunk can be above the surface, for he blows with his trunk and breathes through it.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 46

claims.label: Hens that beat a cock become cock-like, even growing spurs
claims.statement: Hens that have beaten the cock in a fight crow like a cock, try to tread him, raise a crest and tail-feathers, and sometimes grow small spurs.
claims.quote: Hens, for instance, when they have beaten the cock in a fight, will crow like the cock and endeavour to tread him; the crest rises up on their head and the tail-feathers on the rump, so that it becomes difficult to recognize that they are hens; in some cases there is a growth of small spurs.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 49

claims.label: Castrated cocks lose their crest colour, crowing and sexual drive
claims.statement: A full-grown cock castrated by cauterizing the rump loses the colour of its crest, stops crowing and loses sexual desire; if castrated young, it never develops these male traits.
claims.quote: If you burn this twice or thrice with hot irons, then, if the bird be full-grown, his crest grows sallow, he ceases to crow, and foregoes sexual passion; but if you cauterize the bird when young, none of these male attributes propensities will come to him as he grows up.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Boys castrated before puberty keep a high voice; eunuchs never go bald
claims.statement: Men castrated in boyhood never grow the later hair and keep a high-pitched voice, and a eunuch never goes bald.
claims.quote: if you mutilate them in boyhood, the later-growing hair never comes, and the voice never changes but remains high-pitched
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Stags castrated before growing horns never grow them
claims.statement: Stags castrated before they have horns never grow horns, and stags castrated when they have horns keep them unchanged in size and do not shed them.
claims.quote: If stags be mutilated, when, by reason of their age, they have as yet no horns, they never grow horns at all; if they be mutilated when they have horns, the horns remain unchanged in size, and the animal does not lose them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Animals lacking upper teeth are the ones that ruminate
claims.statement: The animals that ruminate are those lacking upper (front) teeth, such as cattle, sheep and goats, though a few with teeth in both jaws also ruminate.
claims.quote: It is the animals that lack the upper teeth that ruminate, such as kine, sheep, and goats.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Many birds change plumage colour and song with the seasons
claims.statement: Many birds change the colour of their plumage and their song with the season; for example, the blackbird turns yellow instead of black and its song changes.
claims.quote: A considerable number of birds change according to season the colour of their plumage and their note; as, for instance, the owsel becomes yellow instead of black, and its note gets altered
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: The redbreast and the redstart are one bird in two seasonal forms
claims.statement: The robin (a winter bird) and the redstart (a summer bird) change into one another and differ only in plumage colour; likewise the beccafico and the blackcap.
claims.quote: The erithacus (or redbreast) and the so-called redstart change into one another; the former is a winter bird, the latter a summer one, and the difference between them is practically limited to the coloration of their plumage.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Ground birds dust-bathe; waterside birds water-bathe
claims.statement: Birds that do not fly but live on the ground take dust-baths, waterside birds and some straight-taloned birds take water-baths, and most crooked-taloned birds take neither.
claims.quote: Birds that do not fly but keep on the ground take the dust-bath, as for instance the hen, the partridge, the francolin, the crested lark, the pheasant; some of the straight-taloned birds, and such as live on the banks of a river, in marshes, or by the sea, take a water-bath
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: The final cause comes before the motor cause in explaining nature
claims.statement: Of the causes at work in the generation of natural things, the final cause (the end or purpose) is prior to the motor cause, in nature as in art.
claims.quote: Plainly, however, that cause is the first which we call the final one. For this is the Reason, and the Reason forms the starting-point, alike in the works of art and in works of nature.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: The vertebrae are not formed by accidental breaking of the foetal backbone
claims.statement: The division of the backbone into vertebrae is not, as Empedocles held, the result of the backbone being broken by the contorted position of the foetus in the womb, nor are animal characters in general mere incidents of development.
